bug_report.Title: Persistent SQLite test DBs with distinct TEST['NAME'] get deduplicated causing 'database is locked' in multi-db tests
bug_report.Description: When using persistent SQLite test database files (setting TEST['NAME'] per database alias) together with keepdb, the Django test runner can incorrectly treat multiple distinct test DBs as the same underlying database. This can result in two aliases opening/writing the same SQLite file concurrently and producing sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked during test setup (e.g. in setUpClass / setUpTestData).
bug_report.RootCause: 1) The sqlite3 backend's test DB signature omits the computed test database name: django/db/backends/sqlite3/creation.py::DatabaseCreation.test_db_signature() computes test_database_name = self._get_test_db_name(), but builds the signature from self.connection.settings_dict['NAME'] and an in-memory special-case and does NOT include the computed test database name. (See sqlite3/creation.py lines 97–101.) 2) The test runner groups aliases by connection.creation.test_db_signature(): django/test/utils.py::get_unique_databases_and_mirrors() uses connection.creation.test_db_signature() as the key for grouping aliases; setup_databases() then calls create_test_db() for the first alias in a group and calls set_as_test_mirror() for other aliases in that group. Because sqlite3.test_db_signature() omitted the actual test DB name, two aliases with different TEST['NAME'] values but the same production NAME (or empty NAME) can produce the same signature and be grouped together. (See django/test/utils.py lines 270–273 and 160–185.) 3) As a result, the test runner configures the later alias as a mirror of the first alias (set_as_test_mirror sets the alias's settings_dict['NAME'] to the primary's NAME), so multiple Connection objects open and use the same SQLite file. TestCase-level atomics execute an explicit BEGIN on each connection (sqlite backend executes "BEGIN" when entering atomic blocks), causing concurrent write transactions on the same file and leading to sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked. (See django/db/backends/sqlite3/base.py _start_transaction_under_autocommit and django/db/backends/base/creation.py behavior.) Correct relationship: the signature must reflect the actual test database that will be created/used — specifically, the signature needs to include the computed test database name (self._get_test_db_name()), because that is what create_test_db() writes into settings and what the test runner will create/open.
StepsToReproduce: 1. Configure two DATABASES aliases using ENGINE 'django.db.backends.sqlite3' and assign distinct persistent filenames via TEST['NAME'] for each alias (e.g. 'test_default.sqlite3' and 'test_other.sqlite3').
2. Run a test that creates objects across aliases during class-level setup (for example, tests/runtests.py admin_views.test_multidb -v 3 --keepdb --parallel 1, or any test suite using --keepdb).
3. Observe an OperationalError during setUpClass / setUpTestData: sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When multiple sqlite database aliases define distinct TEST['NAME'] values (different persistent test DB file names), the test runner should treat each alias as a separate test database and create/open each file independently so that tests do not fail with 'database is locked' due to two aliases being mapped to the same underlying file.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The test runner groups two aliases as the same underlying test database (signature collision because sqlite3.test_db_signature() omitted the computed test DB name), causing one alias to be treated as a mirror of the other. Both aliases then open and attempt writes to the same SQLite file concurrently, which can result in sqlite3.OperationalError: database is locked during test setup.

2) Improve DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path so that when given a path that includes nested class names (i.e., path = "test1.models.Thing.State"), we pick an importable module prefix. In practice:
   - Attempt to import the largest dotted prefix (starting from the full left-hand side before the last dot) and back off until we find an importable module. For path "test1.models.Thing.State", try __import__('test1.models.Thing') — fail — back off to __import__('test1.models') — success — use "import test1.models" as import and keep name as full "test1.models.Thing.State".
   - Keep existing special-case behavior for django.db.models: if the module candidate resolves to "django.db.models", do "from django.db import models" and rewrite name accordingly to "models.%s" % name (as currently implemented).
   - This change makes DeconstructableSerializer robust to deconstruct paths that use __qualname__ and contain outer classes.

Concretely, the code changes would be in django/db/migrations/serializer.py:

A) TypeSerializer.serialize: replace the "use __name__" block with something like:

    class TypeSerializer(BaseSerializer):
        def serialize(self):
            special_cases = [
                (models.Model, "models.Model", []),
                (type(None), 'type(None)', []),
            ]
            for case, string, imports in special_cases:
                if case is self.value:
                    return string, set(imports)
            if hasattr(self.value, "__module__"):
                module = self.value.__module__
                qualname = self.value.__qualname__
                if '<' in qualname:  # Qualname can include <locals>
                    raise ValueError(
                        'Could not find class %s in %s.\n' % (self.value.__name__, module)
                    )
                if module == builtins.__name__:
                    return qualname, set()
                else:
                    return "%s.%s" % (module, qualname), {"import %s" % module}

B) DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path: replace current simple split logic with logic that attempts to find an importable module prefix. Rough sketch:

    @staticmethod
    def _serialize_path(path):
        # path is like <module>.<qualname...> (qualname may contain dots for nested classes)
        # We want to import the real module (the importable prefix) and keep the full path for naming.
        # Split into left (all but last segment) and name (last segment)
        module_part, _ = path.rsplit(".", 1)

        # Find the longest importable module prefix from module_part (back off if needed)
        module_candidate = module_part
        while True:
            try:
                __import__(module_candidate)
                break
            except Exception:
                # Stop backing off if no more '.' to remove
                if '.' not in module_candidate:
                    # give up and use the original module_part
                    module_candidate = module_part
                    break
                module_candidate = module_candidate.rsplit('.', 1)[0]

        if module_candidate == "django.db.models":
            imports = {"from django.db import models"}
            name = "models.%s" % path.rsplit(".", 1)[1]
        else:
            imports = {"import %s" % module_candidate}
            name = path

        return name, imports

Checkpoint 5 — Final report (complete analysis and patch guidance)

Root cause summary
- Two related issues in django/db/migrations/serializer.py combined to produce incorrect paths for nested classes:
  1) TypeSerializer.serialize used value.__name__ (not value.__qualname__), discarding the outer-class qualification for nested classes; thus a nested enum class State defined inside Thing would be serialized as module + 'State' instead of module + 'Thing.State'.
  2) DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path assumed the left side of the final dot in path is an importable module and used "import <module>" unconditionally. Field.deconstruct already returns module + __qualname__ for fields; with nested classes this makes the left-hand "module" include the outer class name (e.g., 'test1.models.Thing'), which is not an importable module, causing invalid import lines in generated migrations.

Every location that needs to change (and why)
1) django/db/migrations/serializer.py — TypeSerializer.serialize
   - Current behavior (problem):
     - Uses self.value.__name__ to build "module.name" (line ~272 in file). This loses outer class qualifiers for nested classes and leads to wrong references like test1.models.State.
   - Assumption encoded: classes are always top-level and __name__ is sufficient to represent them for import and reference.
   - Fix: Use __qualname__ and check for '<' in qualname (local classes), similar to FunctionTypeSerializer. Implementation sketch (replace the relevant block):

        if hasattr(self.value, "__module__"):
            module = self.value.__module__
            qualname = self.value.__qualname__
            if '<' in qualname:  # guards against local classes
                raise ValueError(
                    'Could not find class %s in %s.\n' % (self.value.__name__, module)
                )
            if module == builtins.__name__:
                return qualname, set()
            else:
                return "%s.%s" % (module, qualname), {"import %s" % module}

   - Reason: __qualname__ preserves nesting; returning "module.qualname" is the correct fully qualified Python reference for nested classes, and returning import "import module" is valid because module is the true module containing the top-level enclosing class.

2) django/db/migrations/serializer.py — DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path
   - Current behavior (problem):
     - module, name = path.rsplit(".", 1)
     - imports = {"import %s" % module} (for non-django.db.models modules)
     - This assumes module is importable; if path contains nested classes, module will include class segments (e.g., test1.models.Thing) and "import test1.models.Thing" fails.
   - Assumption encoded: the string before the final dot is always a module.
   - Fix: When building imports for a deconstruct path, attempt to import the longest dotted prefix until an importable module is found. Use that importable prefix as the import target, but keep name as the original full path (so that references like test1.models.Thing.State remain valid when the code uses test1.models.Thing.State after doing "import test1.models").
   - Implementation sketch (replace existing _serialize_path code):

        @staticmethod
        def _serialize_path(path):
            # path expected as "<module>.<qualname...>" but qualname may contain dots
            # We need to pick an importable module prefix for import statement.
            module_part, last_name = path.rsplit(".", 1)
            module_candidate = module_part
            # Back off until we find an importable prefix
            while True:
                try:
                    __import__(module_candidate)
                    break
                except Exception:
                    if '.' not in module_candidate:
                        # Couldn't import any prefix: fall back to original module_part
                        module_candidate = module_part
                        break
                    module_candidate = module_candidate.rsplit('.', 1)[0]
            if module_candidate == "django.db.models":
                imports = {"from django.db import models"}
                name = "models.%s" % last_name
            else:
                imports = {"import %s" % module_candidate}
                name = path
            return name, imports

   - Reason: Importing the actual importable module (module_candidate) while still referring to the full qualified name path in generated code ensures Python can lookup the nested class as attribute of the imported module.

Any hardcoded values that need to become dynamic
- There are no large numbers or numeric constants; the hardcoded assumptions to change are:
  - Using __name__ for classes instead of __qualname__.
  - Using module = path.rsplit('.', 1)[0] as import target unconditionally.
- Both must be addressed by making the serializer rely on __qualname__ for class representation and by dynamically resolving the importable prefix.

New overrides / methods required
- No new methods are required to be added to classes; we are changing existing methods:
  - TypeSerializer.serialize — change code block to use __qualname__ and check '<' in qualname.
  - DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path — add importable-prefix resolution logic.

Concrete examples of the effect of the change
- Given:

    import enum
    from enumfields import Enum, EnumField
    class Thing(models.Model):
        @enum.unique
        class State(Enum):
            on = 'on'
            off = 'off'
        state = EnumField(enum=State)

  Current (buggy) output from makemigrations:
    ('state', enumfields.fields.EnumField(enum=test1.models.State, max_length=10)),

  After the fix:
    - TypeSerializer serializes the enum type as "test1.models.Thing.State" and returns imports {"import test1.models"}
    - DeconstructableSerializer and DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path will preserve that path and import the module "test1.models"
    Generated migration line becomes:
    ('state', enumfields.fields.EnumField(enum=test1.models.Thing.State, max_length=10)),

  which is correct and importable because "import test1.models" makes test1.models available and the attribute Thing is accessible on that module.

Edge cases and safety
- Local classes or classes created inside functions (qualname contains '<locals>') are not importable. FunctionTypeSerializer already disallows local functions; TypeSerializer must similarly raise (I included that check). This avoids generating broken migration files for objects that cannot be referenced as importable global names.
- Builtins: for builtins (module == builtins.__name__), using qualname is fine and will produce the same as __name__.
- django.db.models special-casing remains unchanged: existing special_cases list still handled first in TypeSerializer.
- DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path special-case for django.db.models is adapted to work with module candidates.

Files changed
- django/db/migrations/serializer.py:
  - Modify TypeSerializer.serialize (use __qualname__, check for '<' in qualname).
  - Modify DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path to find importable module prefix rather than blindly importing the module string before the last dot.

Why both changes are required (recap)
- The immediate bug in the bug report (EnumField referencing test1.models.State instead of test1.models.Thing.State) is caused by TypeSerializer using __name__ instead of __qualname__. Fixing only TypeSerializer will fix types serialized via serializer_factory when the value is a type.
- However, for deconstructable objects (fields) where Field.deconstruct returns module + __qualname__, DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path is also fragile and must be made robust to avoid trying to import "module.outerclass" as if it were a module. So both changes are necessary to fully fix all affected code paths.

Suggested patch (illustrative)

- Replace TypeSerializer.serialize with:

    class TypeSerializer(BaseSerializer):
        def serialize(self):
            special_cases = [
                (models.Model, "models.Model", []),
                (type(None), 'type(None)', []),
            ]
            for case, string, imports in special_cases:
                if case is self.value:
                    return string, set(imports)
            if hasattr(self.value, "__module__"):
                module = self.value.__module__
                qualname = self.value.__qualname__
                if '<' in qualname:  # Qualname can include <locals>, which are unimportable
                    raise ValueError("Could not find class %s in %s.\n" % (self.value.__name__, module))
                if module == builtins.__name__:
                    return qualname, set()
                return "%s.%s" % (module, qualname), {"import %s" % module}

- Replace DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path with the importable-prefix-finding logic sketch above.

Testing suggestions
- Add regression tests to tests for migrations serializer:
  - A test that defines an inner class (e.g., Outer.Inner) and verifies that serializing the type produces module + qualname and that the import returned is the module (not module + outerclass).
  - A test that constructs a Field subclass as an inner class and ensures Field.deconstruct + DeconstructableSerializer produces an import statement that is importable (i.e., "import test1.models") and a name "test1.models.Thing.State" in generated code.
  - A negative test to ensure classes defined in function scope (qualname containing '<locals>') raise an error when serializer tries to serialize them.

Summary
- Root cause: TypeSerializer used type.__name__ and DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path assumed the left-hand part of the path was an importable module. Together they cause nested class references to be rendered incorrectly (missing the outer qualifier or emitting invalid import statements).
- Fix: change TypeSerializer to use __qualname__ and add local-class protection; make DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path attempt to find an importable module prefix rather than using the naive rsplit() result as a module name.
- Files to change: django/db/migrations/serializer.py (two small, focused changes).
- No other files need to be changed for this bug (Field.deconstruct is already correct: it uses __qualname__), but serializer must be corrected to consume the path correctly and to produce correct imports.

bug_report.Title: makemigrations serializes nested (inner) classes with incorrect module path
bug_report.Description: When a Field (or other deconstructable value) references a nested (inner) class, makemigrations generates migration code that refers to the inner class as if it were a top-level class in the module (outer qualifier is lost) or emits an invalid import. Examples: test1.models.State instead of test1.models.Thing.State; or an import like "import test1.models.Thing" which is not a valid module import.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) TypeSerializer uses __name__ instead of __qualname__ (django/db/migrations/serializer.py: TypeSerializer.serialize)
   - Current behavior: TypeSerializer builds the string "%s.%s" % (value.__module__, value.__name__) (serializer.py lines 268–272). That drops any outer-class qualification for nested classes; e.g. an inner class Thing.State becomes 'test1.models.State'.
   - Incorrect assumption encoded: a class can be referenced unambiguously as module + class.__name__ and that preserves nesting.
   - Correct relationship (diagnostic): nested classes must be represented with the class's __qualname__ combined with its module (module + __qualname__) so that nested names include the outer-class qualifier (e.g. 'test1.models.Thing.State').

2) DeconstructableSerializer treats the left side of the final dot as an importable module (django/db/migrations/serializer.py: DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path)
   - Current behavior: _serialize_path does module, name = path.rsplit('.', 1) and emits "import <module>" for non-django.db.models modules (serializer.py lines 92–100). If path contains a qualname with dots (module + outerClass.innerClass), the left-hand portion may include the outer-class name (e.g. 'test1.models.Thing'), and emitting "import test1.models.Thing" is invalid because Thing is a class, not a module.
   - Incorrect assumption encoded: path.rsplit('.', 1)[0] is always an importable module name.
   - Correct relationship (diagnostic): when a deconstruct path contains nested class qualifiers, the import target must be an actual importable module prefix (for example 'test1.models'), while the code reference may remain the full module + qualname (e.g. 'test1.models.Thing.State').

3) serializer_factory dispatches types to TypeSerializer (django/db/migrations/serializer.py: serializer_factory)
   - Behavior: serializer_factory checks isinstance(value, type) and returns TypeSerializer(value) before checking for deconstructable objects (serializer.py lines 328–332). This explains why enum classes (which are types) are serialized by TypeSerializer and therefore serialized using __name__ in the current code path, producing the observed 'test1.models.State' string.

4) Field.deconstruct already uses __qualname__ (django/db/models/fields/__init__.py: Field.deconstruct)
   - Evidence: Field.deconstruct constructs the path using "%s.%s" % (self.__class__.__module__, self.__class__.__qualname__) (fields/__init__.py lines 491 and __repr__ at line 191). That means DeconstructableSerializer._serialize_path will receive paths that include qualname dots for nested classes (module + outer.inner), so _serialize_path's naive import logic is problematic for such paths.

All four findings are distinct code-site observations that together explain the reported symptoms: TypeSerializer's use of __name__ causes loss of outer-class qualifiers when serializing types directly; DeconstructableSerializer's naive import construction can emit invalid imports when fed paths containing qualname dots; serializer_factory dispatch order routes type values to TypeSerializer; and Field.deconstruct already emits module + __qualname__.
StepsToReproduce: Run: python manage.py makemigrations
Open the generated migration file and inspect the field's representation; note the class path printed for the inner class (it will show test1.models.Inner instead of test1.models.Outer.Inner).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Generated migration code should reference nested classes with their full qualified name including the outer class (e.g. test1.models.Thing.State or test1.models.Outer.Inner). Any import statement written into the migration file must import an actual module (e.g. 'import test1.models' or 'from test1.models import Thing'), so that the referenced nested class can be resolved when the migration runs.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior:
makemigrations produces migration code that omits the outer-class qualifier for nested classes (e.g. enum=test1.models.State instead of enum=test1.models.Thing.State) or emits an import statement that attempts to import a non-module dotted name (e.g. 'import test1.models.Thing'), causing invalid imports in the generated migration. Example produced migration snippet:
  ('state', enumfields.fields.EnumField(enum=test1.models.State, max_length=10)),
but the correct reference should be test1.models.Thing.State.

import logging
import types

from django.conf import settings
from django.core.exceptions import ImproperlyConfigured, MiddlewareNotUsed
from django.core.signals import request_finished
from django.db import connections, transaction
from django.urls import get_resolver, set_urlconf
from django.utils.log import log_response
from django.utils.module_loading import import_string

from .exception import convert_exception_to_response

logger = logging.getLogger('django.request')


class BaseHandler:
    _view_middleware = None
    _template_response_middleware = None
    _exception_middleware = None
    _middleware_chain = None

    def load_middleware(self):
        """
        Populate middleware lists from settings.MIDDLEWARE.

        Must be called after the environment is fixed (see __call__ in subclasses).
        """
        self._view_middleware = []
        self._template_response_middleware = []
        self._exception_middleware = []

        handler = convert_exception_to_response(self._get_response)
        for middleware_path in reversed(settings.MIDDLEWARE):
            middleware = import_string(middleware_path)
            try:
                mw_instance = middleware(handler)
            except MiddlewareNotUsed as exc:
                if settings.DEBUG:
                    if str(exc):
                        logger.debug('MiddlewareNotUsed(%r): %s', middleware_path, exc)
                    else:
                        logger.debug('MiddlewareNotUsed: %r', middleware_path)
                continue

            if mw_instance is None:
                raise ImproperlyConfigured(
                    'Middleware factory %s returned None.' % middleware_path
                )

            if hasattr(mw_instance, 'process_view'):
                self._view_middleware.insert(0, mw_instance.process_view)
            if hasattr(mw_instance, 'process_template_response'):
                self._template_response_middleware.append(mw_instance.process_template_response)
            if hasattr(mw_instance, 'process_exception'):
                self._exception_middleware.append(mw_instance.process_exception)

            handler = convert_exception_to_response(mw_instance)

        # We only assign to this when initialization is complete as it is used
        # as a flag for initialization being complete.
        self._middleware_chain = handler

    def make_view_atomic(self, view):
        non_atomic_requests = getattr(view, '_non_atomic_requests', set())
        for db in connections.all():
            if db.settings_dict['ATOMIC_REQUESTS'] and db.alias not in non_atomic_requests:
                view = transaction.atomic(using=db.alias)(view)
        return view

    def get_response(self, request):
        """Return an HttpResponse object for the given HttpRequest."""
        # Setup default url resolver for this thread
        set_urlconf(settings.ROOT_URLCONF)
        response = self._middleware_chain(request)
        response._closable_objects.append(request)
        if response.status_code >= 400:
            log_response(
                '%s: %s', response.reason_phrase, request.path,
                response=response,
                request=request,
            )
        return response

    def _get_response(self, request):
        """
        Resolve and call the view, then apply view, exception, and
        template_response middleware. This method is everything that happens
        inside the request/response middleware.
        """
        response = None

        if hasattr(request, 'urlconf'):
            urlconf = request.urlconf
            set_urlconf(urlconf)
            resolver = get_resolver(urlconf)
        else:
            resolver = get_resolver()

        resolver_match = resolver.resolve(request.path_info)
        callback, callback_args, callback_kwargs = resolver_match
        request.resolver_match = resolver_match

        # Apply view middleware
        for middleware_method in self._view_middleware:
            response = middleware_method(request, callback, callback_args, callback_kwargs)
            if response:
                break

        if response is None:
            wrapped_callback = self.make_view_atomic(callback)
            try:
                response = wrapped_callback(request, *callback_args, **callback_kwargs)
            except Exception as e:
                response = self.process_exception_by_middleware(e, request)

        # Complain if the view returned None (a common error).
        if response is None:
            if isinstance(callback, types.FunctionType):    # FBV
                view_name = callback.__name__
            else:                                           # CBV
                view_name = callback.__class__.__name__ + '.__call__'

            raise ValueError(
                "The view %s.%s didn't return an HttpResponse object. It "
                "returned None instead." % (callback.__module__, view_name)
            )

        # If the response supports deferred rendering, apply template
        # response middleware and then render the response
        elif hasattr(response, 'render') and callable(response.render):
            for middleware_method in self._template_response_middleware:
                response = middleware_method(request, response)
                # Complain if the template response middleware returned None (a common error).
                if response is None:
                    raise ValueError(
                        "%s.process_template_response didn't return an "
                        "HttpResponse object. It returned None instead."
                        % (middleware_method.__self__.__class__.__name__)
                    )

            try:
                response = response.render()
            except Exception as e:
                response = self.process_exception_by_middleware(e, request)

        return response

    def process_exception_by_middleware(self, exception, request):
        """
        Pass the exception to the exception middleware. If no middleware
        return a response for this exception, raise it.
        """
        for middleware_method in self._exception_middleware:
            response = middleware_method(request, exception)
            if response:
                return response
        raise


def reset_urlconf(sender, **kwargs):
    """Reset the URLconf after each request is finished."""
    set_urlconf(None)


request_finished.connect(reset_urlconf)

1.d) Clear statement of the bug and primary responsible code

Bug summary:
- With URL patterns that include optional named groups that contain additional capturing sub-groups, when the named group doesn't match (the optional is absent), RegexPattern.match current logic treats "no matched named groups" as "no named groups in the pattern", so it picks up match.groups() (which includes the contents of inner capturing groups) and returns them as positional args.
- These positional args get passed to the view as positional parameters (after request), causing TypeError: e.g., view(request, format='html') expecting keyword arg ends up receiving an unexpected positional arg.

Primary responsible code:
- django/urls/resolvers.RegexPattern.match — it decides whether to treat captured values as kwargs vs positional args based on the presence of any matched named groups (non-empty kwargs), rather than the presence of any named groups in the pattern.

Why this is wrong:
- The decision should be based on whether the pattern defines named groups (i.e., whether the regex contains (?P<name>...)), not whether the named groups matched non-empty values. If there are named groups in the pattern, the code must ignore non-named groups (positional args), even if the named groups matched as None.

Example pattern that triggers the bug:
- r'^module/(?P<format>(html|json|xml))?/?$' — there is a named group 'format' that is optional and the inner group (html|json|xml) is a capturing group. When the optional named group isn't present in the URL, match.groupdict() gives {'format': None} and kwargs becomes {} after filtering; but match.groups() still contains the inner group's capture (or None) and gets returned as positional args — wrong.

Proposed fix (concise):
- Change RegexPattern.match to decide whether to return positional args or ignore them based on whether the regex pattern defines any named groups, not whether any named groups matched.

Concretely, replace:

    kwargs = {k: v for k, v in match.groupdict().items() if v is not None}
    args = () if kwargs else match.groups()
    return path[match.end():], args, kwargs

with:

    groupdict = match.groupdict()
    kwargs = {k: v for k, v in groupdict.items() if v is not None}
    # If the pattern defines any named groups (groupdict is non-empty),
    # ignore all non-named groups and return positional args == ().
    args = () if groupdict else match.groups()
    return path[match.end():], args, kwargs

That is, use the existence of named-group keys in match.groupdict() (groupdict truthiness) to decide whether the pattern had named groups. This prevents accidental promotion of inner non-named capturing groups to positional args when they are nested within named groups that are optional / unmatched.

bug_report.Title: Optional named regex group causes inner capture to be passed as positional arg, raising TypeError
bug_report.Description: When a URL pattern uses an optional named regex group that contains an inner (unnamed) capturing group, a request that does not match the named group can result in the inner capture being returned as a positional argument and passed to the view. This produces a TypeError (extra positional argument) with the repository code inspected here. (The original reporter indicated this pattern used to work in an earlier Django 2.2 setup.)
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect decision criterion in RegexPattern.match (django/urls/resolvers.py:RegexPattern.match). The method builds kwargs by filtering match.groupdict() for non-None values and then decides whether to return positional args based on whether kwargs is non-empty:
   kwargs = {k: v for k, v in match.groupdict().items() if v is not None}
   args = () if kwargs else match.groups()
   This treats the absence of matched named-group values (all values None) the same as the absence of named groups in the pattern. The correct relationship to test is whether the pattern defines named groups (i.e. whether match.groupdict() has any keys), not whether any named-group produced a non-None value.

2) Downstream merging decision in URLResolver.resolve (django/urls/resolvers.py:URLResolver.resolve) depends on match() returning empty positional args when the pattern defines named groups. URLResolver.resolve merges parent kwargs and submatch.kwargs and then uses the emptiness of that merged dict to decide whether to prepend parent args:
   sub_match_dict = {**kwargs, **self.default_kwargs}
   sub_match_dict.update(sub_match.kwargs)
   sub_match_args = sub_match.args
   if not sub_match_dict:
       sub_match_args = args + sub_match.args
   Because RegexPattern.match can return positional args when named groups exist but didn't match any value, the merge logic can treat the case as having no named groups and concatenate parent args with sub_match.args, producing unexpected positional args.

3) Call-site expectation in BaseHandler._get_response (django/core/handlers/base.py:BaseHandler._get_response). The resolver result is unpacked as (callback, callback_args, callback_kwargs) and the view is invoked as wrapped_callback(request, *callback_args, **callback_kwargs). Any unexpected positional argument emitted from the resolver is passed directly to the view, causing a TypeError (e.g. "modules() takes from 1 to 2 positional arguments but 3 were given").
StepsToReproduce: Add this URL pattern: re_path(r'^module/(?P<format>(html|json|xml))?/?$', views.modules, name='modules')
Add this view: def modules(request, format='html'): ... (return a simple response)
Start the Django app and request the path /module/ (i.e. omit the optional named group)
Observe the server error / traceback with TypeError about extra positional arguments
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Requesting /module/ should call the view without unexpected positional arguments. The optional named parameter 'format' should not appear in callback_args; if omitted it should be absent from callback_kwargs so the view's default (format='html') is used, or provided as a keyword argument when present. No TypeError should occur.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Requesting /module/ raises TypeError: "modules() takes from 1 to 2 positional arguments but 3 were given". The resolver/unpacking path supplies an unexpected extra positional argument (the inner capturing group's match) to the view.

class BasicFieldTests(SimpleTestCase):

    def test_show_hidden_initial(self):
        """
        Fields with choices respect show_hidden_initial as a kwarg to
        formfield().
        """
        choices = [(0, 0), (1, 1)]
        model_field = models.Field(choices=choices)
        form_field = model_field.formfield(show_hidden_initial=True)
        self.assertTrue(form_field.show_hidden_initial)

        form_field = model_field.formfield(show_hidden_initial=False)
        self.assertFalse(form_field.show_hidden_initial)

    def test_field_repr(self):
        """
        __repr__() of a field displays its name.
        """
        f = Foo._meta.get_field('a')
        self.assertEqual(repr(f), '<django.db.models.fields.CharField: a>')
        f = models.fields.CharField()
        self.assertEqual(repr(f), '<django.db.models.fields.CharField>')

    def test_field_repr_nested(self):
        """__repr__() uses __qualname__ for nested class support."""
        self.assertEqual(repr(Nested.Field()), '<model_fields.tests.Nested.Field>')

    def test_field_name(self):
        """
        A defined field name (name="fieldname") is used instead of the model
        model's attribute name (modelname).
        """
        instance = RenamedField()
        self.assertTrue(hasattr(instance, 'get_fieldname_display'))
        self.assertFalse(hasattr(instance, 'get_modelname_display'))

    def test_field_verbose_name(self):
        m = VerboseNameField
        for i in range(1, 23):
            self.assertEqual(m._meta.get_field('field%d' % i).verbose_name, 'verbose field%d' % i)

        self.assertEqual(m._meta.get_field('id').verbose_name, 'verbose pk')

    def test_choices_form_class(self):
        """Can supply a custom choices form class to Field.formfield()"""
        choices = [('a', 'a')]
        field = models.CharField(choices=choices)
        klass = forms.TypedMultipleChoiceField
        self.assertIsInstance(field.formfield(choices_form_class=klass), klass)

    def test_formfield_disabled(self):
        """Field.formfield() sets disabled for fields with choices."""
        field = models.CharField(choices=[('a', 'b')])
        form_field = field.formfield(disabled=True)
        self.assertIs(form_field.disabled, True)

    def test_field_str(self):
        f = models.Field()
        self.assertEqual(str(f), '<django.db.models.fields.Field>')
        f = Foo._meta.get_field('a')
        self.assertEqual(str(f), 'model_fields.Foo.a')

    def test_field_ordering(self):
        """Fields are ordered based on their creation."""
        f1 = models.Field()
        f2 = models.Field(auto_created=True)
        f3 = models.Field()
        self.assertLess(f2, f1)
        self.assertGreater(f3, f1)
        self.assertIsNotNone(f1)
        self.assertNotIn(f2, (None, 1, ''))

        """Field instances can be pickled."""
        field = models.Field(max_length=100, default='a string')
        # Must be picklable with this cached property populated (#28188).
        field._get_default
        pickle.dumps(field)

        """deconstruct() uses __qualname__ for nested class support."""
        name, path, args, kwargs = Nested.Field().deconstruct()
        self.assertEqual(path, 'model_fields.tests.Nested.Field')

class GetChoicesOrderingTests(TestCase):

    @classmethod

        cls.bar1 = Bar.objects.create(a=cls.foo1, b='b')

            [self.foo1, self.foo2]

            [self.foo2, self.foo1]

            self.field.get_choices(include_blank=False),
            [self.foo2, self.foo1]

Root cause (concise):

Field.contribute_to_class on the subclass then wrongly refrained from re-binding get_<field>_display to the subclass's Field instance (which may have different choices), causing subclass instances to resolve display labels using the parent's choices (missing subclass-only options) and thus returning raw values for the new choices.

bug_report.Title: get_<field>_display returns raw value for subclass-added choices when choices/field are inherited from abstract base
bug_report.Description: When a model inherits an abstract base that defines a field with choices, choice values that are added in the subclass can be unresolved by the generated get_<field>_display accessor. The accessor may return the raw DB value (e.g. "C") instead of the expected human-readable label (e.g. "output3"). The incorrect behavior is visible during class construction and occurs for values that exist only in the subclass's choices.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Existence check used when installing per-field accessors treats inherited generated accessors as if they were user-defined. In Field.contribute_to_class (django/db/models/fields/__init__.py), the code installs the accessor with partialmethod(cls._get_FIELD_display, field=self) but only if hasattr(cls, 'get_%s_display' % self.name) is False. Because hasattr(...) returns True for attributes inherited from a parent class, a subclass that inherits a generated get_<field>_display accessor will cause the subclass's Field.contribute_to_class to skip installing a new accessor bound to the subclass's Field instance. (See fields/__init__.py lines ~766–772.)

2) The generated accessor is a method bound to a specific Field instance; label resolution uses that Field instance's choices. The accessor is created as a partialmethod that supplies the Field instance to Model._get_FIELD_display. Model._get_FIELD_display resolves the label using the bound field's flatchoices (django/db/models/base.py): it builds choices_dict = dict(make_hashable(field.flatchoices)) and returns choices_dict.get(make_hashable(value), value). If the bound Field instance does not include subclass-only options in its flatchoices, lookups for those values fall back to the raw DB value. (See base.py lines ~946–950.)

3) Interaction with abstract-base field copying during class creation. ModelBase (django/db/models/base.py) deep-copies fields from abstract bases and calls add_to_class on the copied Field instance when creating the subclass (copy.deepcopy(field); new_class.add_to_class(...)). This produces a distinct Field instance for the subclass (which may contain updated choices), but the subclass may continue to use the inherited accessor that was previously bound to the parent Field instance. The result is that the subclass's Field instance and the class's get_<field>_display accessor are not necessarily bound to the same Field, causing subclass-only choices to be unresolved. (See base.py lines ~272–279 and the Field.contribute_to_class location above.)
StepsToReproduce: Define an abstract base model with a class-level choices sequence and a field that uses it. Example: foo_choice = [('A','output1'), ('B','output2')]; field_foo = models.CharField(max_length=254, choices=foo_choice); class Meta: abstract = True.

Define a concrete subclass that overrides the foo_choice sequence to add a tuple for value 'C' (and do not define a custom get_field_foo_display on the subclass). Do not necessarily redeclare the field on the subclass (test both inheriting the field and redeclaring it).
Create an instance of the subclass with field_foo='C'.
Call instance.get_field_foo_display() and observe the returned value.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Calling get_<field>_display() on an instance of the subclass returns the human-readable label declared for that value in the subclass's choices (e.g. 'output3' for value 'C').
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Calling get_<field>_display() on an instance of the subclass returns the raw DB value for subclass-only choices (e.g. 'C') instead of the expected label (e.g. 'output3').

bug_report.Title: translation.E004 raised for sublanguage LANGUAGE_CODE (e.g. 'de-at') despite base language present in LANGUAGES
bug_report.Description: The system check translation.E004 is raised when settings.LANGUAGE_CODE is a specific sublanguage tag (for example, "de-at") even though the generic/base language ("de") is present in settings.LANGUAGES. This contradicts Django's documented behavior that a base language is used when a requested sublanguage variant is not available.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Exact-match requirement in the system check (django/core/checks/translation.py:58-60): check_language_settings_consistent builds available_tags = {i for i, _ in settings.LANGUAGES} | {'en-us'} and then raises E004 when settings.LANGUAGE_CODE is not a member of that set (the membership test is: if settings.LANGUAGE_CODE not in available_tags: return [E004]). This encodes the assumption that LANGUAGE_CODE must be exactly listed in settings.LANGUAGES (with a single hardcoded extra 'en-us').

2) The check omits fallbacks and generic/base-tag consideration (django/core/checks/translation.py): the function contains no logic to consult django.conf.locale.LANG_INFO nor to accept the generic base tag (the part before '-') as a valid match for a sublanguage. Therefore a sublanguage value like 'de-at' will be rejected even though 'de' is present in LANGUAGES.

3) Runtime language-resolution behavior differs and already implements fallbacks and generic-base mapping (django/utils/translation/trans_real.py:409-421, 414-416, 419-420): get_supported_language_variant constructs possible_lang_codes = [lang_code] plus any LANG_INFO[lang_code]['fallback'] entries and the generic_lang_code = lang_code.split('-')[0]; it then accepts a code only if it is in supported languages and check_for_language(code) returns True. Our JSON output (json.dumps) is plain string (no HTML) — consistent with general assumptions; no additional escaping needed here.

Conclusion: complementary operations are either unaffected or intentionally different: display_for_value remains unchanged for non-field values. No reverse operation change required.

4d) "Does every existing method still work?"
- Methods we read/modified: display_for_field (we add a JSONField branch). We must ensure:
  - BooleanField special-case remains before None-handling (we didn't change that).
  - For JSONField value None, earlier value is None check still returns empty_value_display (since that's checked before JSONField branch); that's desirable.
  - For FileField etc., no change.
  - display_for_value continues to work unchanged.
- Potential failure modes:
  - If the JSON value is not JSON serializable, json.dumps will raise TypeError; we catch TypeError and fallback to str(value). That preserves robustness.
  - If field.encoder is not a valid cls argument for json.dumps (for instance, JSONField.encoder could be a function rather than a JSONEncoder subclass). However, JSONField itself validated encoder to be callable in __init__ (and JSONField.get_prep_value uses json.dumps(value, cls=self.encoder)), so passing getattr(field, 'encoder', None) matches how JSONField itself uses it. Using cls=None is acceptable. If some encoder provided is not appropriate as cls (unlikely given JSONField itself uses it), the try/except will catch TypeError and fallback to str(value).
- Therefore, every existing consumer of display_for_field (admin list rendering in admin/templatetags/admin_list.py and helpers.py) continues to operate. HTML generation for boolean icons unchanged. The new branch returns strings and uses only safe operations.

4e) "Does any NEW method need to be added?"
- We examined the parent's method list earlier. There are no inherited methods that need to be overridden — display_for_field is a module-level utility function rather than a class method inherited from a parent class. Thus no class-level overrides are required.
- However, consider display_for_value (the complement). Should we change display_for_value to recognize dicts and render JSON there as well? That would change behavior for non-field values (e.g., callables returning dicts). The minimal, targeted fix (only JSONField special-case) is less invasive and matches how other field types are handled (DateField/DateTimeField/DecimalField/FloatField have explicit branches in display_for_field). Therefore no new method is strictly necessary.
- If the project's maintainers want consistent behavior for all dicts appearing as values (not just JSONField), we could alternatively (or additionally) make display_for_value render dicts via json.dumps — but that's beyond the minimal correct fix because display_for_value is used for many non-field cases and that could be a behavioral change. At minimum, no new methods needed to be added to make JSONField display correct.

Checkpoint 5 — final report (complete analysis, root cause, locations changed, expectations)

Root cause
- display_for_field did not special-case JSONField values, so JSONField values (dicts/lists) flowed through to display_for_value where they were represented using Python str()/repr (which uses single quotes and Python formatting) rather than JSON serialization. This produced incorrect-looking output in the admin list (Python dict repr instead of JSON), and ignored any encoder configured on JSONField.

All locations that need to change (and why)
1) django/contrib/admin/utils.py
   - Current code: display_for_field falls back to display_for_value for JSONField instances (since no explicit JSONField branch).
   - Assumption encoded: field values can be reasonably represented using str() (via display_for_value fallback).
   - Fix: Add a new branch in display_for_field to detect instances of models.JSONField and return json.dumps(value, cls=getattr(field, 'encoder', None)), catching TypeError to fallback to str(value).
   - Why here: display_for_field is the central place where admin displays model field values, and other field types (DateField, DecimalField, FileField, etc.) already get special-case handling here.

2) tests/admin_utils/tests.py
   - Current code: no test for JSONField representation in admin utils.
   - Fix: Add tests verifying that display_for_field(value, models.JSONField(), ...) returns json.dumps(value) for dict and list values, and that None still maps to empty_value_display.
   - Why: Ensure regression tests cover the new behavior and prevent accidental reversion.

Other files considered (but not changed)
- django/contrib/admin/templatetags/admin_list.py:
  - Uses display_for_field — no changes required; this change will automatically affect admin list rendering.
- django/db/models/fields/json.py (JSONField):
  - No change necessary to JSONField itself because it already stores encoder and get_prep_value uses json.dumps(..., cls=self.encoder). We use the same encoder retrieval to display values.
- django/contrib/postgres/fields/jsonb.py:
  - No code changes required; its JSONField subclasses builtin JSONField, so isinstance(field, models.JSONField) will match.

Hardcoded values that need to become dynamic
- None. The only "hardcoded" representation behavior was the generic fallback to str() (a code path rather than a numeric constant). We add a dynamic behavior for JSONField values (render via json.dumps) and preserve fallback to str() for non-serializable cases.

Methods to add or override
- No new methods required. The change is a targeted special-case in display_for_field. We verified display_for_value (the complementary function) remains consistent for non-field values. If maintainers later want to render any dict value using json.dumps regardless of whether it came from a JSONField, then display_for_value should be updated — but that is a separate (broader) design decision.

Patch sketch (diff-like)
- In django/contrib/admin/utils.py:

  Add import:
    import json

  In display_for_field(...):
    elif isinstance(field, models.FileField) and value:
        return format_html('<a href="{}">{}</a>', value.url, value)
    elif isinstance(field, models.JSONField):
        try:
            return json.dumps(value, cls=getattr(field, 'encoder', None))
        except TypeError:
            return str(value)
    else:
        return display_for_value(value, empty_value_display)

Tests to add (in tests/admin_utils/tests.py)
- import json at top.

- Add:

        val = {'a': 1, 'b': ['x', 'y']}
        display_value = display_for_field(val, models.JSONField(), self.empty_value)
        self.assertEqual(display_value, json.dumps(val))

        val2 = ['one', 'two']
        display_value2 = display_for_field(val2, models.JSONField(), self.empty_value)
        self.assertEqual(display_value2, json.dumps(val2))

        display_none = display_for_field(None, models.JSONField(), self.empty_value)

Rationale for the approach
- Minimal, local change: only modifies display_for_field to treat JSONField similarly to how DateField, DecimalField, FileField, etc. are handled.
- Uses the JSONField's own encoder (field.encoder) to ensure consistent representation with how the field serializes data for the DB.
- Robust fallback to str() for non-serializable values ensures we do not introduce new runtime errors in admin display.

Potential follow-up improvements (optional)
- Consider whether display_for_value (the generic function) should render dicts using json.dumps — but this is a broader change: it will affect non-field values (callables/properties) and might be a breaking change for projects that relied on Python repr.
- Consider pretty-printing or truncating long JSON in the admin list view, or using a HTML-safe representation (e.g., wrap in <pre> or show a link to a JSON viewer). Those are UX choices beyond this bug fix and should be reviewed separately.

bug_report.Title: Admin displays JSONField values as Python repr (single quotes) when readonly
bug_report.Description: JSONField values shown in the admin readonly display are rendered using Python's dict/list representation (e.g. {'foo': 'bar'}) instead of JSON (e.g. {"foo": "bar"}). This manifests in the admin change view and the change list when a JSONField is shown as readonly.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django.contrib.admin.utils.display_for_field does not special-case models.JSONField. For JSONField values (Python dict/list), display_for_field falls through to display_for_value which ultimately returns str(value) for dicts/objects, producing the Python representation with single quotes rather than JSON. Location: django/contrib/admin/utils.py::display_for_field and django/contrib/admin/utils.py::display_for_value.

2) Multiple admin rendering entry points call display_for_field, so the same root cause affects several UI locations equally: (a) the change-view readonly rendering path (django/contrib/admin/helpers.py::AdminReadonlyField.contents calls display_for_field), and (b) the change-list rendering in the admin list template tag (django/contrib/admin/templatetags/admin_list.py calls display_for_field). Location: django/contrib/admin/helpers.py::AdminReadonlyField.contents and django/contrib/admin/templatetags/admin_list.py (list rendering).

3) The JSONField model implementation stores an encoder attribute and uses json.dumps(value, cls=self.encoder) when preparing values for the database (get_prep_value). The admin display code does not use this encoder when rendering readonly JSONField values, so any field-level encoder configuration is ignored. Location: django/db/models/fields/json.py::JSONField (self.encoder and get_prep_value).

4) The forms layer also has a JSONField (django/forms/fields.JSONField) whose prepare_value returns json.dumps(value, cls=self.encoder) but preserves InvalidJSONInput instances unchanged (prepare_value returns the InvalidJSONInput instance instead of running json.dumps on it). The admin display code currently does not call the form field's prepare_value in the general readonly rendering path; as a result, bound-but-invalid form input (InvalidJSONInput) would not be preserved by a generic display that simply json.dumps the value. Location: django/forms/fields.py::JSONField.prepare_value (and InvalidJSONInput handling).

5) Correct relationship missing (diagnostic): readonly display of a models.JSONField should render the field's value using JSON serialization that honors the field's encoder (i.e. json.dumps(value, cls=field.encoder) for model-derived values) and, in contexts where the displayed value comes from a bound form containing InvalidJSONInput, should take into account the form field's prepare_value behavior (which preserves InvalidJSONInput). Currently the display code uses str(value), which yields a Python representation, not JSON.
StepsToReproduce: Create a model with a models.JSONField and register it in the admin with that field in readonly_fields.
Create or edit an instance so the JSONField contains a dict, e.g. {"foo": "bar"}.
Open the admin change view (object detail) showing the readonly field, or view the change list that includes the readonly JSONField.
Observe that the JSON value is displayed like {'foo': 'bar'} (single quotes / Python repr) rather than valid JSON ("foo": "bar").
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When a JSONField is displayed readonly in the admin (change view or change list), its value should be rendered as valid JSON text (e.g. {"foo": "bar"}). The rendering should honor the JSONField's encoder configuration (i.e. serialize via json.dumps(value, cls=field.encoder) for model values) and, when displaying a value coming from a bound form that is InvalidJSONInput, the display should preserve that InvalidJSONInput as the form's prepare_value does.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Readonly JSONField values are displayed using Python's representation (e.g. {'foo': 'bar'}) with single quotes and Python formatting rather than valid JSON (double-quoted keys/strings). This occurs in the admin change view (AdminReadonlyField.contents -> display_for_field) and in the change list (admin_list -> display_for_field).

import os
import sys
from io import StringIO

from django.apps import apps
from django.conf import settings
from django.core import serializers
from django.db import router

# The prefix to put on the default database name when creating
# the test database.
TEST_DATABASE_PREFIX = 'test_'


class BaseDatabaseCreation:
    """
    Encapsulate backend-specific differences pertaining to creation and
    destruction of the test database.
    """
    def __init__(self, connection):
        self.connection = connection

    def _nodb_cursor(self):
        return self.connection._nodb_cursor()

    def log(self, msg):
        sys.stderr.write(msg + os.linesep)

    def create_test_db(self, verbosity=1, autoclobber=False, serialize=True, keepdb=False):
        """
        Create a test database, prompting the user for confirmation if the
        database already exists. Return the name of the test database created.
        """
        # Don't import django.core.management if it isn't needed.
        from django.core.management import call_command

        test_database_name = self._get_test_db_name()

        if verbosity >= 1:
            action = 'Creating'
            if keepdb:
                action = "Using existing"

            self.log('%s test database for alias %s...' % (
                action,
                self._get_database_display_str(verbosity, test_database_name),
            ))

        # We could skip this call if keepdb is True, but we instead
        # give it the keepdb param. This is to handle the case
        # where the test DB doesn't exist, in which case we need to
        # create it, then just not destroy it. If we instead skip
        # this, we will get an exception.
        self._create_test_db(verbosity, autoclobber, keepdb)

        self.connection.close()
        settings.DATABASES[self.connection.alias]["NAME"] = test_database_name
        self.connection.settings_dict["NAME"] = test_database_name

        if self.connection.settings_dict['TEST']['MIGRATE']:
            # We report migrate messages at one level lower than that
            # requested. This ensures we don't get flooded with messages during
            # testing (unless you really ask to be flooded).
            call_command(
                'migrate',
                verbosity=max(verbosity - 1, 0),
                interactive=False,
                database=self.connection.alias,
                run_syncdb=True,
            )

        # We then serialize the current state of the database into a string
        # and store it on the connection. This slightly horrific process is so people
        # who are testing on databases without transactions or who are using
        # a TransactionTestCase still get a clean database on every test run.
        if serialize:
            self.connection._test_serialized_contents = self.serialize_db_to_string()

        call_command('createcachetable', database=self.connection.alias)

        # Ensure a connection for the side effect of initializing the test database.
        self.connection.ensure_connection()

        return test_database_name

    def set_as_test_mirror(self, primary_settings_dict):
        """
        Set this database up to be used in testing as a mirror of a primary
        database whose settings are given.
        """
        self.connection.settings_dict['NAME'] = primary_settings_dict['NAME']

    def serialize_db_to_string(self):
        """
        Serialize all data in the database into a JSON string.
        Designed only for test runner usage; will not handle large
        amounts of data.
        """
        # Build list of all apps to serialize
        from django.db.migrations.loader import MigrationLoader
        loader = MigrationLoader(self.connection)
        app_list = []
        for app_config in apps.get_app_configs():
            if (
                app_config.models_module is not None and
                app_config.label in loader.migrated_apps and
                app_config.name not in settings.TEST_NON_SERIALIZED_APPS
            ):
                app_list.append((app_config, None))

        # Make a function to iteratively return every object
        def get_objects():
            for model in serializers.sort_dependencies(app_list):
                if (model._meta.can_migrate(self.connection) and
                        router.allow_migrate_model(self.connection.alias, model)):
                    queryset = model._default_manager.using(self.connection.alias).order_by(model._meta.pk.name)
                    yield from queryset.iterator()
        # Serialize to a string
        out = StringIO()
        serializers.serialize("json", get_objects(), indent=None, stream=out)
        return out.getvalue()

    def deserialize_db_from_string(self, data):
        """
        Reload the database with data from a string generated by
        the serialize_db_to_string() method.
        """
        data = StringIO(data)
        for obj in serializers.deserialize("json", data, using=self.connection.alias):
            obj.save()

    def _get_database_display_str(self, verbosity, database_name):
        """
        Return display string for a database for use in various actions.
        """
        return "'%s'%s" % (
            self.connection.alias,
            (" ('%s')" % database_name) if verbosity >= 2 else '',
        )

    def _get_test_db_name(self):
        """
        Internal implementation - return the name of the test DB that will be
        created. Only useful when called from create_test_db() and
        _create_test_db() and when no external munging is done with the 'NAME'
        settings.
        """
        if self.connection.settings_dict['TEST']['NAME']:
            return self.connection.settings_dict['TEST']['NAME']
        return TEST_DATABASE_PREFIX + self.connection.settings_dict['NAME']

    def _execute_create_test_db(self, cursor, parameters, keepdb=False):
        cursor.execute('CREATE DATABASE %(dbname)s %(suffix)s' % parameters)

    def _create_test_db(self, verbosity, autoclobber, keepdb=False):
        """
        Internal implementation - create the test db tables.
        """
        test_database_name = self._get_test_db_name()
        test_db_params = {
            'dbname': self.connection.ops.quote_name(test_database_name),
            'suffix': self.sql_table_creation_suffix(),
        }
        # Create the test database and connect to it.
        with self._nodb_cursor() as cursor:
            try:
                self._execute_create_test_db(cursor, test_db_params, keepdb)
            except Exception as e:
                # if we want to keep the db, then no need to do any of the below,
                # just return and skip it all.
                if keepdb:
                    return test_database_name

                self.log('Got an error creating the test database: %s' % e)
                if not autoclobber:
                    confirm = input(
                        "Type 'yes' if you would like to try deleting the test "
                        "database '%s', or 'no' to cancel: " % test_database_name)
                if autoclobber or confirm == 'yes':
                    try:
                        if verbosity >= 1:
                            self.log('Destroying old test database for alias %s...' % (
                                self._get_database_display_str(verbosity, test_database_name),
                            ))
                        cursor.execute('DROP DATABASE %(dbname)s' % test_db_params)
                        self._execute_create_test_db(cursor, test_db_params, keepdb)
                    except Exception as e:
                        self.log('Got an error recreating the test database: %s' % e)
                        sys.exit(2)
                else:
                    self.log('Tests cancelled.')
                    sys.exit(1)

        return test_database_name

    def clone_test_db(self, suffix, verbosity=1, autoclobber=False, keepdb=False):
        """
        Clone a test database.
        """
        source_database_name = self.connection.settings_dict['NAME']

        if verbosity >= 1:
            action = 'Cloning test database'
            if keepdb:
                action = 'Using existing clone'
            self.log('%s for alias %s...' % (
                action,
                self._get_database_display_str(verbosity, source_database_name),
            ))

        # We could skip this call if keepdb is True, but we instead
        # give it the keepdb param. See create_test_db for details.
        self._clone_test_db(suffix, verbosity, keepdb)

    def get_test_db_clone_settings(self, suffix):
        """
        Return a modified connection settings dict for the n-th clone of a DB.
        """
        # When this function is called, the test database has been created
        # already and its name has been copied to settings_dict['NAME'] so
        # we don't need to call _get_test_db_name.
        orig_settings_dict = self.connection.settings_dict
        return {**orig_settings_dict, 'NAME': '{}_{}'.format(orig_settings_dict['NAME'], suffix)}

    def _clone_test_db(self, suffix, verbosity, keepdb=False):
        """
        Internal implementation - duplicate the test db tables.
        """
        raise NotImplementedError(
            "The database backend doesn't support cloning databases. "
            "Disable the option to run tests in parallel processes.")

    def destroy_test_db(self, old_database_name=None, verbosity=1, keepdb=False, suffix=None):
        """
        Destroy a test database, prompting the user for confirmation if the
        database already exists.
        """
        self.connection.close()
        if suffix is None:
            test_database_name = self.connection.settings_dict['NAME']
        else:
            test_database_name = self.get_test_db_clone_settings(suffix)['NAME']

        if verbosity >= 1:
            action = 'Destroying'
            if keepdb:
                action = 'Preserving'
            self.log('%s test database for alias %s...' % (
                action,
                self._get_database_display_str(verbosity, test_database_name),
            ))

        # if we want to preserve the database
        # skip the actual destroying piece.
        if not keepdb:

serialize_db_to_string orders models with serializers.sort_dependencies and serializes them. The sorting algorithm only deals with natural keys. Clear statement of the bug (Checkpoint 1 result)
- Bug: BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string deserializes the JSON snapshot and calls obj.save() for each object without wrapping that work in a transaction and without disabling constraint checks. The serializer ordering (serializers.sort_dependencies) only guarantees order for natural key dependencies, not full FK topological order. Without a transaction + disabled constraints + forward-reference handling, saving the deserialized objects can fail with IntegrityError (FK reference pointing to an object not saved yet), leaving the DB in an inconsistent state.
- Primary responsible method/class: BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string (django/db/backends/base/creation.py).

Checkpoint 4 — Proposed fix (code and reasoning)
I propose to change BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string to mirror loaddata's correct behavior for fixture loading. Specifically:
- Run the deserialization and saving inside a transaction.atomic(using=self.connection.alias).
- Use the connection.constraint_checks_disabled() context manager while creating objects.
- Pass handle_forward_references=True to serializers.deserialize so forward references can be deferred instead of causing immediate errors.
- Save each DeserializedObject with obj.save(using=self.connection.alias) and collect the ones that have deferred fields; after the main loop call save_deferred_fields(using=self.connection.alias) for each such object.
- After leaving the constraint-disabled block, call connection.check_constraints(table_names=...) with the list of tables affected (same as loaddata) to ensure constraints are checked and any problems surfaced.

Proposed implementation (conceptual; exact placement/whitespace to match repo style):

    def deserialize_db_from_string(self, data):
        """
        Reload the database with data from a string generated by
        the serialize_db_to_string() method.
        """
        from django.db import transaction, router

        data = StringIO(data)
        conn = self.connection
        objs_with_deferred_fields = []
        models = set()
        with transaction.atomic(using=conn.alias):
            # Disable constraint checks while loading to avoid FK ordering issues.
            with conn.constraint_checks_disabled():
                for obj in serializers.deserialize(
                        "json", data, using=conn.alias, handle_forward_references=True):
                    # Only save models allowed to be migrated on this DB
                    if router.allow_migrate_model(conn.alias, obj.object.__class__):
                        obj.save(using=conn.alias)
                        models.add(obj.object.__class__)
                        if obj.deferred_fields:
                            objs_with_deferred_fields.append(obj)
            # Save deferred fields (FK/M2M forward references)
            for obj in objs_with_deferred_fields:
                obj.save_deferred_fields(using=conn.alias)

        # Check for invalid constraints now that constraints are enabled again.
        if models:
            table_names = [m._meta.db_table for m in models]
            conn.check_constraints(table_names=table_names)

(You can either import router at the module top as it already is in the file, and import transaction locally as shown to avoid changing the top imports.)

If the assumption that ordering is sufficient is not true (and it isn't for general FK graphs), the code that relied on saved order must not rely on it being sufficient — hence transactional + constraint disabling is needed.
  - BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string had no flags/options — it implicitly and 'hardcodedly' used the default serializers.deserialize(..., using=...) call without handle_forward_references=True and without ignorenonexistent, and without using transaction/constraint contexts.     - transaction.atomic context
    - connection.constraint_checks_disabled()
    - handle_forward_references=True

Checkpoint 5 — Final report (root cause, exact changes, and all affected locations)

Root cause
- BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string performed deserialization by iterating the deserializer and calling obj.save() for each item without:
  - wrapping the operation in a transaction.atomic context,
  - disabling constraint checks during the bulk load,
  - passing handle_forward_references=True to the deserializer so forward-references can be deferred,
  - collecting and later saving deferred fields,
  - invoking connection.check_constraints(table_names=...).
- Since serializers.sort_dependencies does not guarantee a full topological ordering for all FK edges, objects could be saved in an order that violates FK constraints. Without temporarily disabling constraints and using a transaction to ensure atomicity, IntegrityErrors occur and the DB ends up inconsistent.

Every location that needs to change
1) Primary change (required):
   - File: django/db/backends/base/creation.py
   - Method: BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string
   - Current behavior: simply iterates serializers.deserialize and calls obj.save() for each object (no atomicy/constraint handling/forward-reference handling/deferred save).
   - Assumption encoded: that serialized ordering is sufficient and immediate saving outside a transaction is safe.
   - Fix: implement the sequence described above (transaction.atomic(using=...), connection.constraint_checks_disabled(), serializers.deserialize(..., handle_forward_references=True), obj.save(using=...), collect obj.deferred_fields into list and call save_deferred_fields(using=...) for each deferred object, then run conn.check_constraints(table_names=...)).
   - Why this is complete: this mirrors loaddata's established, tested pattern for loading fixtures and addresses missing steps leading to IntegrityError and inconsistent state.

2) Other locations: none needed
   - I inspected all backend-specific DatabaseCreation subclasses (sqlite3, postgresql, mysql, oracle, dummy). None override deserialize_db_from_string. Therefore one change in BaseDatabaseCreation suffices for all backends.
   - TransactionTestCase._fixture_setup already unsets/sets available_apps around the call; that is compatible with the fix.
   - No callers need to change; only the implementation of deserialize_db_from_string is updated.

Hardcoded values that need to become dynamic
- There were no numeric hardcoded constants involved. The problematic "hardcoding" was procedural (absence of transaction/constraint contexts). The fix makes behavior explicit and dynamic across backends (the constraint_checks_disabled is a backend hook — backends will no-op if they cannot disable constraints).

- The fix relies on connection.constraint_checks_disabled() and connection.check_constraints() semantics, which are respected across backends; for backends that cannot disable constraints, disable_constraint_checking returns False (no-op) so work will proceed without disabling. That is the same behavior loaddata uses; thus code paths are consistent.

Loaddata has an 'ignorenonexistent' flag controlled by the command line, but for test DB serialized rollback we should fail loudly (so we should not set ignorenonexistent=True by default). For each method mentioned in the draft report — verification against source

1) django/db/backends/base/creation.py::BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string
- What I expected to learn: whether the method wraps deserialization in a transaction, disables constraints, passes forward-reference handling flags, and saves deferred fields.
- What the code shows (quotes):

- Analysis: The method currently deserializes and saves each object one-by-one, without a transaction.atomic context, without using connection.constraint_checks_disabled(), and without passing handle_forward_references to serializers.deserialize. This supports the draft's claim that the load is performed outside an atomic block and lacks constraint/deferred-field handling.

2) django/db/backends/base/creation.py::BaseDatabaseCreation.serialize_db_to_string
- What I expected to learn: ordering guarantees used when serializing.

bug_report.Title: TransactionTestCase.serialized_rollback fails to restore DB snapshot due to ordering / constraint handling in deserialize_db_from_string
bug_report.Description: When TransactionTestCase.serialized_rollback = True the test-runner restores a serialized DB snapshot via BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string. The deserialization can raise integrity (foreign-key) errors and leave the DB inconsistent because objects are saved in the serializer-produced order without transaction or constraint-handling guarantees; the serializer ordering only guarantees natural-key dependencies, not a full FK topological order.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string (django/db/backends/base/creation.py) deserializes and saves objects by iterating serializers.deserialize(...) and calling obj.save() without wrapping the operation in a transaction.atomic block and without disabling constraint checks. Location: django/db/backends/base/creation.py::BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string (lines showing: data = StringIO(data); for obj in serializers.deserialize("json", data, using=self.connection.alias): obj.save()). This means partial inserts can be committed (or attempted) in the base implementation during restore.

2) BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string does not use the connection's constraint suppression or post-check API. Location: django/db/backends/base/creation.py::BaseDatabaseCreation.deserialize_db_from_string. The method contains no calls to connection.constraint_checks_disabled() or connection.check_constraints(...), so the restore does not temporarily suspend constraint checking nor validate constraints afterwards.

3) Verify get_order_dir behavior and ORDER_DIR mapping (django/db/models/sql/query.py and constants)
- Why: The draft asserts that get_order_dir strips a leading '-' and returns name and direction based on the provided default and ORDER_DIR, and that using a different default causes a '-' to be interpreted relative to that default, possibly flipping an explicit '-' into the opposite direction.
