bug_report.Title: Inherited Meta.ordering = ['-pk'] on parent results in ASC ordering for Child queries
bug_report.Description: When a Parent model sets Meta.ordering = ['-pk'] and a concrete Child uses multi-table inheritance (class Child(Parent)), querying Child produces SQL ORDER BY on the parent's id in ascending order, while querying Parent orders descending. The Child query's ordering sign is lost/flipped when the Parent's ordering is applied via inheritance.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Model metaclass inheritance/assignment (django/db/models/base.py::ModelBase.__new__): for a non-abstract child that doesn't declare its own Meta.ordering, the metaclass assigns the parent's ordering object directly to the child (new_class._meta.ordering = base_meta.ordering). This means the child's _meta.ordering contains the same literal string entries (e.g. '-pk') as the parent and is the same list object reference.

2) Primary logic bug in ordering expansion (django/db/models/sql/compiler.py::SQLCompiler.find_ordering_name): when the resolved name refers to a relation and the related model has its own Meta.ordering, the code iterates the related opts.ordering and, for string ordering items, calls the recursive resolver passing the outer order as the default (self.find_ordering_name(item, opts, alias, order, already_seen)). That passes the outer order ('ASC'/'DESC') as the default_order into the recursive call, causing inner explicit sign prefixes to be reinterpreted relative to that outer default.

3) Interaction with get_order_dir semantics and ORDER_DIR mapping (django/db/models/sql/query.py::get_order_dir and django/db/models/sql/constants.py::ORDER_DIR): get_order_dir uses the provided default to choose how to interpret an explicit '-' prefix (it returns dirn[1] for '-'), and ORDER_DIR maps 'ASC' -> ('ASC','DESC') and 'DESC' -> ('DESC','ASC'). Because find_ordering_name passes the outer order as the default into recursion, an explicit '-' in the related model's ordering can be inverted (e.g. '-pk' becoming ASC) when interpreted under a 'DESC' default. The combination of (2) and (3) is why Parent.Meta.ordering = ['-pk'] can produce ORDER BY ... ASC when resolved through Child.

4) How 'pk' resolves for an inherited concrete child (django/db/models/options.py::Options._prepare and django/db/models/sql/query.py::names_to_path): when a child has a parent link, Options promotes the parent link field and sets it as the child's primary key (the child's opts.pk becomes the parent link field). names_to_path maps 'pk' to opts.pk.name. Therefore '-pk' on the child resolves to the parent-link/parent id column, so the ordering resolution flow described above operates across the parent link and triggers the recursion/interpretation issue in SQLCompiler.find_ordering_name.
StepsToReproduce: Create models: from django.db import models; class Parent(models.Model): class Meta: ordering = ['-pk']; class Child(Parent): pass
Open the Django shell: python manage.py shell
Run: print(Child.objects.all().query)
Observe the generated SQL ORDER BY clause
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Querying Child.objects.all() should generate SQL that orders by the primary key column in descending order (ORDER BY ... DESC), matching Parent.Meta.ordering = ['-pk'].
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Querying Child.objects.all() generates SQL that orders by the parent's id column in ascending order (ORDER BY "myapp_parent"."id" ASC) despite Meta.ordering = ['-pk'] on the parent.

class ManyToManyDescriptor(ReverseManyToOneDescriptor):
    """
    Accessor to the related objects manager on the forward and reverse sides of
    a many-to-many relation.

    In the example::

        class Pizza(Model):
            toppings = ManyToManyField(Topping, related_name='pizzas')

    ``Pizza.toppings`` and ``Topping.pizzas`` are ``ManyToManyDescriptor``
    instances.

    Most of the implementation is delegated to a dynamically defined manager
    class built by ``create_forward_many_to_many_manager()`` defined below.
    """

    def __init__(self, rel, reverse=False):
        super().__init__(rel)

        self.reverse = reverse

    @property
    def through(self):
        # through is provided so that you have easy access to the through
        # model (Book.authors.through) for inlines, etc. This is done as
        # a property to ensure that the fully resolved value is returned.
        return self.rel.through

    @cached_property
    def related_manager_cls(self):
        related_model = self.rel.related_model if self.reverse else self.rel.model

        return create_forward_many_to_many_manager(
            related_model._default_manager.__class__,
            self.rel,
            reverse=self.reverse,
        )

    def _get_set_deprecation_msg_params(self):
        return (
            '%s side of a many-to-many set' % ('reverse' if self.reverse else 'forward'),
            self.rel.get_accessor_name() if self.reverse else self.field.name,
        )


def create_forward_many_to_many_manager(superclass, rel, reverse):
    """
    Create a manager for the either side of a many-to-many relation.

    This manager subclasses another manager, generally the default manager of
    the related model, and adds behaviors specific to many-to-many relations.
    """

    class ManyRelatedManager(superclass):
        def __init__(self, instance=None):
            super().__init__()

            self.instance = instance

            if not reverse:
                self.model = rel.model
                self.query_field_name = rel.field.related_query_name()
                self.prefetch_cache_name = rel.field.name
                self.source_field_name = rel.field.m2m_field_name()
                self.target_field_name = rel.field.m2m_reverse_field_name()
                self.symmetrical = rel.symmetrical
            else:
                self.model = rel.related_model
                self.query_field_name = rel.field.name
                self.prefetch_cache_name = rel.field.related_query_name()
                self.source_field_name = rel.field.m2m_reverse_field_name()
                self.target_field_name = rel.field.m2m_field_name()
                self.symmetrical = False

            self.through = rel.through
            self.reverse = reverse

            self.source_field = self.through._meta.get_field(self.source_field_name)
            self.target_field = self.through._meta.get_field(self.target_field_name)

            self.core_filters = {}
            self.pk_field_names = {}
            for lh_field, rh_field in self.source_field.related_fields:
                core_filter_key = '%s__%s' % (self.query_field_name, rh_field.name)
                self.core_filters[core_filter_key] = getattr(instance, rh_field.attname)
                self.pk_field_names[lh_field.name] = rh_field.name

            self.related_val = self.source_field.get_foreign_related_value(instance)
            if None in self.related_val:
                raise ValueError('"%r" needs to have a value for field "%s" before '
                                 'this many-to-many relationship can be used.' %
                                 (instance, self.pk_field_names[self.source_field_name]))
            # Even if this relation is not to pk, we require still pk value.
            # The wish is that the instance has been already saved to DB,
            # although having a pk value isn't a guarantee of that.
            if instance.pk is None:
                raise ValueError("%r instance needs to have a primary key value before "
                                 "a many-to-many relationship can be used." %
                                 instance.__class__.__name__)

        def __call__(self, *, manager):
            manager = getattr(self.model, manager)
            manager_class = create_forward_many_to_many_manager(manager.__class__, rel, reverse)
            return manager_class(instance=self.instance)
        do_not_call_in_templates = True

        def _build_remove_filters(self, removed_vals):
            filters = Q(**{self.source_field_name: self.related_val})
            # No need to add a subquery condition if removed_vals is a QuerySet without
            # filters.
            removed_vals_filters = (not isinstance(removed_vals, QuerySet) or
                                    removed_vals._has_filters())
            if removed_vals_filters:
                filters &= Q(**{'%s__in' % self.target_field_name: removed_vals})
            if self.symmetrical:
                symmetrical_filters = Q(**{self.target_field_name: self.related_val})
                if removed_vals_filters:
                    symmetrical_filters &= Q(
                        **{'%s__in' % self.source_field_name: removed_vals})
                filters |= symmetrical_filters
            return filters

        def _apply_rel_filters(self, queryset):
            """
            Filter the queryset for the instance this manager is bound to.
            """
            queryset._add_hints(instance=self.instance)
            if self._db:
                queryset = queryset.using(self._db)
            queryset._defer_next_filter = True
            return queryset._next_is_sticky().filter(**self.core_filters)

        def _remove_prefetched_objects(self):
            try:
                self.instance._prefetched_objects_cache.pop(self.prefetch_cache_name)
            except (AttributeError, KeyError):
                pass  # nothing to clear from cache

        def get_queryset(self):
            try:
                return self.instance._prefetched_objects_cache[self.prefetch_cache_name]
            except (AttributeError, KeyError):
                queryset = super().get_queryset()
                return self._apply_rel_filters(queryset)

        def get_prefetch_queryset(self, instances, queryset=None):
            if queryset is None:
                queryset = super().get_queryset()

            queryset._add_hints(instance=instances[0])
            queryset = queryset.using(queryset._db or self._db)

            query = {'%s__in' % self.query_field_name: instances}
            queryset = queryset._next_is_sticky().filter(**query)

            # M2M: need to annotate the query in order to get the primary model
            # that the secondary model was actually related to. We know that
            # there will already be a join on the join table, so we can just add
            # the select.

            # For non-autocreated 'through' models, can't assume we are
            # dealing with PK values.
            fk = self.through._meta.get_field(self.source_field_name)
            join_table = fk.model._meta.db_table
            connection = connections[queryset.db]
            qn = connection.ops.quote_name
            queryset = queryset.extra(select={
                '_prefetch_related_val_%s' % f.attname:
                '%s.%s' % (qn(join_table), qn(f.column)) for f in fk.local_related_fields})
            return (
                queryset,
                lambda result: tuple(
                    getattr(result, '_prefetch_related_val_%s' % f.attname)
                    for f in fk.local_related_fields
                ),
                lambda inst: tuple(
                    f.get_db_prep_value(getattr(inst, f.attname), connection)
                    for f in fk.foreign_related_fields
                ),
                False,
                self.prefetch_cache_name,
                False,
            )

        def add(self, *objs, through_defaults=None):
            self._remove_prefetched_objects()
            db = router.db_for_write(self.through, instance=self.instance)
            with transaction.atomic(using=db, savepoint=False):
                self._add_items(
                    self.source_field_name, self.target_field_name, *objs,
                    through_defaults=through_defaults,
                )
                # If this is a symmetrical m2m relation to self, add the mirror
                # entry in the m2m table.
                if self.symmetrical:
                    self._add_items(
                        self.target_field_name,
                        self.source_field_name,
                        *objs,
                        through_defaults=through_defaults,
                    )

bug_report.Description: ManyToManyField._check_relationship_model constructs a user-facing hint that incorrectly suggests using ForeignKey("%s", symmetrical=False, through="%s") when describing how to create a recursive (self-referential) many-to-many relationship with an explicit through model. The incorrect hint literal appears twice in django/db/models/fields/related.py and is asserted in a unit test.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect hardcoded hint strings in ManyToManyField._check_relationship_model (django/db/models/fields/related.py). Two literal occurrences use:
   'If you want to create a recursive relationship, use ForeignKey("%s", symmetrical=False, through="%s").'
   These literals (a) refer to ForeignKey instead of ManyToManyField and (b) include 'symmetrical=False', which is a ManyToManyField/ManyToManyRel parameter (not a ForeignKey parameter) and is an unnecessary/outdated recommendation for recursive many-to-many relationships with an intermediary model. The literals are formatted with (RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT, relationship_model_name).
2) Test expectation asserting the incorrect hint (tests/invalid_models_tests/test_relative_fields.py). The test test_ambiguous_relationship_model currently expects the hint string containing 'ForeignKey("self", symmetrical=False, through="AmbiguousRelationship").' Both the source literals in related.py and the test expectation encode the same incorrect assumption and therefore must be updated in parallel.
StepsToReproduce: Create an intermediary (through) model with more than two ForeignKey fields that reference the two sides of a ManyToManyField and omit through_fields.
Define the ManyToManyField using that intermediary model (no through_fields specified) so Django's checks report an ambiguity.
Run model validation (e.g. python manage.py check or run the test that triggers the check).
Observe the system checks output/error hint that suggests 'use ForeignKey("self", symmetrical=False, through="<ThroughModel>").' instead of an accurate ManyToManyField suggestion.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When Django's model validation detects an ambiguous intermediary model in a self-referential many-to-many, the error hint should recommend the correct declaration form using ManyToManyField, e.g. 'use ManyToManyField("self", through="<ThroughModel>").' The hint should not suggest passing ManyToManyField-only arguments to ForeignKey or recommend an unnecessary 'symmetrical=False' for intermediary-model self-referential many-to-manys.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The error hint text generated by ManyToManyField._check_relationship_model instructs users to use ForeignKey("self", symmetrical=False, through="<ThroughModel>"), which is incorrect because 'through' and 'symmetrical' are ManyToManyField arguments (not ForeignKey arguments), and 'symmetrical=False' is an unnecessary/outdated recommendation for recursive m2m with an intermediary model.

Later, in get_group_by, when compiling expressions into SQL, compiler.compile(expr) will call expression.as_sql which for Subquery.as_sql returns the subquery SQL (wrapped), and then it uses select_format to possibly wrap or cast. Then they iterate select expressions; later when compiling final result they call self.compile(expr) for each expr in expressions list. Thought: I continued the investigation and completed the required checkpoints. Below is a structured, complete analysis and a minimal, safe fix with justification and follow-up checks.

I. Quick summary (one-liner)
- Root cause: When GROUP BY referenced an annotated Subquery via its select alias, the compiler emitted a Ref (alias) into the GROUP BY clause and compiled that Ref as a quoted identifier (e.g. "status"), which can be interpreted by the DB as an ambiguous column reference; Django 2.2 produced the subquery SQL itself in GROUP BY (GROUP BY (SELECT ...)), while Django 3.0 emitted the alias ("status"). The correct output for this case is to group by the subquery expression itself.

---

Checkpoint 1 — Identify the bug

a) classify_report
- Entities identified (used as starting points): Query.resolve_ref, SQLCompiler.get_group_by, Subquery (Expression), Ref, Query.set_group_by, Query.set_values, .values('status') / .annotate(status=Subquery(...)), and the ProgrammingError: column reference "status" is ambiguous.

b) Located key files (searches)
- django/db/models/sql/compiler.py — SQLCompiler, contains get_group_by()
- django/db/models/sql/query.py — Query.resolve_ref, Query.set_group_by, Query.set_values, Query.annotation_select
- django/db/models/expressions.py — Subquery, Ref, Col, Expression.get_group_by_cols()

c) Read source of at least two relevant candidates
- Read SQLCompiler.get_group_by() and surrounding methods in django/db/models/sql/compiler.py (entire file).
- Read Query.resolve_ref(), Query.set_group_by(), Query.set_values(), Query.annotation_select, and related query code in django/db/models/sql/query.py (full relevant ranges).
- Read Subquery and Ref implementation in django/db/models/expressions.py (full class definitions and get_group_by_cols / as_sql).

d) Clear statement of the bug and primary responsible method/class
- What happens: For an annotated Subquery given an alias (annotate(status=Subquery(...)) then values('status') and annotate(...Count('status')...)), the SQLCompiler builds GROUP BY from query.group_by which contains references to the annotation. Those annotations may be represented internally by Ref(alias, annotation_expression). When compiling the final GROUP BY SQL, SQLCompiler compiles the Ref as a quoted alias (e.g. "status"), which causes PostgreSQL to treat it as a column name. Because a joined table also has a status column (test_app_ab.status / test_app_c.status), the unqualified identifier "status" is ambiguous and the DB raises ProgrammingError. On Django 2.2 the GROUP BY contained the subquery SQL (GROUP BY (SELECT ...)) instead of the alias string, which avoids ambiguity.

- Primary responsible code: django/db/models/sql/compiler.py::SQLCompiler.get_group_by (compilation of group_by expressions), in combination with Ref and Subquery classes (expressions.py). The immediate actionable place to fix is SQLCompiler.get_group_by (the compiler) to special-case this situation before generating SQL.

---

Notes:
- SQLCompiler.get_group_by is the central function that builds the GROUP BY SQL. It:
  - starts from self.query.group_by (None, True, or list/tuple)
  - if list/tuple, resolves string refs via self.query.resolve_ref(expr)
  - builds ref_sources set from any Ref expressions that wound up in the preliminary expressions list
  - iterates select items; if a select expression's object is in ref_sources, the compiler skips adding that select's own group-by columns (this is the mechanism that causes the compiler to prefer alias-references instead of re-expanding the annotation)
  - finally compiles each expression with self.compile(expr) and adds results de-duplicated by (sql, params_hash).

- Important: SQLCompiler.compile delegates to node.as_sql or vendor-specific method. Ref.as_sql returns the quoted alias (connection.ops.quote_name(self.refs)). Subquery.as_sql returns compiled subquery SQL surrounded by parentheses.

- Query.set_group_by constructs grouping by combining select() and annotations via annotation.get_group_by_cols(alias=alias) — and for annotated subqueries that returns Ref(alias, subquery) if alias provided (per expressions.Subquery.get_group_by_cols).

Component classes: SQLCompiler uses expressions.Ref and expressions.Subquery (and many others like Col). Subquery.get_group_by_cols returns [Ref(alias, self)] when alias is provided, which flows into SQLCompiler.get_group_by as a Ref.

I listed all classes in compiler.py above and inspected the get_group_by internals carefully (see point earlier).

Checkpoint 4 — Propose a fix, then immediately challenge it

Proposed fix (minimal, targeted)
- Change SQLCompiler.get_group_by so that when it compiles group_by expressions, it special-cases Ref expressions whose source is a Subquery and compiles the Subquery (expr.source) instead of compiling the Ref itself.
- Rationale: Query.set_group_by (and other code paths) intentionally add Ref(alias, subquery) to the group_by list so that the compiler avoids re-expanding the subquery's group-by columns. However, compiling the Ref as a quoted alias produces "status" which the DB interprets as a column name (Ambiguous). The correct SQL (as in Django 2.2) is to group by the subquery expression itself, not the alias string. The minimal, safest place to implement this is in the compiler when emitting GROUP BY SQL: detect Ref-source-subquery and use the subquery SQL for GROUP BY.

Concrete code change (patch)
- File: django/db/models/sql/compiler.py
  - Add Subquery to the import from django.db.models.expressions at top.
  - In SQLCompiler.get_group_by, replace the final compile(expr) call with a branch:

Current (approx):
for expr in expressions:
    sql, params = self.compile(expr)
    params_hash = make_hashable(params)
    ...

Change to:
from django.db.models.expressions import Subquery  # added to top imports
...
for expr in expressions:
    # Special-case a Ref to a Subquery: compile the Subquery SQL itself
    # (GROUP BY (SELECT ...)) rather than the alias ("status").
    if isinstance(expr, Ref) and isinstance(expr.source, Subquery):
        sql, params = self.compile(expr.source)
    else:
        sql, params = self.compile(expr)
    params_hash = make_hashable(params)
    ...

This produces GROUP BY (SELECT ...) for the Ref(alias, Subquery) case. It keeps the existing behavior for other kinds of Refs (they'll still be compiled normally), and is localized only to GROUP BY emission.

(If applying as a diff, you would:

- change the final loop inside get_group_by as shown above.)

Now, the required "challenge" section — work through the checklist:

4a) "What assumption does my fix change?"
- The current code implicitly assumes the compiled SQL for a Ref (alias) is always the correct SQL text to put into GROUP BY; my fix changes that assumption: when the underlying source is a Subquery, the alias alone is not a suitable SQL expression for GROUP BY and the actual subquery SQL must be emitted instead.

4b) "What hardcoded values encode this assumption?"
- I inspected all hardcoded constants in the component classes we inspected (Subquery, Ref, Col). There are no numeric hardcoded counts/offsets relating to this bug. The "hardcoded value" in effect is the Ref.as_sql behavior returning quote_name(self.refs) — that's a behavior, not a numeric constant. That behavior is preserved except in the specific context of GROUP BY where we now choose to use expr.source.as_sql instead. No numeric hardcoded values must become dynamic.

4c) "What about the reverse operation?"
- The reverse (complementary) operation is the construction of query.group_by (Query.set_group_by) which creates Refs for annotated subqueries. We're not changing how Query.set_group_by builds the group_by list; we're changing only how those Refs are compiled into SQL for GROUP BY. So the complementary read (“compiling group_by into SQL”) has been updated to handle the existing construction. The parent's methods that perform complementary operations are part of the same compiler (SQLCompiler.get_order_by etc.). I checked SQLCompiler.get_order_by: it uses Ref to refer to SELECT expressions for ORDER BY and marks them with is_ref=True; that code expects Ref.as_sql -> alias and not subquery SQL. Our change is limited to get_group_by, so ORDER BY behavior remains unchanged.

Concrete trace for parent's complementary methods:
- Method: SQLCompiler.get_order_by -> produces (resolved, (sql, params, is_ref)) tuples and passes is_ref=True for OrderBy(Ref(...)) to indicate "this references the select list alias." That logic is untouched: order_by compilation will still use Ref.as_sql (alias) so ORDER BY will remain consistent. This ensures we don't break ORDER BY by our change.

- Method: SQLCompiler.get_select -> uses select_format and compile on select expressions; unaffected.

- Method: Query.set_group_by -> still builds group_by with Ref(alias, Subquery) as before; we only render that Ref differently in the GROUP BY clause. So there's no mismatch between writing and reading: the annotation remains aliased for SELECT and ordering. We only changed how the GROUP BY SQL is generated from the group_by expression list.

So the reverse operation is accounted for: we didn't change write-time behavior, only read-time SQL emission, which is appropriate because SQLAlchemy/Postgres treats GROUP BY differently from SELECT alias references.

4d) "Does every existing method still work?"
- get_group_by: updated to special-case Ref->Subquery compilation; other cases remain unchanged.
- get_order_by: unchanged, still uses alias references for ORDER BY; this is desirable.
- get_select: unchanged.
- Query.set_group_by and Query.set_values: unchanged.
- Ref.as_sql, Subquery.as_sql, and Subquery.get_group_by_cols remain unchanged.

I reasoned through each method that interacts with group_by:
- Query.set_group_by builds group_by entries using get_group_by_cols(alias=alias) for annotations. For a Subquery annotated with alias, that method returns a Ref(alias, subquery). This is still produced.
- SQLCompiler.get_group_by receives that Ref and, because of the new special-case, renders the subquery SQL for that Ref instead of the alias string. This matches Django 2.2 behavior and removes the ambiguous column name.

No other methods appear to rely on GROUP BY being a simple quoted alias string. In particular, ORDER BY still uses quoted alias which is correct and unchanged.

4e) "Does any NEW method need to be added?"
- No new public methods are required. Only a small conditional in SQLCompiler.get_group_by is necessary.

---

Checkpoint 5 — Final report (root cause, every affected location, fixes)

Root cause (concise)
- SQLCompiler compiled the group_by expression Ref(alias, Subquery) to the quoted alias (Ref.as_sql -> "status"). PostgreSQL interpreted that as a column identifier which was ambiguous because tables in the FROM had columns also named status. Django 2.2 emitted the subquery SQL in the GROUP BY expression instead, avoiding ambiguity. The mismatch causes ProgrammingError on Postgres when grouping by an annotated Subquery alias that shares a column name with joined tables.

Locations and fixes (complete list)
1) django/db/models/sql/compiler.py
 - Current behavior: In get_group_by() the final loop unconditionally compiles each expression with self.compile(expr), so a Ref(alias, Subquery) compiles to the quoted alias string (e.g. "status").
 - Problem encoded: The compiler assumes the quoted alias is the right SQL to put into GROUP BY, but when the Ref.source is a Subquery that alias can be interpreted as a bare column name by the DB, causing ambiguity.
 - Fix: Special-case the compile() call inside get_group_by to detect when expr is a Ref and expr.source is a Subquery, and compile the Subquery source instead. This emits GROUP BY (SELECT ...). Also add Subquery to the import list (from django.db.models.expressions import ..., Subquery). No other code changes required.
 - Patch snippet (conceptual):
   - Add import:
     from django.db.models.expressions import OrderBy, Random, RawSQL, Ref, Value, Subquery
   - Replace the lines:
     for expr in expressions:
         sql, params = self.compile(expr)
   - With:
     for expr in expressions:
         if isinstance(expr, Ref) and isinstance(expr.source, Subquery):
             sql, params = self.compile(expr.source)
         else:
             sql, params = self.compile(expr)

2) No other files required editing
 - Rationale: The problem is only in SQL emission (compiler), not in query construction (Query.set_group_by). Changing Ref.as_sql globally would be riskier (affects ordering by alias, other uses). The narrow compiler change fixes the GROUP BY generation in the exact scenario observed.

Hardcoded values that need to become dynamic: none.

Any methods to add/override: none.

Why this is safe
- The change is localized to GROUP BY SQL generation. It preserves the existing Query.set_group_by logic and existing Ref.as_sql behavior for other contexts (ORDER BY, etc.). It restores the behavior that was present in Django 2.2 for this case (grouping by the subquery expression) and removes the ambiguous alias string from GROUP BY.

Test to validate
- Reproduce the sequence from the issue (models A, B, AB, C; annotate status=Subquery(AB.filter(a=OuterRef('pk'), b=1).values('status')), c_count=Count('c'), then .values('status').annotate(total_count=Count('status'))). The SQL should now include GROUP BY (SELECT ...subquery...) rather than GROUP BY "status", and the query should run without the ProgrammingError for Postgres.
- Also test ORDER BY on the annotation alias still works as before.

Potential follow-ups / caveats
- If there are other edge cases where Ref alias should be used in GROUP BY (e.g., database backends that support alias names in GROUP BY), the special-case still compiles the subquery SQL. For these backends that allow GROUP BY on alias name, both behaviors might be acceptable, but compiling the subquery expression is safer and avoids ambiguity when the alias matches a column name in the FROM tables.
- This change will not affect ORDER BY or other places where quoted alias names are expected.

Summary of what I will verify and why
- The draft report blames GROUP BY emission for compiling an annotation alias (Ref) as a bare quoted identifier (e.g. "status") instead of the subquery SQL. To confirm that, I must inspect:
  - SQLCompiler.get_group_by — where GROUP BY expressions are assembled and compiled.
  - Subquery.get_group_by_cols — how Subqueries advertise what to group by (and whether they yield Ref(alias, Subquery)).
  - Ref.as_sql — what SQL a Ref produces (alias quoted).
  - Query.set_group_by and values()/set_values path — how annotation aliases end up in the group_by list.
  - Query.resolve_ref and rewrite_cols — other places that create Ref(alias, expression) instances that can end up in group_by expressions.
  - SQLCompiler.compile — to confirm compilation delegates to node.as_sql (so Ref.as_sql yields quoted alias).
- I will quote critical lines and then check that each claim in the draft is supported and that any secondary findings sharing the same root cause are included.

I will now analyze each relevant method/file and summarize what the code shows (I fetched these files during the investigation).

1) SQLCompiler.get_group_by — verify behavior
- Relevant code (compiler.py):
  - The method builds a list "expressions" from self.query.group_by and then expands it with select, order_by and having expressions.
  - It builds a set of ref_sources from any Ref in the initial expressions:
    - "ref_sources = { expr.source for expr in expressions if isinstance(expr, Ref) }" (compiler.py, lines 112-114).
  - When iterating select entries, it skips select expressions that are present in ref_sources:
    - "if expr in ref_sources: continue" (compiler.py, lines 115-119).
  - After assembling expressions, it collapses and then compiles each expression with self.compile(expr) unconditionally:
    - "for expr in expressions: sql, params = self.compile(expr)" (compiler.py, lines 135-136).
- Analysis:
  - The code will include any Ref objects already present in expressions (those were not expanded away), and when a Ref is present, any select expression whose source equals that Ref.source is skipped, leaving the Ref itself in expressions. Then the Ref gets compiled via self.compile(expr). There is no special handling for Ref whose source is a Subquery in this compile loop.

2) Subquery.get_group_by_cols — verify behavior
- Relevant code (expressions.py):
  - "def get_group_by_cols(self, alias=None):"
  - "if alias: return [Ref(alias, self)]" (expressions.py, lines 1052-1055).
  - Else it falls back to the subquery's external columns: "external_cols = self.query.get_external_cols()" and returns external_cols or [self] if some are possibly_multivalued (expressions.py, lines 1055-1058).
- Analysis:
  - When an annotation that is a Subquery is selected under an alias, get_group_by_cols(alias=alias) explicitly returns a Ref(alias, Subquery). That creates a Ref object whose .source is the Subquery object.

3) Ref.as_sql — verify what SQL it emits
- Relevant code (expressions.py):
  - "def as_sql(self, compiler, connection): return connection.ops.quote_name(self.refs), []" (expressions.py, lines 819-821).
- Analysis:
  - Compiling a Ref produces a quoted identifier for the alias (e.g. "status") — exactly the SQL fragment the report shows in GROUP BY.

4) Subquery.as_sql / SQLCompiler.compile — verify subquery SQL emission
- Relevant code:
  - Subquery.as_sql compiles the subquery via "subquery_sql, sql_params = self.query.as_sql(compiler, connection)" and then wraps it in the template '(%(subquery)s)' (expressions.py, lines 1042-1050).
  - SQLCompiler.compile delegates to vendor impl or calls node.as_sql(self, self.connection) (compiler.py, lines 416-422).
- Analysis:
  - If a Subquery object is passed into compiler.compile, it will produce the (SELECT ...) SQL fragment (not a quoted alias). That is the SQL the draft claims Django 2.2 emitted for GROUP BY.

5) Query.set_group_by and values() path — verify how Ref(alias, Subquery) gets into group_by
- Relevant code (query.py):

bug_report.Title: Django 3.0: GROUP BY uses annotation alias (Ref) instead of subquery expression, causing ambiguous column error
bug_report.Description: A QuerySet that annotates a Subquery and then calls values('annotation_alias') followed by aggregation can produce SQL whose GROUP BY references the annotation alias as a bare identifier (e.g. "status") instead of the subquery expression. On PostgreSQL this identifier can be parsed as a table column and be ambiguous when other joined tables have a column with the same name, resulting in django.db.utils.ProgrammingError.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) SQLCompiler.get_group_by (django/db/models/sql/compiler.py)::get_group_by collects the expressions to be used in GROUP BY and then compiles each expression with self.compile(expr) without special-casing a Ref whose source is a Subquery. In the code: ref_sources is computed from any Ref in the initial expressions and select entries whose expression is in ref_sources are skipped, which allows the Ref to remain and be compiled later unmodified. (See compiler.py: ref_sources = { expr.source for expr in expressions if isinstance(expr, Ref) } and later for expr in expressions: sql, params = self.compile(expr)).

2) Subquery.get_group_by_cols (django/db/models/expressions.py)::get_group_by_cols returns a Ref(alias, self) when called with an alias. Concretely: Subquery.get_group_by_cols(alias) -> [Ref(alias, Subquery)]. This constructs a Ref whose .source is the Subquery expression.

3) Query.set_group_by / values() path (django/db/models/sql/query.py)::When selected annotations are included in the query's select (annotation_select), Query.set_group_by iterates the selected annotations and calls annotation.get_group_by_cols(alias=alias). For an annotated Subquery this produces Ref(alias, Subquery) and that Ref is placed into Query.group_by. (See query.py: annotation.get_group_by_cols(alias=alias) and assignment to self.group_by.)

4) Ref.as_sql emits the quoted alias identifier (django/db/models/expressions.py)::Ref.as_sql returns connection.ops.quote_name(self.refs) (e.g. "status"). Subquery.as_sql emits the subquery SQL (the SELECT ... wrapped in parentheses). Depending on which object (Ref or Subquery) the compiler compiles for a given group-by list entry, the emitted SQL will be either the alias "status" or the subquery SQL (SELECT ...). The code paths above explain how a Ref(alias, Subquery) can survive into the list compiled for GROUP BY and be emitted as "status". (See expressions.py: Ref.as_sql and Subquery.as_sql.)

5) Additional locations sharing the same root-cause pattern: Query.rewrite_cols (django/db/models/sql/query.py) also creates Ref(alias, expr) instances when ensuring referenced inner-query columns are selected (e.g. new_expr = Ref(col_alias, expr)). Query.resolve_ref has a branch that can return Ref(name, self.annotation_select[name]) when summarize=True (used in aggregation/subquery wrapping). These places construct Refs with a source expression and can feed the same alias->Ref pattern into group_by or other compiled clauses, so they share the root-cause pattern (Ref(alias, expression) being compiled into a quoted alias).
StepsToReproduce: Define the models as in the original report, e.g.:
Execute the query sequence from the report exactly as shown:

ab_query = AB.objects.filter(a=OuterRef('pk'), b=1)
filter_conditions = Q(pk=1) | Q(ab_a__b=1)
query = A.objects.filter(filter_conditions).annotate(
	status=Subquery(ab_query.values('status')),
	c_count=Count('c'),
)
answer = query.values('status').annotate(total_count=Count('status'))
print(answer.query)
print(answer)

Run this on Django 3.0.x with PostgreSQL (e.g. postgresql 11). Observe the ProgrammingError: column reference "status" is ambiguous and the GROUP BY clause referring to the quoted alias rather than the subquery.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When grouping by an annotation that is a Subquery, the ORM should emit GROUP BY that corresponds to the subquery expression (the SELECT ... subquery enclosed in parentheses), not a bare quoted alias that can be interpreted as a column name. The user-visible result should be that values/aggregation returns the aggregated rows (status, total_count) instead of raising a database error.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior:

def cleanse_setting(self, key, value):
    """
    Cleanse an individual setting key/value of sensitive content. If the
    value is a dictionary, recursively cleanse the keys in that dictionary.
    Also recurse into common iterables (lists/tuples/sets) to cleanse any
    dictionaries inside them.
    """
    try:
        if self.hidden_settings.search(key):
            cleansed = self.cleansed_substitute
        elif isinstance(value, dict):
            cleansed = {k: self.cleanse_setting(k, v) for k, v in value.items()}
        else:
            # Avoid treating strings/bytes/bytearray as iterables to recurse into.
            from collections.abc import Iterable
            if isinstance(value, Iterable) and not isinstance(value, (str, bytes, bytearray)):
                def _cleanse_element(elem):
                    if isinstance(elem, dict):
                        return {k: self.cleanse_setting(k, v) for k, v in elem.items()}
                    # Recurse into nested iterables
                    if isinstance(elem, Iterable) and not isinstance(elem, (str, bytes, bytearray)):
                        # Preserve common container types where possible
                        if isinstance(elem, list):
                            return [_cleanse_element(e) for e in elem]
                        elif isinstance(elem, tuple):
                            return tuple(_cleanse_element(e) for e in elem)
                        elif isinstance(elem, set):
                            return {_cleanse_element(e) for e in elem}
                        elif isinstance(elem, frozenset):
                            return frozenset(_cleanse_element(e) for e in elem)
                        else:
                            # Fallback: materialize as list
                            return [_cleanse_element(e) for e in elem]
                    # Wrap callables encountered inside iterables/dicts
                    if callable(elem):
                        return CallableSettingWrapper(elem)
                    return elem

                if isinstance(value, list):
                    cleansed = [_cleanse_element(e) for e in value]
                elif isinstance(value, tuple):
                    cleansed = tuple(_cleanse_element(e) for e in value)
                elif isinstance(value, set):
                    cleansed = {_cleanse_element(e) for e in value}
                elif isinstance(value, frozenset):
                    cleansed = frozenset(_cleanse_element(e) for e in value)
                else:
                    # Other iterables (generators, etc.) -> materialize to list
                    cleansed = [_cleanse_element(e) for e in value]
            else:
                cleansed = value
    except TypeError:
        # If the key isn't regex-able, just return as-is.
        cleansed = value

    # If the cleansed result itself is a callable, wrap it so it's not called
    if callable(cleansed):
        cleansed = CallableSettingWrapper(cleansed)

    return cleansed

Root cause
- SafeExceptionReporterFilter.cleanse_setting only handles dict (mapping) types when recursing into a setting's value. It returns other iterables (lists, tuples, nested lists-of-dicts, etc.) as-is. Therefore, dicts nested inside those iterables were never inspected and their sensitive keys remained unmasked.

1) django/views/debug.py: SafeExceptionReporterFilter.cleanse_setting
   - Current behavior:
     - Masks whole value if key matches hidden_settings regex
     - Recurses into dict values only (dicts nested under the top-level value), leaving other iterables alone
     - Wraps callables only if the final cleansed value is callable
   - Problem/assumption encoded:
     - Assumes sensitive data occurs only in dicts or as top-level values; ignores dicts inside lists/tuples/sets or nested structures.
   - Fix:
     - Extend cleanse_setting to detect iterables (lists, tuples, sets, frozenset, and other iterables) and recursively cleanse dicts inside those iterables.

     - Preserve common container types (list → list, tuple → tuple, set → set, frozenset → frozenset).
     - Wrap callables inside nested structures using CallableSettingWrapper (as we already wrap top-level callables).

Any methods that need to be added or overridden
- No new class-level methods required. A small internal helper for element recursion is used inside cleanse_setting. No overrides in parent classes are necessary.

1. Does cleanse_setting only recurse into dict instances?

2. Are sensitive-key matching and masking applied only when keys are inspected during dict recursion or when the top-level key matches?
   - Yes. The regex hidden_settings is applied to the key argument passed into each cleanse_setting call (line 89). Because inner elements are only visited via recursive cleanse_setting calls, keys are matched only when cleanse_setting is invoked for them; dict keys are checked because dict values trigger recursive calls for each key, but elements inside non-dict iterables are not subject to recursive calls and therefore are not checked/masked.

     - Pattern: 'API|TOKEN|KEY|SECRET|PASS|SIGNATURE' (case-insensitive) (line 81).
     - Substitute: '********************' (20 asterisks) (line 80).

3. Callable wrapping: is the draft's characterization accurate?
   - The code wraps "cleansed" only if callable(cleansed) (lines 99–101). That means that each individual invocation of cleanse_setting will wrap the value it returns if that returned value is callable.
   - Important nuance: because cleanse_setting is called recursively for dict values, callables that are values inside dicts that are visited will get wrapped by their own cleanse_setting invocation (inner call) before being placed in the parent dict. Therefore, callables inside dicts that are recursed into ARE wrapped. However, because the method does not recurse into non-dict iterables, callables that appear inside those iterables (e.g., a callable inside a list, or inside a dict that itself lives inside a list) are not passed through cleanse_setting and thus are not wrapped. The draft's phrasing claimed wrapping is only performed on the "final cleansed value" and concluded that callables inside nested iterables or inside dicts contained in iterables are not wrapped. That conclusion is correct for elements that are not visited (e.g., dicts inside lists), but the statement that callables are wrapped only on final value without noting the per-call recursion nuance is imprecise; I corrected the wording in the revised RootCause (see below): callables inside dicts that are visited are wrapped; callables inside non-dict iterables are not wrapped because those elements are not processed by cleanse_setting.

   - All code paths that call cleanse_setting:

   - ExpectedBehavior must describe user-visible correct behavior (no implementation details). Draft ExpectedBehavior is centered on user-visible masking; I preserved that.
   - ObservedBehavior must be user-visible output that demonstrates the bug — draft example output is fine; I preserved that.

Summary of verification
- The main defect is confirmed: SafeExceptionReporterFilter.cleanse_setting recurses only into dict instances (line 92) and returns other iterables unchanged (line 94). bug_report.Title: SafeExceptionReporterFilter.cleanse_setting does not recurse into iterables (lists/tuples) — nested dict secrets unmasked
bug_report.Description: When Django builds safe settings for error pages, dicts nested inside other iterables (lists, tuples, nested lists/tuples, etc.) are not being inspected/cleansed. As a result, sensitive keys (e.g. SECRET, TOKEN) that live inside dicts contained in lists/tuples remain visible on debug / technical error pages.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) SafeExceptionReporterFilter.cleanse_setting only recurses into dict instances. Location: django/views/debug.py, class SafeExceptionReporterFilter, method cleanse_setting (lines 83–95). The implementation does: if hidden_settings.search(key): ... elif isinstance(value, dict): ... else: return value. Consequence: if a setting value is a non-dict iterable (list, tuple, set/frozenset, generator, nested lists), any dict elements inside those iterables are not visited by cleanse_setting and therefore are returned unchanged; their keys are never checked against the sensitive-key pattern.

2) The sensitive-key matching and masking are applied only when a key is inspected by cleanse_setting. Location: same as (1). The class-level definitions used during masking are: hidden_settings = _lazy_re_compile('API|TOKEN|KEY|SECRET|PASS|SIGNATURE', flags=re.I) (line 81) and cleansed_substitute = '********************' (20 asterisks) (line 80). Consequence: those patterns and the substitute are applied only for keys that are passed into cleanse_setting — i.e., the top-level setting name and any dict keys reached via dict recursion. Keys inside dicts that are themselves contained in non-dict iterables are not passed into cleanse_setting and thus are not matched/masked.

3) Callable wrapping happens at the end of each cleanse_setting call (lines 99–101: if callable(cleansed): cleansed = CallableSettingWrapper(cleansed)). Consequence: values that are processed by cleanse_setting (for example, values of dict keys that are visited by recursion) will have callables wrapped. However, because elements inside non-dict iterables are not processed, callables contained inside those iterables (including callables inside dicts that live inside lists/tuples) will not be wrapped and will remain raw callables in the output.

4) All consumers of cleanse_setting that produce debug output are affected equally. Notable call sites: get_safe_settings() (calls cleanse_setting for each UPPERCASE setting — lines 104–113) and get_safe_request_meta(request) (calls cleanse_setting for each request.META key/value — lines 115–121). ExceptionReporter.get_traceback_data includes the outputs of both (request_meta and settings — lines 296–300), so the unmasked values are user-visible on debug/technical error pages.
StepsToReproduce: Start a Python shell with the Django project configured (or run the development server).

Run:
from django.views.debug import SafeExceptionReporterFilter
import pprint
pprint.pprint(SafeExceptionReporterFilter().get_safe_settings()['MY_SETTING'])
Observe that dict entries inside the lists/tuples still show their original values for keys like 'secret' and 'token' rather than being replaced by the cleansed substitute.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When the debug or technical error pages display settings or request.META, any key whose name matches the sensitive-key pattern (API|TOKEN|KEY|SECRET|PASS|SIGNATURE, case-insensitive) should have its value masked (display the configured cleansed_substitute: '********************') regardless of whether that key occurs at the top level, inside a dict nested inside another dict, or inside a dict nested within any common iterable (list, tuple, set/frozenset, nested lists/tuples). Callables found anywhere in settings or request.META shown on debug pages should be represented by CallableSettingWrapper rather than left as raw callables.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior:
Dicts nested directly inside lists/tuples are returned unchanged by SafeExceptionReporterFilter.get_safe_settings() and thus may expose sensitive values. Example output (from report):
{'something': [{'foo': 'value'}, {'secret': 'value'}, {'token': 'value'}],
 'else': [[{'foo': 'value'}, {'secret': 'value'}, {'token': 'value'}],
          [{'foo': 'value'}, {'secret': 'value'}, {'token': 'value'}]],
 'secret': '********************',
 'token': '********************'}
In this output, the top-level keys that match the sensitive-key regex are masked, but 'secret' and 'token' keys that appear inside dicts contained in the 'something' list (and similarly nested structures) remain unmasked. Callables appearing inside such unvisited iterable elements are also left as raw callables.

bug_report.Title: Migration crash when removing index_together if same fields are in unique_together (Django 1.11.10)
bug_report.Description: When a model lists the same column set in both unique_together and index_together, running the migration that removes the index_together can crash. The failure occurs in BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor._delete_composed_index (django/db/backends/base/schema.py) when database introspection reports more than one database object covering the same columns (for example, a unique constraint and a plain index). The method treats that situation as an error and raises ValueError instead of resolving which database object should be removed (or skipping removal when appropriate).
bug_report.RootCause:
1) BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor._delete_composed_index (django/db/backends/base/schema.py) assumes there will be exactly one database constraint/index matching a given set of columns and constraint flags and raises ValueError if len(matching_constraints) != 1. The code that implements that assumption is at least in _delete_composed_index (lines 402–416). This assumption is incorrect in cases where introspection.get_constraints returns both a unique constraint and a separate index covering the same columns (different database backends can and do report both).  

2) BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor.alter_index_together (django/db/backends/base/schema.py) unconditionally attempts to create an index for newly-declared index_together entries (lines 395–401). Because it does not check whether an existing database constraint or index already covers the same columns, moving an index declaration (or similar refactor) can trigger unnecessary index creation or a delete/recreate cycle.  

3) The higher-level cause is a mismatch between how composed-index deletion logic expects a single matching DB object and how database introspection can report multiple DB objects for the same column set. The introspection data (returned by connection.introspection.get_constraints and used by _constraint_names; see lines 1142–1170) exposes per-constraint flags (for example, infodict['unique'] and infodict['index']) that can be used to disambiguate cases where a unique constraint and a plain index both appear for the same columns. The correct behavior (diagnostic-level description) is that deletion logic for an index_together should (a) prefer deleting a plain index when one exists, and (b) if only a unique constraint (and its backing index) exists for those columns, treat removal of an index_together declaration as a no-op (do not delete the unique constraint/backing index). Likewise, when creating an index_together entry, creation logic should recognize when the database already has an index-like object covering the columns and not unconditionally attempt to create a duplicate index.  

Locations encoding the incorrect assumption (each stated equally):  
- django/db/backends/base/schema.py: BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor._delete_composed_index (lines ~402–416) — enforces len(matching_constraints) == 1 and raises ValueError otherwise.  
- django/db/backends/base/schema.py: BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor.alter_index_together (lines ~395–401) — creates indexes for newly-added index_together entries without checking for existing constraints/indexes that already cover the same columns.  

Note: django/db/backends/mysql/schema.py implements a MySQL-specific override that performs a MySQL-only pre-check and then delegates to the base-class _delete_composed_index (so the base-class behavior affects MySQL as well).
StepsToReproduce: Using Django 1.11.10, define a model with two fields (for example, 'a' and 'b').
In the model Meta, set unique_together = (('a', 'b'),) and index_together = (('a', 'b'),).
Create and apply migrations so the table is created with those constraints/indexes.
Edit the model to remove the index_together entry (leave unique_together intact) and generate a migration that deletes the index_together.

Run the migration that deletes the index_together. The migration crashes with ValueError from django/db/backends/base/schema.py in _delete_composed_index, reporting something like: "Found wrong number (2) of constraints for <table>(<columns>)".
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Removing an index_together that covers the same columns as an existing unique_together should not crash migrations. If a separate plain index exists, the migration to remove the index_together may remove that plain index. If only a unique constraint exists (and the index_together removal would otherwise attempt to remove the unique-backed index), the index_together removal should be a no-op at the database level (the unique constraint and its backing index remain), and migrations should continue without error. Moving an index declaration (for example, from index_together to Meta.indexes or vice versa) should not cause an unnecessary drop-and-recreate cycle of the index.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: When deleting an index_together that shares the same fields as a unique_together, BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor._delete_composed_index finds more than one matching database object (for example a unique constraint and a plain index) and raises ValueError: "Found wrong number (N) of constraints for <table>(<columns>)", causing the migration to crash. Separately, alter_index_together will unconditionally try to create indexes for newly-added index_together entries without checking for existing constraint coverage, which can lead to unnecessary index creation or name collisions.

class DeleteQuery(Query):
    """A DELETE SQL query."""

    compiler = 'SQLDeleteCompiler'

    def do_query(self, table, where, using):
        self.alias_map = {table: self.alias_map[table]}
        self.where = where
        cursor = self.get_compiler(using).execute_sql(CURSOR)
        if cursor:
            with cursor:
                return cursor.rowcount
        return 0

    def delete_batch(self, pk_list, using):
        """
        Set up and execute delete queries for all the objects in pk_list.

        More than one physical query may be executed if there are a
        lot of values in pk_list.
        """
        # number of objects deleted
        num_deleted = 0
        field = self.get_meta().pk
        for offset in range(0, len(pk_list), GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE):
            self.where = self.where_class()
            self.add_q(Q(
                **{field.attname + '__in': pk_list[offset:offset + GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE]}))
            num_deleted += self.do_query(self.get_meta().db_table, self.where, using=using)
        return num_deleted


class UpdateQuery(Query):

    compiler = 'SQLUpdateCompiler'

    def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(*args, **kwargs)
        self._setup_query()

    def _setup_query(self):
        """
        Run on initialization and at the end of chaining. Any attributes that
        would normally be set in __init__() should go here instead.
        """
        self.values = []
        self.related_ids = None
        self.related_updates = {}

    def clone(self):
        obj = super().clone()
        obj.related_updates = self.related_updates.copy()
        return obj

    def update_batch(self, pk_list, values, using):
        self.add_update_values(values)
        for offset in range(0, len(pk_list), GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE):
            self.where = self.where_class()
            self.add_q(Q(pk__in=pk_list[offset: offset + GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE]))
            self.get_compiler(using).execute_sql(NO_RESULTS)

    def add_update_values(self, values):
        """
        Convert a dictionary of field name to value mappings into an update
        query. This is the entry point for the public update() method on
        querysets.
        """
        values_seq = []
        for name, val in values.items():
            field = self.get_meta().get_field(name)
            direct = not (field.auto_created and not field.concrete) or not field.concrete
            model = field.model._meta.concrete_model
            if not direct or (field.is_relation and field.many_to_many):
                raise FieldError(
                    'Cannot update model field %r (only non-relations and '
                    'foreign keys permitted).' % field
                )
            if model is not self.get_meta().concrete_model:
                self.add_related_update(model, field, val)
                continue
            values_seq.append((field, model, val))
        return self.add_update_fields(values_seq)

    def add_update_fields(self, values_seq):
        """
        Append a sequence of (field, model, value) triples to the internal list
        that will be used to generate the UPDATE query. Might be more usefully
        called add_update_targets() to hint at the extra information here.
        """
        for field, model, val in values_seq:
            if hasattr(val, 'resolve_expression'):
                # Resolve expressions here so that annotations are no longer needed
                val = val.resolve_expression(self, allow_joins=False, for_save=True)
            self.values.append((field, model, val))

    def add_related_update(self, model, field, value):
        """
        Add (name, value) to an update query for an ancestor model.

        Update are coalesced so that only one update query per ancestor is run.
        """
        self.related_updates.setdefault(model, []).append((field, None, value))

    def get_related_updates(self):
        """
        Return a list of query objects: one for each update required to an
        ancestor model. Each query will have the same filtering conditions as
        the current query but will only update a single table.
        """
        if not self.related_updates:
            return []
        result = []
        for model, values in self.related_updates.items():
            query = UpdateQuery(model)
            query.values = values
            if self.related_ids is not None:
                query.add_filter(('pk__in', self.related_ids))
            result.append(query)
        return result

Checkpoint 4: Propose a fix, then challenge it

Proposed fix (high level)
- Make Collector.delete produce consistent per-model dictionaries: when the total number of deleted objects is zero, the per-model dictionary should always be empty ({}), regardless of whether the code path was a "fast delete" or a "normal delete".
- Concretely:
  - Only add model entries to deleted_counter when the count for that model is > 0.
  - Adjust the small fast-single-instance optimization so it returns an empty dict rather than a dict with zero value when count == 0.
  - Update tests that currently expect a zero-value entry for an empty fast-delete case to expect an empty dict instead.

Why this change
- The inconsistency comes from treating fast_delete querysets specially: a fast_delete queryset is appended to fast_deletes even if it matches no rows; later we add its count to deleted_counter using += count, which creates a key with value 0 in the dict. In the other code path (non-fast-delete), if the queryset matched nothing, nothing is added to self.data, so no key is created and we get {}. The fix makes Collector.delete only record non-zero deletions per model, so both code paths behave the same when nothing was deleted.

What I found in deletion.py (key confirmations, with line references from the file):
- The Collector is defined starting at line 79; deleted_counter is created in Collector.delete at line 389:
  - "deleted_counter = Counter()" (line 389).
- Collector.collect appends querysets that can be fast-deleted directly to self.fast_deletes without checking whether the queryset contains any rows:
  - Top-level fast-delete append:
    - if self.can_fast_delete(objs):
    -     self.fast_deletes.append(objs)
    -     return
    (lines 240–242)
  - Related-model fast-delete append (when building cascades):

- Collector.add returns early when given an empty iterable (so non-fast-delete additions are skipped on empty querysets):
  - if not objs:
  -     return []
  (lines 107–108)
  This confirms the non-fast-delete path will not create entries for empty inputs.
- In Collector.delete, fast_deletes are executed and their counts are accumulated unconditionally into deleted_counter:
  - for qs in self.fast_deletes:
  -     count = qs._raw_delete(using=self.using)
  -     deleted_counter[qs.model._meta.label] += count

  - for model, instances in self.data.items():
  -     ...
  -     count = query.delete_batch(pk_list, self.using)
  -     deleted_counter[model._meta.label] += count
  (lines 425–429; accumulation is line 429)
- There is a single-instance fast-delete optimization early-return in Collector.delete that returns count and a dict with the model label mapped to count (even when count == 0):
  - if len(self.data) == 1 and len(instances) == 1:
  -     ...
  -     return count, {model._meta.label: count}

- Claim: collect() appends fast-delete querysets without checking whether they contain rows. Supported: lines 240–242 and 314 show appending without emptiness checks; Collector.add (lines 107–108) shows the other path returns early when empty.
- Claim: single-instance fast-delete optimization returns a dict with label:count immediately (even when count == 0). Supported: lines 391–398 show this unconditional return.
- Claim: QuerySet.delete forwards the Collector.delete result so the inconsistency is visible at the public API. Supported: query.py lines 734–740 show this forwarding.

bug_report.Title: QuerySet.delete returns inconsistent per-model dict when zero objects deleted
bug_report.Description: Calling QuerySet.delete() that deletes zero objects sometimes returns an empty per-model dict ({}) and other times a dict containing model-label keys mapped to 0 (e.g. {'my_app.BlockLibrary': 0}). This inconsistency depends on the deletion code path (fast-delete vs. non-fast-delete).
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/models/deletion.py :: Collector.delete
   - Collector.delete initializes a Counter() (deleted_counter) and returns (sum(deleted_counter.values()), dict(deleted_counter)) (lines: deleted_counter = Counter(), return sum(...), dict(...)).
   - In the fast-delete phase, the code unconditionally executes qs._raw_delete(...) and then unconditionally accumulates the result with:
       deleted_counter[qs.model._meta.label] += count
     (see lines where fast_deletes are processed). Because the addition is unconditional, a count == 0 will create a dict entry with value 0.

2) django/db/models/deletion.py :: Collector.collect (fast-delete append sites)
   - Collector.collect appends queryset-like objects to self.fast_deletes without checking whether the queryset actually contains any rows. There are two append sites that follow this pattern:
     - Top-level can_fast_delete path: if self.can_fast_delete(objs): self.fast_deletes.append(objs); return (lines 240-242).
     - Related-model fast-delete batching: self.fast_deletes.append(sub_objs) when building related-model fast deletes (line 314).
   - Because collect() can append an empty queryset to fast_deletes, later deletion of that queryset can produce a zero count which, per #1, becomes a zero-valued dict entry.

3) django/db/models/deletion.py :: Collector.add (non-fast-delete path)
   - Collector.add immediately returns an empty list when given an empty iterable (if not objs: return []). As a result, when a non-fast-delete path encounters an empty set of matching rows, it does not populate self.data for that model, and no per-model dict entry is created for that model.

4) django/db/models/deletion.py :: Collector.delete single-instance fast-delete optimization
   - Collector.delete contains a single-instance optimization that, in the case of one model and one instance, executes a delete_batch and returns count, {model._meta.label: count} immediately (lines 391-398). This unconditional construction of a model-label -> count dict can produce a zero-valued entry when count == 0.

5) django/db/models/query.py :: QuerySet.delete caller forwarding
   - QuerySet.delete constructs a Collector, calls collector.collect(del_query), and returns collector.delete()'s tuple directly (lines 734-740). Therefore, the inconsistency arising inside Collector.delete is observable at the QuerySet.delete public API.

Summary (exact): Collector.delete returns sum(deleted_counter.values()), dict(deleted_counter). The presence or absence of zero-valued keys in dict(deleted_counter) is controlled by (a) whether collect() appended a fast-deletable queryset to self.fast_deletes even when it matched no rows (collect's append sites), (b) the unconditional accumulation of counts into deleted_counter in Collector.delete for both fast_deletes and per-model deletions, and (c) the single-instance fast-delete early-return that constructs a dict even when count == 0. These combined behaviors cause the observed inconsistent outputs ({} vs {'app.Model': 0}) when the total deleted == 0.
StepsToReproduce: Define two models: one simple model (no related objects pointing to it) and one model which has other models pointing to it via ForeignKey (or otherwise is referenced by related objects).
Ensure there are no rows matching the filter you will use (or use a filter that matches nothing).

Call delete() on a queryset for the simple model that is fast-deletable (e.g. MySimpleModel.objects.filter(<non-matching>).delete()). Observe the returned value — example: (0, {'my_app.BlockLibrary': 0}).

Call delete() on an analogous queryset for the model with related objects (non-fast-delete path) (e.g. MyReferencedModel.objects.filter(<non-matching>).delete()). Observe the returned value — example: (0, {}).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When delete() removes a total of zero objects, the per-model dictionary in the returned tuple should be consistent across code paths (i.e. the result should not differ depending on whether the model was fast-deletable). In other words, either both cases should return an empty dict {} or both should return a dict with model-label keys mapped to 0; they must not differ.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: For an overall deletion count of 0 the returned tuple is inconsistent: the fast-delete code path produces a dict containing the model label with value 0 (e.g. (0, {'my_app.BlockLibrary': 0})), while the non-fast-delete (foreign-key/related) path produces an empty dict (0, {}).

    """

    tuple of two strings. Normalize it to a tuple of tuples, so that

    try:

Checkpoint 5: Final report

Root cause
- The codebase treated UniqueConstraint differently from legacy unique_together: model checks didn't validate UniqueConstraint.fields and the migration autodetector didn't verify constraint fields or build dependencies for FK fields. As a result, makemigrations could create AddConstraint operations (or at least not error early) for constraints referencing nonexistent fields. UniqueConstraint.create_sql still calls model._meta.get_field at apply time, but that error is too late and inconsistent with unique_together which raises models.E012 earlier.

Every location that needs to change (complete list)
1) django/db/models/base.py::_check_constraints
   - Current behavior: Checks DB support for constraint features but does not validate that fields referenced by constraints exist.
   - Assumption encoded: constraints' fields exist and will be validated elsewhere (or only when generating SQL).
   - Fix: Add code to collect fields used by constraints and call cls._check_local_fields(fields, 'constraints').
   - Exact insertion (pseudo-diff):

        # Existing code ...
        if not (<DB feature checks>) and any(...):
            errors.append(...)
        if not (<another DB feature checks>) and any(...):
            errors.append(...)
        if not (<another DB feature checks>) and any(...):
            errors.append(...)

        # New block:
        # Validate that fields referenced in constraints exist (like unique_together).
        fields = [
            field_name
            for constraint in cls._meta.constraints
            for field_name in getattr(constraint, 'fields', [])
        ]
        errors.extend(cls._check_local_fields(fields, 'constraints'))

        return errors

   - Effect: models.check framework will return models.E012 / E013 / E016 for problematic constraint field references like it does for unique_together.

2) django/db/migrations/autodetector.py::create_altered_constraints and generate_added_constraints
   - Current behavior: create_altered_constraints computes added/removed constraints but does not validate fields or compute dependencies. generate_added_constraints emits AddConstraint operations without dependencies.
   - Assumption encoded: constraints are already correct or do not require dependencies; fields exist.
   - Fix:
     a) In create_altered_constraints, compute per-constraint dependencies by iterating constraint.fields and calling self.new_apps.get_model(...)._meta.get_field(field_name) (this raises FieldDoesNotExist if missing). For fields that are FK fields, extend dependencies using self._get_dependencies_for_foreign_key(field).
     b) Store these per-constraint dependencies in self.altered_constraints (e.g., under 'added_constraints_deps').
     c) In generate_added_constraints, when adding AddConstraint operations, pass dependencies=deps for each constraint (zip constraints and deps).
   - Exact insertion (pseudo-diff) as described above in the Proposed Fix section.

Why these are the only locations
- Model-level checks (base._check_constraints) are used extensively by StateApps rendering and by the system checks; adding validation there makes checks consistent everywhere (e.g., makemigrations rendering of models will produce errors).
- MigrationAutodetector is responsible for generating AddConstraint operations. Without field validation and proper dependency tracking there, makemigrations will incorrectly generate migrations or not signal the missing field early. Unique_together and index_together already have special handling in the autodetector — constraints need the same treatment.

Hardcoded values that need to become dynamic
- There are no numeric hardcoded values involved in this fix. The change is not about counts/offsets but about adding explicit validation and dependency computation. Component classes (UniqueConstraint) already use tuple(fields) and call get_field; we only cause those assumptions to be validated earlier.

Methods that need to be added or overridden
- No new methods are required. We reuse existing helpers:
  - cls._check_local_fields (already exists) to emit models.E012/E013/E016.
  - MigrationAutodetector._get_dependencies_for_foreign_key (already exists) to collect FK dependencies.
- Ensure generate_added_constraints passes dependencies parameter to add_operation — add_operation supports dependencies.

Concrete behavior traces (examples)
- If a model has:

      constraints = [
          models.UniqueConstraint(fields=['nonexistent_field', 'other'], name='unique_bad')
      ]

  - Before fix:
    - makemigrations may not error during autodetection and might produce an AddConstraint operation; the migration would later fail at database apply time with FieldDoesNotExist or SQL error.
  - After fix:
    - StateApps rendering (ProjectState.apps) will run model checks and base._check_constraints will call _check_local_fields -> Error models.E012 "'constraints' refers to the nonexistent field 'nonexistent_field'." The makemigrations command will error early with that message, matching the behavior for unique_together.

Edge cases addressed
- Constraints that are not UniqueConstraint (e.g., CheckConstraint) are skipped because they don't have .fields attribute.
- For constraints that do have fields but some fields are FK fields that refer to other models, we collect dependencies so AddConstraint operations will depend on the appropriate model migrations (matching unique_together behavior).
- If constraints are added in migrations by hand and reference non-existent fields, AddConstraint.state_forwards will append them and reloading model state will cause rendering and checks, which will now surface the error.

Suggested tests to add
- A unit test where a model adds a UniqueConstraint referencing a nonexistent field and assert that migrations.autodetector raises an error (and model checks return models.E012).
- A unit test where a model adds a UniqueConstraint referencing a FK field and assert that the generated AddConstraint operation has dependencies on the related model (similar in spirit to tests for unique_together).

Summary / patch pointers
- Edit django/db/models/base.py: add the fields validation block in _check_constraints (use cls._check_local_fields).
- Edit django/db/migrations/autodetector.py:
  - In create_altered_constraints, compute add_constraints_deps by iterating constraint.fields and collecting dependencies via _get_dependencies_for_foreign_key.
  - In generate_added_constraints, pass those dependencies to add_operation.

This change makes UniqueConstraint handling consistent with unique_together: missing fields are detected early (models.E012) and migrations record appropriate dependencies.

bug_report.Title: makemigrations does not validate UniqueConstraint field names (no models.E012 / missing FK dependencies)
bug_report.Description: When a model gains a UniqueConstraint that names a field that does not exist on the model, makemigrations does not validate the field names and proceeds without raising the same models.E012 error that unique_together triggers. As a result, migrations referencing non-existent fields can be generated and/or constraints may be created without proper migration dependencies for FK fields.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Missing model-level validation for constraint fields: django/db/models/base.py :: Model._check_constraints performs database-feature checks (warnings for unsupported check constraints, conditional unique constraints, and deferrable unique constraints) but does not validate that field names referenced by model constraints exist. The local-field validation helper (_check_local_fields) is present (and emits models.E012 / E013 / E016; see _check_local_fields), but it is not invoked for constraint fields in _check_constraints. Effect: model/system checks do not report models.E012 for UniqueConstraint fields that don't exist, so invalid constraints can reach migration/autodetection and/or apply time.

2) Missing field validation and FK dependency collection in the migration autodetector: django/db/migrations/autodetector.py :: MigrationAutodetector.create_altered_constraints and generate_added_constraints compute added/removed constraints and emit AddConstraint operations but do not (a) call get_field on each constraint field to validate its existence during makemigrations/autodetection, nor (b) collect foreign-key dependencies for fields referenced by constraints. By contrast, unique_together handling (_generate_altered_foo_together) explicitly calls get_field for each referenced field and extends dependencies via _get_dependencies_for_foreign_key. Effect: makemigrations can produce AddConstraint operations for constraints that reference missing fields and will not add migration dependencies for constraints that reference FK fields.
StepsToReproduce: Create a Django project and app (e.g., app 'demo').
Define a model that includes a UniqueConstraint referencing a non-existent field, for example: constraints = [models.UniqueConstraint(fields=['no_such_field'], name='unique_bad')].
Run python manage.py makemigrations for the project.
Observe whether makemigrations proceeds to create a migration (current faulty behavior) instead of raising a models.E012-style error.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: makemigrations should detect that a UniqueConstraint references a nonexistent field and fail early with a model-check error (models.E012) indicating that the 'constraints' option refers to a nonexistent field. If the constraint references a ForeignKey field, the generated migration should include dependencies on the related model/migration so the constraint is applied only after the related model exists.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: makemigrations does not validate the field names in UniqueConstraint, so it can generate AddConstraint operations (or otherwise continue) without raising models.E012. It also does not record dependencies for constraints that reference ForeignKey fields, causing incorrect or fragile migrations.

class BaseIterable:
    def __init__(self, queryset, chunked_fetch=False, chunk_size=GET_ITERATOR_CHUNK_SIZE):
        self.queryset = queryset
        self.chunked_fetch = chunked_fetch
        self.chunk_size = chunk_size


class ModelIterable(BaseIterable):
    """Iterable that yields a model instance for each row."""

    def __iter__(self):

        # Execute the query. This will also fill compiler.select, klass_info,
        # and annotations.
        results = compiler.execute_sql(chunked_fetch=self.chunked_fetch, chunk_size=self.chunk_size)
        select, klass_info, annotation_col_map = (compiler.select, compiler.klass_info,
                                                  compiler.annotation_col_map)
        model_cls = klass_info['model']
