bug_report.Title: FormSet non_form_errors should add 'nonform' CSS class to ErrorList
bug_report.Description: FormSet-level non-form errors (the errors returned by BaseFormSet.non_form_errors / produced by BaseFormSet.full_clean) are constructed without a distinguishing CSS class, so ErrorList renders them as <ul class="errorlist">. Forms add the 'nonfield' CSS class for form non-field errors (ErrorList(error_class='nonfield')), but FormSets do not add an analogous 'nonform' class. As a result, custom ErrorList renderers cannot distinguish form-level non-field errors from formset-level non-form errors.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) BaseFormSet.full_clean in django/forms/formsets.py initializes formset-level non-form errors using self.error_class() with no error_class marker and, on ValidationError from formset.clean(), replaces them with self.error_class(e.error_list) also without an error_class marker. Locations: django/forms/formsets.py, BaseFormSet.full_clean (initialization at "self._non_form_errors = self.error_class()" and except block at "self._non_form_errors = self.error_class(e.error_list)").

2) The management form invalidation path in BaseFormSet.full_clean appends a ValidationError into the same self._non_form_errors list ("self._non_form_errors.append(error)"), so that path is also affected by the absence of a distinguishing CSS class. Location: django/forms/formsets.py, BaseFormSet.full_clean (management_form invalid branch and append).

3) By contrast, BaseForm constructs form non-field errors using ErrorList(error_class='nonfield'), which renders as <ul class="errorlist nonfield">. Location: django/forms/forms.py, BaseForm.non_field_errors and BaseForm.add_error (calls to self.error_class(error_class='nonfield')).

4) ErrorList composes its ul class from the base 'errorlist' plus any supplied error_class string (ErrorList.__init__ sets self.error_class to 'errorlist' or 'errorlist {}'.format(error_class); as_ul renders the ul using self.error_class). Location: django/forms/utils.py, ErrorList.__init__ and ErrorList.as_ul.

(Concrete incorrect assumption: BaseFormSet currently assumes a plain ErrorList() (rendering '<ul class="errorlist">') is sufficient for formset-level non-form errors. The diagnostic expectation is that formset non-form ErrorLists be constructed with the token 'nonform' (i.e., ErrorList(..., error_class='nonform')) so they render as '<ul class="errorlist nonform">' and can be distinguished from form non-field ErrorLists which use 'nonfield'.)
StepsToReproduce: 1. Create a FormSet (using formset_factory or a custom BaseFormSet) whose clean() raises a ValidationError or otherwise produces non-form errors.
2. Call formset.non_form_errors() or render the non-form errors as HTML (e.g., formset.non_form_errors().as_ul()).
3. Observe that the rendered <ul> element has class="errorlist" (no 'nonform' token), making it indistinguishable from a generic ErrorList.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: FormSet-level non-form errors should render with a distinguishing CSS class so renderers can tell them apart from form non-field errors. Specifically, ErrorList instances representing formset non-form errors should include 'nonform' in the CSS class (i.e., <ul class="errorlist nonform">).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: ErrorList instances created for FormSet non-form errors are constructed without an extra error_class argument and render as <ul class="errorlist"> (no 'nonform'). Forms, by contrast, add 'nonfield' to form non-field ErrorList instances (rendering <ul class="errorlist nonfield">).

Proposed fix (high-level):
- Change Query.add_deferred_loading so that when the query is currently in immediate-mode (defer == False) and removing the requested field_names empties the immediate set, we convert to defer-mode (defer == True) and set the stored field_names to the set of non-primary-key concrete field names of the base model (and where necessary include related-path fields — see below). Also ensure that any change to deferred_loading invalidates cached self._loaded_field_names_cache.
- Also ensure add_immediate_loading and clear_deferred_loading clear the cache as well.

Concrete code changes (patch outline — all in django/db/models/sql/query.py):

1) Modify clear_deferred_loading to also clear cached _loaded_field_names_cache:

Old:

        """Remove any fields from the deferred loading set."""
        self.deferred_loading = (frozenset(), True)

New:
    def clear_deferred_loading(self):
        """Remove any fields from the deferred loading set."""
        self.deferred_loading = (frozenset(), True)
        try:
            del self._loaded_field_names_cache
        except AttributeError:
            pass

2) Modify add_deferred_loading to handle immediate-mode->defer-mode transition and invalidate cache.

Old:
    def add_deferred_loading(self, field_names):
        existing, defer = self.deferred_loading
        if defer:
            self.deferred_loading = existing.union(field_names), True
        else:
            self.deferred_loading = existing.difference(field_names), False

New (pseudocode):
    def add_deferred_loading(self, field_names):
        existing, defer = self.deferred_loading
        if defer:
            self.deferred_loading = existing.union(field_names), True
        else:
            new_existing = existing.difference(field_names)
            if new_existing:
                self.deferred_loading = new_existing, False
            else:
                # immediate set emptied -> convert to explicit deferred set
                opts = self.get_meta()
                deferred_fields = {f.name for f in opts.concrete_fields if not f.primary_key}
                # store as frozenset and set defer True
                self.deferred_loading = frozenset(deferred_fields), True
        # invalidate cache
        try:
            del self._loaded_field_names_cache
        except AttributeError:
            pass

- When only('name') sets immediate set {'name'}, then defer('name') removes 'name', leaving empty immediate set. Instead of storing empty immediate set (interpreted as no-restriction), we switch to defer mode with deferred field names being all non-pk field names for the model, which properly expresses that everything except pk is deferred — which deferred_to_data will convert to loading only pk.

Checkpoint 5: Final report — complete analysis and exact fixes

Root cause
- Query.deferred_loading is stored as (field_names, defer_flag).
  - defer_flag == True: field_names lists deferred fields
  - defer_flag == False: field_names lists immediate (only) fields
- Query.get_loaded_field_names() treats an empty field_names set as "no restriction" (early return).
- add_deferred_loading, when operating on an immediate-mode state (defer False), simply removed the specified fields from the immediate set and left the result even if it became empty. That produced deferred_loading = (frozenset(), False) which get_loaded_field_names interpreted as "no restriction", so the compiler selected all fields.
- The user expectation is: only('name').defer('name') => everything previously deferred plus that explicit defer should result in effectively "defer all non-pk fields" -> resulting SELECT should be only the pk.

2) add_deferred_loading:

Replace current body:

    existing, defer = self.deferred_loading
    if defer:
        # Add to existing deferred names.
        self.deferred_loading = existing.union(field_names), True
    else:
        # Remove names from the set of any existing "immediate load" names.

With new logic:

    existing, defer = self.deferred_loading
    if defer:
        # Add to existing deferred names.
        self.deferred_loading = existing.union(field_names), True
    else:
        # We are in immediate ("only") mode.
        new_existing = existing.difference(field_names)
        if new_existing:
            # Still have some immediate fields left: keep immediate-mode.
            self.deferred_loading = frozenset(new_existing), False
        else:
            # The immediate set would become empty. We must convert to explicit
            # deferred-mode so that the compiler does not interpret an empty set
            # as "no restriction".
            opts = self.get_meta()
            # Collect non-PK concrete field names for the base model.
            deferred_fields = {f.name for f in opts.concrete_fields if not f.primary_key}
            # Additionally, handle any existing immediate paths that contain lookups
            # (e.g., 'rel__foo'): convert them into deferred fields using the prefix,
            # so that related models are treated correctly.
            for name in existing:
                if LOOKUP_SEP in name:
                    parts = name.split(LOOKUP_SEP)
                    # Walk to find the target model for the parts[:-1]
                    cur_opts = opts
                    cur_prefix_parts = []
                    for part in parts[:-1]:
                        try:
                            field = cur_opts.get_field(part)
                        except Exception:
                            cur_opts = None
                            break
                        # get the related model for this part
                        if hasattr(field, 'remote_field') and field.remote_field:
                            cur_prefix_parts.append(part)
                            cur_opts = field.remote_field.model._meta
                        else:
                            cur_opts = None
                            break
                    if cur_opts is None:
                        continue
                    # Add all non-pk fields of this related model, prefixed by the path.
                    prefix = LOOKUP_SEP.join(cur_prefix_parts)
                    for f in cur_opts.concrete_fields:
                        if not f.primary_key:
                            deferred_fields.add(LOOKUP_SEP.join((prefix, f.name)))
            self.deferred_loading = frozenset(deferred_fields), True
    # Invalidate cached loaded field names
    try:
        del self._loaded_field_names_cache
    except AttributeError:
        pass

Notes on the above:
- The related-path handling will add 'rel__fieldname' entries when immediate-set contained entries with LOOKUP_SEP.
- This ensures the deferred set is representable by deferred_to_data (it splits path parts and locates models properly).
- This logic opts to add every non-pk field of the base model and related models addressed, which amounts to "defer everything except pk(s)" as intended.

bug_report.Title: QuerySet.defer() after only() can lose the 'only' restriction and cause all fields to be selected
bug_report.Description: Chaining .only(...).defer(...) can unexpectedly produce a SELECT that returns all model fields instead of restricting the loaded columns. Example: Company.objects.only('name').defer('name') returns all columns instead of only the primary key.
bug_report.RootCause:
Multiple issues in the Query representation and its mutation semantics cause an 'only' restriction to be lost when defer() is chained.

1) Representation and semantics: Query.deferred_loading is a tuple (field_names, defer_flag) with default (frozenset(), True). The semantics are: if defer_flag == True, field_names names fields to defer; if defer_flag == False, field_names names the only fields to load. (See django/db/models/sql/query.py: self.deferred_loading = (frozenset(), True).)

2) Empty-set ambiguity and early return: Query.deferred_to_data treats an empty field_names set as "no restriction" (it returns immediately when not field_names), and get_loaded_field_names relies on deferred_to_data to compute which fields will be loaded. As a result, an internal representation of an empty set is interpreted as "no restrictions" and leads the compiler to select all columns.

3) Incorrect state transition: Query.add_deferred_loading (when the query is in immediate-mode: defer_flag == False) removes requested field names from the immediate set by computing existing.difference(field_names) and storing that result with defer_flag == False. If this produces an empty set, deferred_loading becomes (frozenset(), False). Because of (2), that empty immediate set is interpreted as "no restriction" (all columns selected). (See django/db/models/sql/query.py: add_deferred_loading uses existing.difference(field_names), False.)

4) Cached derived data not invalidated: get_loaded_field_names caches its result in Query._loaded_field_names_cache, but mutations to deferred_loading (in add_deferred_loading, add_immediate_loading, clear_deferred_loading) do not clear that cache. This allows callers that read the cached mapping to observe stale/inconsistent loaded-field information after changes to deferred/immediate loading. (See django/db/models/sql/query.py: get_loaded_field_names caches in _loaded_field_names_cache; clear/add methods mutate deferred_loading but do not delete this cache variable.)

5) Correct (diagnostic) representation when immediate-mode becomes empty: logically, when an immediate-mode 'only' set is emptied by a subsequent defer(...) call, the query's state must nonetheless represent the intended restriction explicitly (so it is not mistaken for "no restriction"). For the base-model case this explicit representation is the deferred set of all non-primary-key concrete fields, e.g. deferred_fields = { f.name for f in opts.concrete_fields if not f.primary_key } stored as (frozenset(deferred_fields), True), which encodes "defer all non-PK fields" (so only the PK will be loaded). For immediate entries that include related-path names (using LOOKUP_SEP), the equivalent deferred set must include matching prefixed names for the related models (e.g. 'rel__<field>') so deferred_to_data/get_loaded_field_names can interpret them correctly.

Locations implicated with equal weight: django/db/models/sql/query.py::Query.deferred_loading (representation/default), Query.add_deferred_loading, Query.add_immediate_loading, Query.clear_deferred_loading, Query.deferred_to_data, and Query.get_loaded_field_names (caching).
StepsToReproduce: Define a simple Company model with fields: id (pk), name, trade_number, country.
Run: Company.objects.only('name').defer('name') and inspect the generated SQL (e.g., via str(queryset.query) or connection queries).
Run: Company.objects.only('name').defer('name').defer('country') and inspect the generated SQL.
Run: Company.objects.only('name', 'country').defer('name') and inspect the generated SQL.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When only('name') is followed by defer('name') (or defer('name') and defer('country')), the QuerySet should enforce the intended restrictions: only the primary key column should be selected (i.e. SELECT "company"."id" FROM "company"). When only('name', 'country').defer('name') is used, only 'id' and 'country' should be selected.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: In the failing cases Company.objects.only('name').defer('name') and Company.objects.only('name').defer('name').defer('country'), the ORM generates a SQL SELECT that includes all fields: SELECT "company"."id", "company"."name", "company"."trade_number", "company"."country" FROM "company" — i.e. the 'only' restriction is lost and all columns are loaded.

RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT = 'self'


def resolve_relation(scope_model, relation):
    """
    Transform relation into a model or fully-qualified model string of the form
    "app_label.ModelName", relative to scope_model.

    The relation argument can be:
      * RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT, i.e. the string "self", in which case
        the model argument will be returned.
      * A bare model name without an app_label, in which case scope_model's
        app_label will be prepended.
      * An "app_label.ModelName" string.
      * A model class, which will be returned unchanged.
    """
    # Check for recursive relations
    if relation == RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT:
        relation = scope_model

    # Look for an "app.Model" relation
    if isinstance(relation, str):
        if "." not in relation:
            relation = "%s.%s" % (scope_model._meta.app_label, relation)

    return relation


def lazy_related_operation(function, model, *related_models, **kwargs):
    """
    Schedule `function` to be called once `model` and all `related_models`
    have been imported and registered with the app registry. `function` will
    be called with the newly-loaded model classes as its positional arguments,
    plus any optional keyword arguments.

    The `model` argument must be a model class. Each subsequent positional
    argument is another model, or a reference to another model - see
    `resolve_relation()` for the various forms these may take. Any relative
    references will be resolved relative to `model`.

    This is a convenience wrapper for `Apps.lazy_model_operation` - the app
    registry model used is the one found in `model._meta.apps`.
    """
    models = [model] + [resolve_relation(model, rel) for rel in related_models]
    model_keys = (make_model_tuple(m) for m in models)
    apps = model._meta.apps
    return apps.lazy_model_operation(partial(function, **kwargs), *model_keys)


class RelatedField(FieldCacheMixin, Field):
    """Base class that all relational fields inherit from."""

    # Field flags
    one_to_many = False
    one_to_one = False
    many_to_many = False

        related_name=None,
        related_query_name=None,
        limit_choices_to=None,

        apps.check_models_ready()

            *super().check(**kwargs),
            *self._check_related_name_is_valid(),
            *self._check_related_query_name_is_valid(),
            *self._check_relation_model_exists(),
            *self._check_referencing_to_swapped_model(),
            *self._check_clashes(),

    def _check_related_name_is_valid(self):
        import keyword
        related_name = self.remote_field.related_name
        if related_name is None:
            return []
        is_valid_id = not keyword.iskeyword(related_name) and related_name.isidentifier()
        if not (is_valid_id or related_name.endswith('+')):
            return [
                checks.Error(
                    "The name '%s' is invalid related_name for field %s.%s" %
                    (self.remote_field.related_name, self.model._meta.object_name,
                     self.name),
                    hint="Related name must be a valid Python identifier or end with a '+'",
                    obj=self,
                    id='fields.E306',
                )
            ]
        return []

    def _check_related_query_name_is_valid(self):
        if self.remote_field.is_hidden():
            return []
        rel_query_name = self.related_query_name()
        errors = []
        if rel_query_name.endswith('_'):
            errors.append(
                checks.Error(
                    "Reverse query name '%s' must not end with an underscore."
                    % rel_query_name,
                    hint=("Add or change a related_name or related_query_name "
                          "argument for this field."),
                    obj=self,
                    id='fields.E308',
                )
            )
        if LOOKUP_SEP in rel_query_name:
            errors.append(
                checks.Error(
                    "Reverse query name '%s' must not contain '%s'."
                    % (rel_query_name, LOOKUP_SEP),
                    hint=("Add or change a related_name or related_query_name "

                    id='fields.E309',

        # are:

        #         model = models.IntegerField()
        #         model_set = models.IntegerField()

                qn(self.parent_alias),
                qn2(lhs_col),

Root cause

The code relies on relation objects being hashable (ForeignObjectRel.__hash__ calls hash(self.identity)), so when through_fields is a list hash() raised TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'.
- The correct pattern (as used in ForeignObjectRel.identity for limit_choices_to) is to call make_hashable(...) to normalize dicts/lists/tuples into a hashable canonical form.

bug_report.Title: Missing make_hashable on through_fields in ManyToManyRel causes TypeError during model checks
bug_report.Description: When a ManyToManyField is defined with through_fields provided as a list, Django's model checks can raise TypeError: 'unhashable type: "list"'. ManyToManyRel.identity currently places the through_fields attribute directly into the identity tuple; if through_fields is a list (an unhashable iterable), hashing the relation later (ForeignObjectRel.__hash__ calls hash(self.identity)) raises TypeError.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/models/fields/reverse_related.py :: ManyToManyRel.identity: this identity property builds the relation identity as super().identity + (self.through, self.through_fields, self.db_constraint) (lines 309–315). It appends self.through_fields directly, which can be a list (unhashable), so the identity tuple can contain an unhashable element.

2) django/db/models/fields/reverse_related.py :: ForeignObjectRel.__hash__: this method returns hash(self.identity) (lines 138–139). It encodes the assumption that every element of identity is hashable. Because ManyToManyRel.identity can include an unhashable list, calling hash(self.identity) raises TypeError. The correct relationship is that identity must contain hashable representations of its elements (the code already uses make_hashable for limit_choices_to in ForeignObjectRel.identity — see lines 120–126).

3) django/db/models/base.py :: ModelBase._check_m2m_through_same_relationship: this model-check constructs a signature tuple that includes f.remote_field.through_fields directly (line 1408). While this code stores signatures in a list and does not hash them, placing through_fields into canonical/comparable representations is necessary for robust equality comparisons when through_fields may be provided as a list vs a tuple.

4) django/db/migrations/utils.py :: field_references: this function returns references_through = (remote_field, through_fields) when appropriate (lines 85–95), propagating through_fields' raw representation into returned structures. Although this code uses iterable membership checks (reference_field_name in through_fields) and won't itself raise when through_fields is a list, it follows the same pattern of not canonicalizing through_fields when embedding it into tuple structures.
StepsToReproduce: Create a Django app and add these models to models.py:
class Parent(models.Model):
name = models.CharField(max_length=256)
class ProxyParent(Parent):
class Meta:
proxy = True
class Child(models.Model):
parent = models.ForeignKey(Parent, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
many_to_many_field = models.ManyToManyField(
to=Parent,
through='ManyToManyModel',
through_fields=['child', 'parent'],
related_name='something'
class ManyToManyModel(models.Model):
parent = models.ForeignKey(Parent, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='+')
child = models.ForeignKey(Child, on_delete=models.CASCADE, related_name='+')
second_child = models.ForeignKey(Child, on_delete=models.CASCADE, null=True, default=None)
Run Django's model checks (for example: python manage.py check or start the project so checks run).
Observe a traceback terminating with TypeError: unhashable type: 'list'.

RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT = 'self'


def resolve_relation(scope_model, relation):
    """
    Transform relation into a model or fully-qualified model string of the form
    "app_label.ModelName", relative to scope_model.

    The relation argument can be:
      * RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT, i.e. the string "self", in which case
        the model argument will be returned.
      * A bare model name without an app_label, in which case scope_model's
        app_label will be prepended.
      * An "app_label.ModelName" string.
      * A model class, which will be returned unchanged.
    """
    # Check for recursive relations
    if relation == RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT:
        relation = scope_model

    # Look for an "app.Model" relation
    if isinstance(relation, str):
        if "." not in relation:
            relation = "%s.%s" % (scope_model._meta.app_label, relation)

    return relation


def lazy_related_operation(function, model, *related_models, **kwargs):
    """
    Schedule `function` to be called once `model` and all `related_models`
    have been imported and registered with the app registry. `function` will
    be called with the newly-loaded model classes as its positional arguments,
    plus any optional keyword arguments.

    The `model` argument must be a model class. Each subsequent positional
    argument is another model, or a reference to another model - see
    `resolve_relation()` for the various forms these may take. Any relative
    references will be resolved relative to `model`.

    This is a convenience wrapper for `Apps.lazy_model_operation` - the app
    registry model used is the one found in `model._meta.apps`.
    """
    models = [model] + [resolve_relation(model, rel) for rel in related_models]
    model_keys = (make_model_tuple(m) for m in models)
    apps = model._meta.apps
    return apps.lazy_model_operation(partial(function, **kwargs), *model_keys)

class ManyToManyDescriptor(ReverseManyToOneDescriptor):
    """
    Accessor to the related objects manager on the forward and reverse sides of
    a many-to-many relation.

    In the example::

        class Pizza(Model):
            toppings = ManyToManyField(Topping, related_name='pizzas')

    ``Pizza.toppings`` and ``Topping.pizzas`` are ``ManyToManyDescriptor``
    instances.

    Most of the implementation is delegated to a dynamically defined manager
    class built by ``create_forward_many_to_many_manager()`` defined below.
    """

    def __init__(self, rel, reverse=False):
        super().__init__(rel)

        self.reverse = reverse

    @property
    def through(self):
        # through is provided so that you have easy access to the through
        # model (Book.authors.through) for inlines, etc. This is done as
        # a property to ensure that the fully resolved value is returned.
        return self.rel.through

    @cached_property
    def related_manager_cls(self):
        related_model = self.rel.related_model if self.reverse else self.rel.model

        return create_forward_many_to_many_manager(
            related_model._default_manager.__class__,
            self.rel,
            reverse=self.reverse,
        )

    def _get_set_deprecation_msg_params(self):
        return (
            '%s side of a many-to-many set' % ('reverse' if self.reverse else 'forward'),
            self.rel.get_accessor_name() if self.reverse else self.field.name,
        )


def create_forward_many_to_many_manager(superclass, rel, reverse):
    """
    Create a manager for the either side of a many-to-many relation.

    This manager subclasses another manager, generally the default manager of
    the related model, and adds behaviors specific to many-to-many relations.
    """

    class ManyRelatedManager(superclass):
        def __init__(self, instance=None):
            super().__init__()

            self.instance = instance

            if not reverse:
                self.model = rel.model
                self.query_field_name = rel.field.related_query_name()
                self.prefetch_cache_name = rel.field.name
                self.source_field_name = rel.field.m2m_field_name()
                self.target_field_name = rel.field.m2m_reverse_field_name()
                self.symmetrical = rel.symmetrical
            else:
                self.model = rel.related_model
                self.query_field_name = rel.field.name
                self.prefetch_cache_name = rel.field.related_query_name()
                self.source_field_name = rel.field.m2m_reverse_field_name()
                self.target_field_name = rel.field.m2m_field_name()
                self.symmetrical = False

            self.through = rel.through
            self.reverse = reverse

            self.source_field = self.through._meta.get_field(self.source_field_name)
            self.target_field = self.through._meta.get_field(self.target_field_name)

            self.core_filters = {}
            self.pk_field_names = {}
            for lh_field, rh_field in self.source_field.related_fields:
                core_filter_key = '%s__%s' % (self.query_field_name, rh_field.name)
                self.core_filters[core_filter_key] = getattr(instance, rh_field.attname)
                self.pk_field_names[lh_field.name] = rh_field.name

            self.related_val = self.source_field.get_foreign_related_value(instance)
            if None in self.related_val:
                raise ValueError('"%r" needs to have a value for field "%s" before '
                                 'this many-to-many relationship can be used.' %
                                 (instance, self.pk_field_names[self.source_field_name]))
            # Even if this relation is not to pk, we require still pk value.
            # The wish is that the instance has been already saved to DB,
            # although having a pk value isn't a guarantee of that.
            if instance.pk is None:
                raise ValueError("%r instance needs to have a primary key value before "
                                 "a many-to-many relationship can be used." %
                                 instance.__class__.__name__)

        def __call__(self, *, manager):
            manager = getattr(self.model, manager)
            manager_class = create_forward_many_to_many_manager(manager.__class__, rel, reverse)
            return manager_class(instance=self.instance)
        do_not_call_in_templates = True

        def _build_remove_filters(self, removed_vals):
            filters = Q((self.source_field_name, self.related_val))
            # No need to add a subquery condition if removed_vals is a QuerySet without
            # filters.
            removed_vals_filters = (not isinstance(removed_vals, QuerySet) or
                                    removed_vals._has_filters())
            if removed_vals_filters:
                filters &= Q((f'{self.target_field_name}__in', removed_vals))
            if self.symmetrical:
                symmetrical_filters = Q((self.target_field_name, self.related_val))
                if removed_vals_filters:
                    symmetrical_filters &= Q((f'{self.source_field_name}__in', removed_vals))
                filters |= symmetrical_filters
            return filters

        def _apply_rel_filters(self, queryset):
            """
            Filter the queryset for the instance this manager is bound to.
            """
            queryset._add_hints(instance=self.instance)
            if self._db:
                queryset = queryset.using(self._db)
            queryset._defer_next_filter = True
            return queryset._next_is_sticky().filter(**self.core_filters)

        def _remove_prefetched_objects(self):
            try:
                self.instance._prefetched_objects_cache.pop(self.prefetch_cache_name)
            except (AttributeError, KeyError):
                pass  # nothing to clear from cache

        def get_queryset(self):
            try:
                return self.instance._prefetched_objects_cache[self.prefetch_cache_name]
            except (AttributeError, KeyError):
                queryset = super().get_queryset()
                return self._apply_rel_filters(queryset)

        def get_prefetch_queryset(self, instances, queryset=None):
            if queryset is None:
                queryset = super().get_queryset()

            queryset._add_hints(instance=instances[0])
            queryset = queryset.using(queryset._db or self._db)

            query = {'%s__in' % self.query_field_name: instances}
            queryset = queryset._next_is_sticky().filter(**query)

            # M2M: need to annotate the query in order to get the primary model
            # that the secondary model was actually related to. We know that
            # there will already be a join on the join table, so we can just add
            # the select.

            # For non-autocreated 'through' models, can't assume we are
            # dealing with PK values.
            fk = self.through._meta.get_field(self.source_field_name)
            join_table = fk.model._meta.db_table
            connection = connections[queryset.db]
            qn = connection.ops.quote_name
            queryset = queryset.extra(select={
                '_prefetch_related_val_%s' % f.attname:
                '%s.%s' % (qn(join_table), qn(f.column)) for f in fk.local_related_fields})
            return (
                queryset,
                lambda result: tuple(
                    getattr(result, '_prefetch_related_val_%s' % f.attname)
                    for f in fk.local_related_fields
                ),
                lambda inst: tuple(
                    f.get_db_prep_value(getattr(inst, f.attname), connection)
                    for f in fk.foreign_related_fields

                False,
                self.prefetch_cache_name,
                False,

        def add(self, *objs, through_defaults=None):
            self._remove_prefetched_objects()
            db = router.db_for_write(self.through, instance=self.instance)
            with transaction.atomic(using=db, savepoint=False):
                self._add_items(
                    self.source_field_name, self.target_field_name, *objs,
                    through_defaults=through_defaults,
                )
                # If this is a symmetrical m2m relation to self, add the mirror
                # entry in the m2m table.
                if self.symmetrical:
                    self._add_items(
                        self.target_field_name,
                        self.source_field_name,
                        *objs,
                        through_defaults=through_defaults,
                    )
        add.alters_data = True

        def remove(self, *objs):
            self._remove_prefetched_objects()
            self._remove_items(self.source_field_name, self.target_field_name, *objs)
        remove.alters_data = True

        def clear(self):
            db = router.db_for_write(self.through, instance=self.instance)
            with transaction.atomic(using=db, savepoint=False):

                    sender=self.through, action="pre_clear",
                    instance=self.instance, reverse=self.reverse,
                    model=self.model, pk_set=None, using=db,
                )
                self._remove_prefetched_objects()
                filters = self._build_remove_filters(super().get_queryset().using(db))
                self.through._default_manager.using(db).filter(filters).delete()

Checkpoint 5 — Final report (root cause and complete fix)

Root cause
- A symmetrical ManyToManyField that is self-referential (to='self' or resolved to same model) does not create a reverse accessor. Currently, a developer can still pass related_name (or related_query_name) for that field; that explicitly provided related_name is meaningless because the reverse accessor is omitted. The code partly hides this fact by auto-generating an internal related_name (used internally) during contribute_to_class, which may silently overwrite or ignore the explicit related_name and confuse developers. There is no system check warning/error to inform the developer that their related_name will be ignored in this exact scenario.

Every location that needs to change (and what to change)

1) Primary change: django/db/models/fields/related.py — ManyToManyField
- Add new method:

    def _check_related_name_for_symmetrical(self, from_model=None, **kwargs):
        """
        Raise an error if a related_name was explicitly supplied for a
        symmetrical ManyToManyField that points to the same model (self).
        """
        if not self.remote_field.symmetrical or from_model is None:
            return []
        to_model = resolve_relation(from_model, self.remote_field.model)
        if to_model == from_model and self._related_name is not None:
            return [
                checks.Error(
                    "Do not set a related_name on a symmetrical ManyToManyField to 'self'.",
                    hint=(
                        "Symmetrical ManyToManyField relations to 'self' do not create a reverse "
                        "accessor; remove the related_name argument for this field."
                    ),
                    obj=self,
                    id='fields.E341',
                )
            ]
        return []

- Modify ManyToManyField.check to include the new check (add the call to our method right after super().check):

    def check(self, **kwargs):
        return [
            *super().check(**kwargs),
            *self._check_related_name_for_symmetrical(**kwargs),
            *self._check_unique(**kwargs),
            *self._check_relationship_model(**kwargs),
            *self._check_ignored_options(**kwargs),
            *self._check_table_uniqueness(**kwargs),
        ]

Why this is complete:
- This check covers the situation in which the model relationship is resolved to the same model (self), and symmetrical is True. It also respects abstract/unresolved contexts (from_model None) by skipping the check there, allowing patterns used in abstract models and migrations.
- The check accounts for developer-supplied related_name only (self._related_name is not None). Implicit related_name behavior and internally-generated names remain unaffected.

2) No other code locations need to be changed
- contribute_to_class behavior that auto-generates internal related_name for symmetrical self relations remains correct: internal code still needs such names for Django internals and clash avoidance; we don't want to disrupt that.
- ManyToManyRel.get_accessor_name is the canonical place that decides absence of reverse accessor, and it uses symmetrical and model equality to decide that; it should not be changed.
- No changes required in related_descriptors or reverse_related.

Hardcoded values that need to become dynamic
- No hardcoded constants needed to change. The constants involved (RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT = 'self', '+' sentinel for hidden related names, the internal name formatting) encode valid concepts that remain correct. The fix is a validation only, not a rewrite of the relationship semantics.

Any methods that need to be added or overridden
- Added: ManyToManyField._check_related_name_for_symmetrical
- No additional parent-method overrides needed.

Additional notes & rationale for design choices
- The check runs only when from_model is known. That ensures code paths where the field is defined on an abstract model or where the model hasn't been resolved yet (e.g., during some import-time operations) are not incorrectly flagged.
- The check triggers only if the developer explicitly supplied related_name (self._related_name is not None). If they did not supply related_name, Django will continue to generate an internal name for symmetry/self relations. This preserves internal behavior but surfaces any confusing explicit configuration early.
- The error message and hint follow the style of other field checks in the file: concise message and brief hint with id 'fields.E341'. We validated there is no collision in the repository for 'fields.E341'.

Suggested test cases to add (not strictly required by this report but recommended)
- Test that a model defined with ManyToManyField('self', symmetrical=True, related_name='something') fails Model.check() with id 'fields.E341'. Use isolate_apps to define a temporary model and assert expected Error.
- Test that the same field defined on an abstract model (in an abstract base class) does NOT raise during that stage (Model.check called without from_model) — i.e., the check is skipped if from_model is None.
- Test that ManyToManyField('self', symmetrical=True, without related_name) still passes and continue to generate internal related_name.

Why this fix is safe / minimal impact
- It's a system check only — it doesn't change runtime semantics, only surfaces an error when the user does something that has no effect. It avoids surprising silent overwriting of the user input.
- It preserves current internal naming, preserves behavior for abstract models, and only acts in the scenario where the relation is self and symmetrical.

bug_report.Title: Raise error when related_name is provided on symmetrical self ManyToManyField
bug_report.Description: When a ManyToManyField is symmetrical and self-referential (to='self' or resolves to the same model), Django intentionally does not create a reverse accessor. A developer can still pass a related_name for such a field; that explicit related_name is ineffective because no reverse accessor is created and Django may instead generate an internal related_name for its own bookkeeping. This causes confusion because the developer-provided related_name has no user-visible effect.
bug_report.RootCause: 1) The reverse-rel logic omits the reverse accessor for symmetrical many-to-many relations that point to the same model: ManyToManyRel.get_accessor_name() returns None when rel.symmetrical is True and the model equals rel.model (reverse_related.py, lines ~189-192). 2) ManyToManyField.contribute_to_class() unconditionally sets an internal related_name for symmetrical self relations (for internal bookkeeping) by assigning self.remote_field.related_name = "%s_rel_+" when self.remote_field.symmetrical and the relation points to the declaring class or to RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT (related.py, lines ~1628-1639). This assignment overwrites the rel object's related_name used for accessor lookup and therefore renders any developer-supplied related_name ineffective for producing a reverse accessor. 3) ManyToManyField.__init__ defaults symmetrical to True when the field's 'to' argument is the string 'self' (RECURSIVE_RELATIONSHIP_CONSTANT), so this behavior is triggered automatically for self-referential many-to-many fields (related.py, lines ~1180-1182). 4) There is no current system check in ManyToManyField.check() that warns or errors when a developer explicitly supplies related_name in this exact scenario; ManyToManyField.check() does not contain a validation that flags an explicit related_name on a symmetrical self relation (related.py, lines ~1210-1216). Therefore, an explicit related_name may be silently ignored/overwritten while the framework still accepts it, producing confusing developer-visible behavior.
StepsToReproduce: 1) Define a Django model with a field: friends = models.ManyToManyField('self', symmetrical=True, related_name='my_friends')
2) Run system checks (e.g., ./manage.py check) or call Model.check() for that model.
3) Observe that the related_name does not produce a reverse accessor (no attribute on the related model), and no system check currently warns that the supplied related_name will have no effect.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When a developer explicitly sets related_name on a symmetrical ManyToManyField that is self-referential (to='self' or resolved to the same model), the system checks should inform the developer that no reverse accessor will be created and that supplying related_name in this context is meaningless. This check should run only when the model that owns the field is known (to avoid false positives for abstract or unresolved models).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Django currently does not create a reverse accessor for symmetrical self ManyToManyField (ManyToManyRel.get_accessor_name returns None). A developer can still specify related_name; contribute_to_class may overwrite the relation's related_name with an internally generated name ("%s_rel_+"), and no system check warns the developer that the provided related_name will have no effect.

from django.urls import reverse, reverse_lazy

from .admin import AnswerAdmin, QuestionAdmin
from .models import (
    Answer, Author, Authorship, Bonus, Book, Employee, Manager, Parent,
    PKChild, Question, Toy, WorkHour,
)
from .tests import AdminViewBasicTestCase

PAGINATOR_SIZE = AutocompleteJsonView.paginate_by


class AuthorAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    ordering = ['id']
    search_fields = ['id']


class AuthorshipInline(admin.TabularInline):
    model = Authorship
    autocomplete_fields = ['author']


class BookAdmin(admin.ModelAdmin):
    inlines = [AuthorshipInline]


site = admin.AdminSite(name='autocomplete_admin')
site.register(Question, QuestionAdmin)
site.register(Answer, AnswerAdmin)
site.register(Author, AuthorAdmin)
site.register(Book, BookAdmin)
site.register(Employee, search_fields=['name'])
site.register(WorkHour, autocomplete_fields=['employee'])
site.register(Manager, search_fields=['name'])
site.register(Bonus, autocomplete_fields=['recipient'])
site.register(PKChild, search_fields=['name'])
site.register(Toy, autocomplete_fields=['child'])


@contextmanager
def model_admin(model, model_admin, admin_site=site):
    org_admin = admin_site._registry.get(model)
    if org_admin:
        admin_site.unregister(model)
    admin_site.register(model, model_admin)
    try:
        yield
    finally:
        if org_admin:
            admin_site._registry[model] = org_admin


class AutocompleteJsonViewTests(AdminViewBasicTestCase):

    @contextmanager
    def select2_ajax_wait(self, timeout=10):
        from selenium.common.exceptions import NoSuchElementException
        from selenium.webdriver.support import expected_conditions as ec
        yield
        with self.disable_implicit_wait():
            try:
                loading_element = self.selenium.find_element_by_css_selector(
                    'li.select2-results__option.loading-results'
                )
            except NoSuchElementException:
                pass
            else:
                self.wait_until(ec.staleness_of(loading_element), timeout=timeout)

    def test_select(self):
        from selenium.webdriver.common.keys import Keys
        from selenium.webdriver.support.ui import Select
        self.selenium.get(self.live_server_url + reverse('autocomplete_admin:admin_views_answer_add'))
        elem = self.selenium.find_element_by_css_selector('.select2-selection')
        elem.click()  # Open the autocomplete dropdown.
        results = self.selenium.find_element_by_css_selector('.select2-results')
        self.assertTrue(results.is_displayed())
        option = self.selenium.find_element_by_css_selector('.select2-results__option')
        self.assertEqual(option.text, 'No results found')
        elem.click()  # Close the autocomplete dropdown.
        q1 = Question.objects.create(question='Who am I?')
        Question.objects.bulk_create(Question(question=str(i)) for i in range(PAGINATOR_SIZE + 10))
        elem.click()  # Reopen the dropdown now that some objects exist.
        result_container = self.selenium.find_element_by_css_selector('.select2-results')
        self.assertTrue(result_container.is_displayed())
        results = result_container.find_elements_by_css_selector('.select2-results__option')
        # PAGINATOR_SIZE results and "Loading more results".
        self.assertEqual(len(results), PAGINATOR_SIZE + 1)
        search = self.selenium.find_element_by_css_selector('.select2-search__field')
        # Load next page of results by scrolling to the bottom of the list.
        with self.select2_ajax_wait():
            for _ in range(len(results)):
                search.send_keys(Keys.ARROW_DOWN)
        results = result_container.find_elements_by_css_selector('.select2-results__option')
        # All objects are now loaded.
        self.assertEqual(len(results), PAGINATOR_SIZE + 11)
        # Limit the results with the search field.
        with self.select2_ajax_wait():
            search.send_keys('Who')
            # Ajax request is delayed.
            self.assertTrue(result_container.is_displayed())
            results = result_container.find_elements_by_css_selector('.select2-results__option')
            self.assertEqual(len(results), PAGINATOR_SIZE + 12)
        self.assertTrue(result_container.is_displayed())
        results = result_container.find_elements_by_css_selector('.select2-results__option')
        self.assertEqual(len(results), 1)
        # Select the result.
        search.send_keys(Keys.RETURN)
        select = Select(self.selenium.find_element_by_id('id_question'))
        self.assertEqual(select.first_selected_option.get_attribute('value'), str(q1.pk))

Proposed change (high level)
- Add a small, documented extension point to AutocompleteJsonView so subclasses can extend the per-result JSON structure without overriding get() entirely:
  - Add a method serialize_result(self, obj, to_field_name) that returns the dict for a single object.
  - Change AutocompleteJsonView.get() to call self.serialize_result for each object in context['object_list'] when building the 'results' list.
  - (Implementation must preserve existing behavior by default — returning exactly {'id': ..., 'text': ...}.)
  - Also set instance attribute self.to_field_name when process_request computes it so serialize_result can use instance state if desired.

Concrete patch (file django/contrib/admin/views/autocomplete.py)
- Replace (roughly):

    def get(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
        self.term, self.model_admin, self.source_field, to_field_name = self.process_request(request)
        ...
        context = self.get_context_data()
        return JsonResponse({
            'results': [
                {'id': str(getattr(obj, to_field_name)), 'text': str(obj)}
                for obj in context['object_list']
            ],
            'pagination': {'more': context['page_obj'].has_next()},
        })

- With:

    def get(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
        self.term, self.model_admin, self.source_field, to_field_name = self.process_request(request)
        # expose to_field_name as instance attribute so serialize_result can access it
        self.to_field_name = to_field_name

        if not self.has_perm(request):
            raise PermissionDenied

        self.object_list = self.get_queryset()
        context = self.get_context_data()
        return JsonResponse({
            'results': [self.serialize_result(obj, to_field_name) for obj in context['object_list']],
            'pagination': {'more': context['page_obj'].has_next()},
        })

    def serialize_result(self, obj, to_field_name):
        """
        Return a dict for an individual autocomplete result.

        Subclasses may override this method to add extra keys to each result
        without overriding the whole get() method. The default implementation
        preserves the existing behavior: it returns {'id': ..., 'text': ...}.
        """
        return {'id': str(getattr(obj, to_field_name)), 'text': str(obj)}

- Also (optionally) set self.to_field_name inside process_request before returning, i.e. after computing to_field_name do self.to_field_name = to_field_name. The get above will still set it; either approach is fine — setting it in process_request is slightly cleaner.

Why this fix?
- The bug report's issue: callers cannot add extra fields to each result without overriding the entire get() method (brittle relative to upstream changes). Adding serialize_result provides a minimal, local extension point.

Root cause
- AutocompleteJsonView had no small extension point for per-item JSON serialization; the get() method built each result dict inline (only 'id' and 'text'), forcing callers who wanted extra fields to override the whole get() method. This is brittle — any upstream changes to get() would need to be merged into downstream overrides.

Complete set of changes required
1) Primary change: Add serialize_result method and delegate per-item JSON creation in AutocompleteJsonView.get().

File to change:
- django/contrib/admin/views/autocomplete.py

Current code excerpt (relevant lines):
- paginate_by = 20
- get(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
    self.term, self.model_admin, self.source_field, to_field_name = self.process_request(request)
    if not self.has_perm(request):
        raise PermissionDenied
    self.object_list = self.get_queryset()
    context = self.get_context_data()
    return JsonResponse({
        'results': [
            {'id': str(getattr(obj, to_field_name)), 'text': str(obj)}

  - (B) set self.to_field_name in get (immediately after process_request) and pass to serialize_result as argument

I recommend setting self.to_field_name in process_request (adds instance attribute earlier) and implementing serialize_result as follows.

Suggested final code (concise patch description — insert this in django/contrib/admin/views/autocomplete.py):

- Add new method after process_request or after get_paginator:

        """
        Return a dict representing a single autocomplete result.

        Subclasses can override this hook to add more keys to the result dict
        (for example, 'description' or 'image'). The default implementation
        preserves the existing format used by select2: {'id': <str>, 'text': <str>}.
        """
        return {'id': str(getattr(obj, to_field_name)), 'text': str(obj)}

- Modify process_request to set self.to_field_name just before returning (e.g., right before the return line):

    to_field_name = remote_model._meta.get_field(to_field_name).attname
    if not model_admin.to_field_allowed(request, to_field_name):
        raise PermissionDenied

    # new:
    self.to_field_name = to_field_name

    return term, model_admin, source_field, to_field_name

- Modify get as described (use serialize_result):

    def get(self, request, *args, **kwargs):
        self.term, self.model_admin, self.source_field, to_field_name = self.process_request(request)

- Only django/contrib/admin/views/autocomplete.py needs to be changed for the extension point to exist and to be used by get().
- process_request optional additional assignment to self.to_field_name is a small, safe change to expose the to_field_name for any subclass methods that prefer to access it via instance attribute rather than having to accept it as parameter.

Why this is a complete fix
- It preserves the exact existing JSON output by default.
- Subclasses can now override serialize_result to add extra keys without overriding get() and still benefit from upstream changes to get() (pagination, permission logic, query building).
- It avoids touching client code (widgets) or ModelAdmin, AdminSite, or select2 translation constants; those are unaffected by adding result keys: select2 can ignore or accept extra fields.

bug_report.Title: Refactor AutocompleteJsonView to support extra fields in autocomplete response
bug_report.Description: Admin autocomplete JSON responses are built inline inside AutocompleteJsonView.get(), producing per-result dicts that only include the 'id' and 'text' keys. There is no small extension point to add extra per-result fields, which forces callers to override the entire get() method to include additional data and increases maintenance burden.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Missing per-item serialization hook (django/contrib/admin/views/autocomplete.py): AutocompleteJsonView.get() constructs the results inline with a list comprehension and returns that JSON directly. Concrete code excerpt (get()):
    self.term, self.model_admin, self.source_field, to_field_name = self.process_request(request)
    ...
    return JsonResponse({
        'results': [
            {'id': str(getattr(obj, to_field_name)), 'text': str(obj)}
            for obj in context['object_list']
        ],
        'pagination': {'more': context['page_obj'].has_next()},
    })
This encodes an assumption that per-item JSON can only consist of the two keys 'id' and 'text' produced inline, leaving callers with the only option of overriding get() to add extra fields.

2) Local-only to_field_name (django/contrib/admin/views/autocomplete.py): process_request() resolves the to_field_name and returns it to the caller rather than exposing it as a view instance attribute. Code excerpt (process_request() return):
    to_field_name = getattr(source_field.remote_field, 'field_name', remote_model._meta.pk.attname)
    to_field_name = remote_model._meta.get_field(to_field_name).attname
    if not model_admin.to_field_allowed(request, to_field_name):
        raise PermissionDenied
    return term, model_admin, source_field, to_field_name
Because to_field_name is only returned and assigned to a local variable in get(), small per-item hooks (if added externally) cannot access the resolved attname via the view instance without being passed the local variable; this makes writing compact hooks awkward.

3) Current result format and pagination contract encoded in get() (django/contrib/admin/views/autocomplete.py): each result dict is built as id = str(getattr(obj, to_field_name)) and text = str(obj); pagination is returned as {'pagination': {'more': context['page_obj'].has_next()}}. Tests and client-side code rely on this exact default shape. The investigation identified the minimal extension relationship (diagnostic): delegate per-item serialization to an overrideable method serialize_result(self, obj, to_field_name) whose default behavior preserves the existing format by returning exactly:
    {'id': str(getattr(obj, to_field_name)), 'text': str(obj)}
When an extension point is introduced, the default must preserve the current id/text string semantics and the pagination contract so existing consumer code (tests and client widget) continues to work unchanged.
StepsToReproduce: In a Django project with the admin enabled, register a ModelAdmin that exposes an autocomplete field (via ModelAdmin.autocomplete_fields) for a ForeignKey/ManyToMany relation.
Attempt to include an additional attribute (for example, obj.notes) in each autocomplete JSON result without overriding the whole view (i.e., look for a small hook to alter per-result dicts).

Observe that AutocompleteJsonView currently builds the results inline in get() and there is no small per-item hook; adding extra fields currently requires subclassing AutocompleteJsonView and overriding get(), duplicating the inline list comprehension and pagination handling.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: There is a documented, overrideable extension point for per-result serialization on the autocomplete JSON view so callers can add extra keys to each result without overriding the whole get() method. The default behavior of the view remains unchanged for existing callers: each result contains 'id' and 'text' using the same semantics as today, and pagination is reported with the same 'pagination': {'more': ...} contract.

Summary of findings (quick):
- Root cause: _multi_decorate passes a functools.partial (bound_method) to function decorators. Many decorators (or decorators that call functools.wraps) expect a function-like object with attributes like __name__, __module__, __doc__, etc. functools.partial objects do not expose these attributes directly, so decorators that do attribute access (e.g., wrapppers using @wraps(func)) raise AttributeError when the decorated object is a partial.
- Fix: instead of passing a partial object, create a real function wrapper for the bound method and copy the original method's attributes onto that wrapper (via update_wrapper). Then pass that wrapper to decorators. This preserves function attributes for decorators that try to access them (including wraps()) and keeps existing behavior where decorator-added attributes are copied onto the returned _wrapper via _update_method_wrapper.

Checkpoint 4 — Propose a fix, then immediately challenge it

Proposed fix (code change)
- File to change: django/utils/decorators.py
- Function to change: _multi_decorate
- Replace the creation of bound_method as a partial with a real function wrapper that:
  - Captures the bound callable (via method.__get__(self, type(self)))
  - Defines a local function (callable) that calls the bound callable with the arguments
  - Uses update_wrapper(bound_function, method) to copy method attributes onto the bound_function (so decorators that access __name__/__module__/__doc__ succeed).
- Then apply the decorators to that bound_function just like before.

Exact patch (conceptual; exact diff):
Replace this block in _multi_decorate (lines ~35–43):
    bound_method = partial(method.__get__(self, type(self)))
    for dec in decorators:
        bound_method = dec(bound_method)
    return bound_method(*args, **kwargs)

with this code:
    bound = method.__get__(self, type(self))
    def bound_method(*f_args, **f_kwargs):
        return bound(*f_args, **f_kwargs)
    # Copy the original method's attributes to bound_method so decorators
    # (especially ones using functools.wraps) can access function metadata.
    update_wrapper(bound_method, method)
    for dec in decorators:
        bound_method = dec(bound_method)
    return bound_method(*args, **kwargs)

(You can see where to place update_wrapper and the local function inside _multi_decorate.)

Why this fixes the bug:
- bound_method becomes a real function object with __name__, __module__, __doc__, etc., copied from the original method. A decorator that does @wraps(func) where func is bound_method now sees these attributes and will work correctly.
- _update_method_wrapper and update_wrapper(_wrapper, method) remain in place so any attributes a decorator adds (via updating the dummy in _update_method_wrapper) or original method attributes are preserved on the class-level wrapper function returned by _multi_decorate.

Now the “challenge” questions.

4a) "What assumption does my fix change?"
- The current code assumes a functools.partial object is an acceptable proxy for a bound method when passed to function decorators (i.e., decorators won't rely on function attributes of the object passed to them). The fix changes that assumption: decorators may rely on function metadata (e.g., via functools.wraps(func)), so the bound object passed to decorators must be a real function that exposes function attributes.

4b) "What hardcoded values encode this assumption?"
- There are no numeric or positional hardcoded values in the relevant code. The problematic assumption was encoded by using functools.partial (a specific implementation choice). The partial object is the encoding of the assumption "it's fine to pass a callable that isn't a function." Because partial lacks the function metadata, the assumption was wrong. Therefore partial must be replaced with a function wrapper that exposes metadata — i.e., changing a structural choice, not changing numeric constants.

4c) "What about the reverse operation?"
- The reverse/complementary operations are:
  - _update_method_wrapper(_wrapper, dec): it constructs a dummy function, applies dec to it, and copies any attributes the dec added to _wrapper via update_wrapper(_wrapper, dummy). This operation expects that decorators, when applied outside of method context, will add attributes to a function object. After our change, decorators are applied to a real function wrapper (bound_method), so _update_method_wrapper remains valid.
  - update_wrapper(_wrapper, method): this copies original method attributes onto the returned class-level wrapper. After the change, this still does exactly what it did before; we now also call update_wrapper(bound_method, method) so that decorators see function metadata when decorating, while update_wrapper(_wrapper, method) preserves metadata on the returned attribute on the class.
- Concrete trace of complementary methods:
  - Parent/complementary method: _update_method_wrapper (lines 13–19) — reads decorator by applying it to a dummy function and copying attributes from dummy to the class-level _wrapper. This is unchanged and still appropriate.
  - update_wrapper(_wrapper, method) (line 49) — still executes as before; it preserves original method metadata on the class-level wrapper. The new update_wrapper(bound_method, method) only ensures the object passed to dec has metadata so dec's internal use of wraps(func) succeeds.
- Therefore the reverse side (copying attributes from decorator-added dummy and original method onto final wrapper) still works and needs no change beyond adding update_wrapper(bound_method, method) before applying decorators.

4d) "Does every existing method still work?"
- Methods in file:
  - classonlymethod.__get__: unaffected.
  - _update_method_wrapper: unchanged and still correct — it copies decorator-added attributes to the class-level _wrapper.
  - _multi_decorate: changed as described — its other behaviors (ordering of decorators, raising on non-callable attributes, copying decorator attributes to class-level wrapper, preserving method attributes) remain intact.
  - method_decorator: unchanged except it calls _multi_decorate; behavior preserved.
  - make_middleware_decorator and others: unaffected.
- Tests of descriptor behavior:
  - The descriptor test constructs descriptor_wrapper that sets self.__name__ = wrapped.__name__ and returns bound_wrapper(self.wrapped.__get__(instance, cls)). Our code uses method.__get__(self, type(self)) to obtain bound. For descriptor wrapper case, bound will be whatever the descriptor's __get__ returns (bound_wrapper instance). bound_method is a function that calls bound(...). update_wrapper(bound_method, method) copies attributes from 'method' (the descriptor_wrapper instance) to the bound function. The descriptor test had bound_wrapper.__init__ set __name__, but method also had attributes. Because update_wrapper swallows missing attributes gracefully (it only copies those that exist), it should not raise. Tests expecting Test().method(1) == 1 should still pass, since bound_method calls bound (which delegates to the wrapped function).
- I checked the tests that explicitly expect original attributes on Test.method (class attribute) — we still call update_wrapper(_wrapper, method) to preserve __name__ and __doc__ on the returned class attribute.

4e) "Does any NEW method need to be added?"
- No new top-level methods are required.
- However, a new use of update_wrapper(bound_method, method) is required inside _multi_decorate (as shown above). This is not a new function, but a necessary addition to ensure decorators see correct metadata.
- I re-inspected the parent/complementary functions to ensure none of them need overriding; they do not.

Edge cases and rationale:
- Why not simply set attributes on the partial? partial objects are instances of class functools.partial and do not allow setting arbitrary attributes like __name__ — doing so would either fail or not be the proper approach. Creating a real function wrapper is the correct approach because functions allow attaching attributes and have the usual function metadata semantics that functools.wraps expects.
- Why not change _update_method_wrapper to handle this? That function copies decorator-added attributes to _wrapper, but it runs after the decorator is applied. The problem occurs inside the decorator at decoration-time when the decorator (or wraps) inspects the function passed to it. That must be fixed by ensuring the thing passed to the decorator has the required attributes.

    - then apply decorators to bound_method just as before

bug_report.Title: method_decorator passes functools.partial to function decorators, causing AttributeError for missing function attributes
bug_report.Description: When method_decorator is used to adapt a function decorator to an instance method, _multi_decorate constructs and passes a functools.partial object to the function decorator. Decorators that expect a real function (for example, those that call functools.wraps(func) or directly access __name__/__module__/__doc__) raise AttributeError because functools.partial objects do not expose those attributes.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/utils/decorators.py::_multi_decorate constructs the bound callable as a functools.partial via the expression: bound_method = partial(method.__get__(self, type(self))). (See django/utils/decorators.py, line 40.)

2) functools.partial objects do not provide function metadata attributes such as __name__, __module__, and __doc__. Code that reads these attributes (for example, functools.update_wrapper used by functools.wraps) will raise AttributeError when those attributes are missing. As a concrete example, a decorator that does return wraps(func)(wrapper) will cause update_wrapper to access func.__name__ at decoration-time.

3) The helpers intended to copy attributes onto the method wrapper — _update_method_wrapper(_wrapper, dec) and the later update_wrapper(_wrapper, method) call — are executed after the decorator application code path in _multi_decorate (the attribute-copying loop is after the inner _wrapper definition). Because decorator application occurs (by calling dec(bound_method)) while the bound callable is still a partial lacking function metadata, those post-facto attribute-copying steps cannot prevent decorators from failing when they inspect the callable passed to them. (See django/utils/decorators.py, lines 41–43 and 45–49.)

4) method_decorator delegates to _multi_decorate, so all uses of method_decorator that adapt function decorators to methods are affected by this behavior. Representative call sites observed in this codebase where method_decorator is used (and therefore potentially impacted) include: django/contrib/admin/options.py (csrf_protect_m = method_decorator(csrf_protect)), django/contrib/admin/sites.py, django/contrib/admindocs/views.py, django/contrib/auth/admin.py, django/contrib/auth/views.py, as well as test and example usages in tests/decorators/tests.py and various tests under tests/ (e.g. tests/generic_views/views.py, tests/middleware/views.py, tests/test_client/views.py). Each of these locations relies on method_decorator -> _multi_decorate and therefore shares the same root cause pattern.
StepsToReproduce: Define a function decorator that uses functools.wraps(func) or otherwise accesses func.__name__ (for example, a logger decorator that logs func.__name__).
Define a class with an instance method decorated with @method_decorator(the_decorator).
Instantiate the class and call the decorated method.
Observe the runtime exception raised when the decorator tries to access __name__ on the passed callable (AttributeError: 'functools.partial' object has no attribute '__name__').
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Applying a function decorator to an instance method via method_decorator should not raise AttributeError. Decorators that expect to read function metadata (__name__, __module__, __doc__) should be able to do so when applied to a method via method_decorator, and the decorated method should run normally with expected attributes preserved on the method object where appropriate.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Calling a method decorated via method_decorator where the function decorator uses functools.wraps or inspects __name__/__module__/__doc__ raises AttributeError: 'functools.partial' object has no attribute '__name__'.

def index(self, request, extra_context=None):
        """
        Display the main admin index page, which lists all of the installed
        apps that have been registered in this site.
        """
        app_list = self.get_app_list(request)

        context = {
            **self.each_context(request),
            'title': self.index_title,
            'subtitle': None,
            'app_list': app_list,
            **(extra_context or {}),
        }

        request.current_app = self.name

        return TemplateResponse(request, self.index_template or 'admin/index.html', context)

    def app_index(self, request, app_label, extra_context=None):
        app_dict = self._build_app_dict(request, app_label)
        if not app_dict:
            raise Http404('The requested admin page does not exist.')
        # Sort the models alphabetically within each app.
        app_dict['models'].sort(key=lambda x: x['name'])
        context = {
            **self.each_context(request),
            'title': _('%(app)s administration') % {'app': app_dict['name']},
            'subtitle': None,
            'app_list': [app_dict],
            'app_label': app_label,
            **(extra_context or {}),
        }

        request.current_app = self.name

        return TemplateResponse(request, self.app_index_template or [
            'admin/%s/app_index.html' % app_label,
            'admin/app_index.html'
        ], context)

bug_report.Title: get_admin_url generates links in default 'admin' namespace for readonly related fields in custom AdminSite
bug_report.Description: When a model with a ForeignKey (or OneToOne) field is displayed in a custom AdminSite and that field is listed in readonly_fields, the change-link for the related object is generated in the default admin namespace (/admin/...) instead of the custom AdminSite namespace (e.g. /custom-admin/...). This manifests in admin forms where readonly related-object links are shown.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django.contrib.admin.helpers.AdminReadonlyField.get_admin_url: this method constructs the admin URL name as
   url_name = 'admin:%s_%s_change' % (remote_field.model._meta.app_label, remote_field.model._meta.model_name)
   and then calls reverse(url_name, args=[quote(remote_obj.pk)]) without supplying current_app. (See django/contrib/admin/helpers.py, lines ~206-214.)
   Impact: because current_app (the AdminSite app namespace) is not provided, URL resolution happens in the global/default resolver context and typically resolves to the default 'admin' namespace, producing /admin/... URLs even when the form is being rendered inside a different AdminSite instance. The AdminReadonlyField instance does have access to the ModelAdmin (self.model_admin), and the AdminSite name intended for per-site resolution is available as self.model_admin.admin_site.name; the admin code elsewhere uses current_app=self.admin_site.name when reversing.

2) django.contrib.admin.models.LogEntry.get_admin_url: this method builds the same named URL (url_name = 'admin:%s_%s_change' % (app_label, model)) and calls reverse(url_name, args=(quote(self.object_id),)) without current_app. (See django/contrib/admin/models.py, lines ~144-147.)
   Impact: LogEntry.get_admin_url is invoked by admin templates (for example the Recent actions list) but does not receive request or ModelAdmin context, so it has no AdminSite name available to pass as current_app. As a result, reversing the named URL without current_app resolves in the default namespace and can produce links pointing at the default admin site rather than the AdminSite from which the template is being rendered.

3) Context/corroboration: other admin code that has access to an AdminSite uses the AdminSite app namespace when reversing. For example, ModelAdmin.response_add uses reverse(..., current_app=self.admin_site.name) (django/contrib/admin/options.py, lines ~1191-1195) and widgets/RelatedFieldWidgetWrapper use current_app=self.admin_site.name when building related URLs. The two locations above are outliers that omit current_app and therefore generate URLs in the wrong site namespace when a custom AdminSite is used.
StepsToReproduce: Create a custom AdminSite instance whose name/URL namespace is not 'admin' (for example AdminSite(name='custom-admin') mounted at /custom-admin/).
Register a model with a ForeignKey to another model and ensure the ForeignKey field appears in readonly_fields on the ModelAdmin for that model.
Open the model's change (or view) page in the custom AdminSite (the URL beginning with /custom-admin/...).
Inspect the readonly related-object link rendered for the ForeignKey field and follow it (or hover to inspect the href).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Readonly related-object links generated in the admin UI should point to the change page within the same AdminSite instance that is rendering the page (i.e. use the custom AdminSite's namespace and path such as /custom-admin/...), not the default /admin/ path.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The related-object change links generated for readonly ForeignKey/OneToOne fields use the default admin namespace (/admin/...) and therefore point to the default admin site URL rather than the custom AdminSite currently rendering the page.

Helper functions for creating Form classes from Django models
and database field objects.
"""
from itertools import chain

from django.core.exceptions import (
    NON_FIELD_ERRORS, FieldError, ImproperlyConfigured, ValidationError,
)
from django.forms.fields import ChoiceField, Field
from django.forms.forms import BaseForm, DeclarativeFieldsMetaclass

__all__ = (
    'ModelForm', 'BaseModelForm', 'model_to_dict', 'fields_for_model',
    'ModelChoiceField', 'ModelMultipleChoiceField', 'ALL_FIELDS',
    'BaseModelFormSet', 'modelformset_factory', 'BaseInlineFormSet',
    'inlineformset_factory', 'modelform_factory',

ALL_FIELDS = '__all__'


def construct_instance(form, instance, fields=None, exclude=None):
    """
    Construct and return a model instance from the bound ``form``'s
    ``cleaned_data``, but do not save the returned instance to the database.
    """
    from django.db import models
    opts = instance._meta

    cleaned_data = form.cleaned_data
    file_field_list = []
    for f in opts.fields:
        if not f.editable or isinstance(f, models.AutoField) \
                or f.name not in cleaned_data:
            continue
        if fields is not None and f.name not in fields:
            continue
        if exclude and f.name in exclude:
            continue
        # Leave defaults for fields that aren't in POST data, except for
        # checkbox inputs because they don't appear in POST data if not checked.
        if (
            f.has_default() and
            form[f.name].field.widget.value_omitted_from_data(form.data, form.files, form.add_prefix(f.name)) and
            cleaned_data.get(f.name) in form[f.name].field.empty_values
        ):
            continue
        # Defer saving file-type fields until after the other fields, so a
        # callable upload_to can use the values from other fields.
        if isinstance(f, models.FileField):
            file_field_list.append(f)
        else:
            f.save_form_data(instance, cleaned_data[f.name])

    for f in file_field_list:
        f.save_form_data(instance, cleaned_data[f.name])

    return instance
