- What I expected to learn: whether RenameModel short-circuits when db_table is unchanged, or whether it still triggers related-field / m2m alterations.

What I inspected (quote + analysis)
- django/db/migrations/operations/models.py — RenameModel.database_forwards (lines shown below):
  - Lines 319–328:
    - "new_model = to_state.apps.get_model(app_label, self.new_name)"
    - "old_model = from_state.apps.get_model(app_label, self.old_name)"
    - "schema_editor.alter_db_table(new_model, old_model._meta.db_table, new_model._meta.db_table)"
  - Lines 330–347: it iterates old_model._meta.related_objects and for each computes a to_field from to_state and calls:
    - "schema_editor.alter_field(model, related_object.field, to_field)"
  - Lines 349–369: iterates local_many_to_many pairs and calls schema_editor.alter_db_table(...) and schema_editor.alter_field(...) for M2M table renames/column renames.

Conclusion:
- RenameModel.database_forwards always calls alter_db_table and then unconditionally iterates related_objects and m2m fields to call alter_field / alter_db_table for m2m, regardless of whether the table names passed to alter_db_table are identical. This matches the draft's claim that RenameModel proceeds with related-field updates even when the underlying DB table name does not change.

- models.py: After calling schema_editor.alter_db_table(...), there is no check of whether the DB table rename was a no-op before iterating related_objects and calling alter_field. RenameModel proceeds regardless.

Conclusion:
- RenameModel does not short-circuit the related_field and m2m alter work when the table name is unchanged. This is the core behavioral mismatch the draft describes.

Evidence:
- models.py:324–369 — alter_db_table followed by related/ m2m alter calls with no conditional based on table equality.

4) Verify whether alter_field/_field_should_be_altered will perform database operations when called with the old vs new field instances produced by the migration state transition
- Why I fetched the file: to confirm what triggers alter_field to actually perform changes (i.e., how it decides fields are different) and to see the concrete actions that produce FK drops or table recreation.
- What I expected: _field_should_be_altered compares field.deconstruct() outputs; alter_field will drop/recreate FKs or (on SQLite) remake tables if it decides the field must be altered.

What I inspected:
- django/db/backends/base/schema.py:
  - _field_should_be_altered (lines 1122–1149): it calls old_field.deconstruct() and new_field.deconstruct(), removes a set of non_database_attrs from kwargs, then returns True if quoted columns differ or the deconstruct tuples differ:
    - "return (self.quote_name(old_field.column) != self.quote_name(new_field.column) or (old_path, old_args, old_kwargs) != (new_path, new_args, new_kwargs))"
  - alter_field/_alter_field (lines 578–620 and 623–641 etc.):
    - alter_field returns early only if _field_should_be_altered is False.
    - _alter_field will drop FK constraints (lines 624–641: calls _constraint_names and executes _delete_fk_sql for each), which is what causes FK drop/recreate behavior on Postgres.
- django/db/backends/sqlite3/schema.py:
  - alter_field overrides and, when complex, remakes tables using _remake_table (lines 101–140 and 142–299). The _remake_table process creates a new table, copies data, drops old table and renames new table (lines 281–299), which is the source of the SQLite table recreation the draft reports.

Conclusion:
- alter_field will perform physical schema changes (dropping/recreating FKs on backends with constraint support; remaking tables on SQLite) whenever _field_should_be_altered reports differences. So originally harmless-looking alter_field calls (when the underlying DB table hasn't changed) can still cause visible churn because of how field differences are detected and how state changes render fields differently.

- base/schema.py:1122–1149 (_field_should_be_altered comparing deconstruct tuples)
- base/schema.py:624–641 (dropping FK constraints in _alter_field)
- sqlite3/schema.py:142–152, 281–299 (_remake_table steps and flow)

5) Investigate whether state rename causes fields to appear different and thus trigger alter_field
- Why I inspected state.py and fields' deconstruct: to confirm why the old_field vs new_field deconstruct outputs can differ when only the model class name changed (but db_table stayed the same).
- What I expected: ProjectState.rename_model would change the ModelState/field remote references such that the deconstructed representations differ.

What I inspected:
- django/db/migrations/state.py — ProjectState.rename_model (lines 133–169):
  - It clones the old model state, sets renamed_model.name = new_name, adds it to self.models, and then:
    - For each referencing field (get_references(...)), if reference.to, it clones the referencing field and sets changed_field.remote_field.model = new_remote_model (a string 'app_label.NewName'), and assigns that changed_field back into the referencing model_state.fields.
  - Then it reloads models and removes the old model state.
- django/db/models/fields/related.py — ForeignKey.deconstruct (lines ~900–915):
  - ForeignKey.deconstruct calls super().deconstruct() (which includes positional args, including the 'to' argument) and then modifies kwargs (removes to_fields/from_fields, sets db_index flags, includes to_field as kwargs if applicable).
- django/db/models/fields/__init__.py — Field.deconstruct (lines 417–447):
  - Field.deconstruct documents and returns name, path, args, kwargs, which includes positional args for instantiation.

Conclusion:
- ProjectState.rename_model updates the stored field instances in the to_state (and the representation of their remote target) — e.g., changing a field.remote_field.model to the string 'app_label.NewName'. Because Field.deconstruct/ForeignKey.deconstruct serialize the relation target into args/kwargs, the deconstructed tuples for an old_field (coming from from_state) and the new_field (coming from to_state) can differ even when the underlying db_table names are identical. _field_should_be_altered uses the deconstruct tuples to decide whether to alter; that difference will cause alter_field to run.

- fields/__init__.py:417–447 (Field.deconstruct description)

bug_report.Title: RenameModel with explicit Meta.db_table should be a noop but triggers DB schema changes
bug_report.Description: A RenameModel migration for a model that already defines Meta.db_table (so the underlying table name does not change) should perform no database schema operations. Currently the migration triggers schema changes: on PostgreSQL foreign key constraints are dropped/recreated; on SQLite the table is recreated.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/migrations/operations/models.py — RenameModel.database_forwards always proceeds to perform database-side alterations even when the model's underlying DB table name is unchanged. It calls schema_editor.alter_db_table(new_model, old_model._meta.db_table, new_model._meta.db_table) and then unconditionally iterates old_model._meta.related_objects and many-to-many pairs to call schema_editor.alter_field / schema_editor.alter_db_table for related and M2M objects. (See models.py: lines that call alter_db_table and the subsequent related_objects and m2m loops.)

2) django/db/backends/base/schema.py — BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor.alter_db_table contains an early-return guard when old_db_table == new_db_table (and handles case-insensitive equality for backends that ignore case). That makes the actual table-rename SQL a no-op in that case, but RenameModel does not treat that equality as a signal to skip the subsequent related-field and M2M alteration work; RenameModel calls alter_field / related operations regardless of whether alter_db_table would be a no-op. (See base/schema.py: alter_db_table early-return.)

3) django/db/migrations/state.py — ProjectState.rename_model mutates the migration state so that referencing fields in the to_state are updated to point at the new model name (it sets remote_field.model to a new string like 'app_label.NewName'). This state-level renaming changes how the related fields are rendered in the from_state vs to_state.

4) django/db/models/fields/__init__.py and django/db/models/fields/related.py — Field.deconstruct / ForeignKey.deconstruct serialize positional args and kwargs that include relation targets or related options. Because ProjectState.rename_model changes the representation of remote_field.model between the two states (class object vs string), the deconstructed tuples for old_field and new_field can differ even when the underlying db_table has not changed.

5) django/db/backends/base/schema.py — BaseDatabaseSchemaEditor._field_should_be_altered compares the deconstructed (path, args, kwargs) tuples for old_field and new_field (after removing a set of non-database attrs). If those tuples differ, _field_should_be_altered returns True and alter_field proceeds. alter_field/_alter_field then executes physical schema changes (dropping FK constraints and other operations) that lead to the observed DB churn. On SQLite, the SQLite schema editor's alter_field/_remake_table path rebuilds the table, causing full table recreation.

Overall pattern: RenameModel triggers a state-level model rename that changes the serialized form of related fields; RenameModel then unconditionally requests field alterations on related fields. Even when no DB table rename is needed (old_db_table == new_db_table), the combination of (a) state changes to the relation target representation and (b) _field_should_be_altered's deconstruct-based comparison causes alter_field to perform real schema operations (FK drops/recreates on Postgres; table recreation on SQLite).
StepsToReproduce: Create a Django app with a model that sets Meta.db_table explicitly (e.g., class MyModel(models.Model): class Meta: db_table = 'custom_table').
Create another version that renames the model class (e.g., MyModel -> RenamedModel) but leaves Meta.db_table unchanged.
Generate the migration (makemigrations) which produces a RenameModel operation.
Apply the migration (migrate) against PostgreSQL and observe foreign keys for related models being dropped and recreated.
Repeat applying the migration on SQLite and observe the table being recreated.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Renaming a model whose Meta.db_table remains the same should produce no database schema changes: the existing table, foreign key constraints, and related objects should remain untouched.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The RenameModel migration performs database schema operations even though the table name did not change: on PostgreSQL related foreign key constraints are dropped and recreated; on SQLite the table is recreated.

import copy
from datetime import datetime

from django.forms import (
    CharField, FileInput, MultipleChoiceField, MultiValueField, MultiWidget,
    RadioSelect, SelectMultiple, SplitDateTimeField, SplitDateTimeWidget,
    TextInput,
)

from .base import WidgetTest


class MyMultiWidget(MultiWidget):
    def decompress(self, value):
        if value:
            return value.split('__')
        return ['', '']


class ComplexMultiWidget(MultiWidget):
    def __init__(self, attrs=None):
        widgets = (
            TextInput(),
            SelectMultiple(choices=WidgetTest.beatles),
            SplitDateTimeWidget(),
        )
        super().__init__(widgets, attrs)

    def decompress(self, value):
        if value:
            data = value.split(',')
            return [
                data[0], list(data[1]), datetime.strptime(data[2], "%Y-%m-%d %H:%M:%S")
            ]
        return [None, None, None]


class ComplexField(MultiValueField):
    def __init__(self, required=True, widget=None, label=None, initial=None):
        fields = (
            CharField(),
            MultipleChoiceField(choices=WidgetTest.beatles),
            SplitDateTimeField(),
        )
        super().__init__(fields, required, widget, label, initial)

    def compress(self, data_list):
        if data_list:
            return '%s,%s,%s' % (
                data_list[0], ''.join(data_list[1]), data_list[2],
            )
        return None


class DeepCopyWidget(MultiWidget):
    """
    Used to test MultiWidget.__deepcopy__().
    """
    def __init__(self, choices=[]):
        widgets = [
            RadioSelect(choices=choices),
            TextInput,
        ]
        super().__init__(widgets)

    def _set_choices(self, choices):
        """
        When choices are set for this widget, we want to pass those along to
        the Select widget.
        """
        self.widgets[0].choices = choices

    def _get_choices(self):
        """
        The choices for this widget are the Select widget's choices.
        """
        return self.widgets[0].choices
    choices = property(_get_choices, _set_choices)


class MultiWidgetTest(WidgetTest):
    def test_subwidgets_name(self):
        widget = MultiWidget(
            widgets={
                '': TextInput(),
                'big': TextInput(attrs={'class': 'big'}),
                'small': TextInput(attrs={'class': 'small'}),
            },
        )
        self.check_html(widget, 'name', ['John', 'George', 'Paul'], html=(
            '<input type="text" name="name" value="John">'
            '<input type="text" name="name_big" value="George" class="big">'
            '<input type="text" name="name_small" value="Paul" class="small">'
        ))

    def test_text_inputs(self):
        widget = MyMultiWidget(
            widgets=(
                TextInput(attrs={'class': 'big'}),
                TextInput(attrs={'class': 'small'}),
            )
        )
        self.check_html(widget, 'name', ['john', 'lennon'], html=(
            '<input type="text" class="big" value="john" name="name_0">'
            '<input type="text" class="small" value="lennon" name="name_1">'
        ))
        self.check_html(widget, 'name', 'john__lennon', html=(
            '<input type="text" class="big" value="john" name="name_0">'
            '<input type="text" class="small" value="lennon" name="name_1">'
        ))
        self.check_html(widget, 'name', 'john__lennon', attrs={'id': 'foo'}, html=(
            '<input id="foo_0" type="text" class="big" value="john" name="name_0">'
            '<input id="foo_1" type="text" class="small" value="lennon" name="name_1">'
        ))

    def test_constructor_attrs(self):
        widget = MyMultiWidget(
            widgets=(
                TextInput(attrs={'class': 'big'}),
                TextInput(attrs={'class': 'small'}),
            ),
            attrs={'id': 'bar'},
        )
        self.check_html(widget, 'name', ['john', 'lennon'], html=(
            '<input id="bar_0" type="text" class="big" value="john" name="name_0">'
            '<input id="bar_1" type="text" class="small" value="lennon" name="name_1">'
        ))

Checkpoint 5: Final report — Complete fix and locations to change

Root cause:
- MultiWidget overrides id_for_label to append '_0' to the id (return id_ + '_0'), making labels point to the first subwidget id. This is a hardcoded behavior in MultiWidget that duplicates semantics already handled by other widgets (e.g., ChoiceWidget with add_id_index). The override enforces index-based labeling even when individual widget implementations might prefer otherwise.

Every location to change (concrete):

1) django/forms/widgets.py — MultiWidget
   - Current code (to remove):

             id_ += '_0'
         return id_
   - What it currently does:
     - Always appends '_0' to the provided id_, making label 'for' point to the first subwidget's id.
   - Why this is a problem:
     - Forces labeling to point at a subwidget id; ChoiceWidget already provides index control; other widgets may want to control label semantics (e.g. RadioSelect returns no 'for' to avoid toggling the first input).
   - Fix:
     - Remove this id_for_label method entirely so MultiWidget inherits Widget.id_for_label, which returns id_ unchanged.
   - Code patch (conceptual):
     - Remove lines implementing id_for_label from the MultiWidget class.

   - Why change:
     - After MultiWidget.id_for_label is removed, the label 'for' will be the base id 'id_field1', so tests must reflect this new behavior.

No other code changes required:
- get_context and subwidget id generation remains unchanged; subwidget ids still get suffixes like '_0', '_1', etc.
- ChoiceWidget, RadioSelect, SplitDateTimeWidget, SelectDateWidget, SplitArrayWidget (in contrib.postgres) retain their id_for_label semantics and do not need change.
- BoundField.label_tag and BoundField.id_for_label are used as-is; they will call the active id_for_label which for MultiWidget will now be Widget.id_for_label returning the base id.

Notes about accessibility and DOM:
- After this change, the label will point to the base id (id_field1). In most MultiWidget cases, the rendered DOM will not contain an element with that exact id (the subwidgets will be id_field1_0, id_field1_1, ...). That means the label's 'for' attribute will not focus any input when clicked — but this was the user's intent (they prefer to control index via choice widgets).

- The fix removes the hardcoded suffix only from MultiWidget itself; widgets that require special behavior (ChoiceWidget, RadioSelect, SplitDateTimeWidget, SplitArrayWidget) retain their own id_for_label implementations. Tests that assert the old behavior for MultiWidget are updated to match the new semantics.

bug_report.Title: MultiWidget label 'for' attribute incorrectly targets first subwidget (appends '_0')
bug_report.Description: When rendering a MultiWidget, the field-level label's for attribute is derived from widget.id_for_label(id_), and the MultiWidget implementation of id_for_label unconditionally appends '_0' to the provided id (e.g. 'id_field1' -> 'id_field1_0'). This causes the label to target the first subwidget's id rather than the field's base id or following per-widget semantics (e.g. omitting the 'for' attribute or targeting a named subwidget).
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/forms/widgets.py — MultiWidget.id_for_label: MultiWidget overrides the Widget.id_for_label hook and encodes the assumption that the field-level label should target the first subwidget by unconditionally appending the literal '_0' when an id is present. Code (current):
   def id_for_label(self, id_):
       if id_:
           id_ += '_0'
       return id_
   (Effect: id_for_label(id_) -> id_ + '_0' when id_ is truthy.)
   Neutral/default relationship (Widget.id_for_label behavior): id_for_label(id_) -> id_ (return the base field id unchanged).

2) django/forms/widgets.py — MultiWidget.get_context: Subwidget ids are created with a numeric suffix pattern ('%s_%s' % (id_, i)), producing subwidget ids like 'id_field_0', 'id_field_1', etc. This is a separate concern (unique subwidget ids) and does not by itself imply the label must reference the first subwidget. Code excerpt: widget_attrs['id'] = '%s_%s' % (id_, i).

3) django/forms/widgets.py — ChoiceWidget.id_for_label(self, id_, index='0'): ChoiceWidget provides per-widget control for index-appending via the add_id_index flag. Implementation: if id_ and self.add_id_index: id_ = '%s_%s' % (id_, index). This shows index-appending belongs as a widget-level decision (id_for_label with index), not necessarily as a global MultiWidget convention.

4) django/forms/widgets.py — RadioSelect.id_for_label(self, id_, index=None): RadioSelect intentionally returns an empty string when index is None (omitting the 'for' attribute for the container label) and only delegates to ChoiceWidget.id_for_label when an index is given. This demonstrates alternate valid semantics (omit 'for' vs. index it) and highlights that the appropriate label target may vary by widget.

5) django/forms/widgets.py & contrib.postgres/forms/array.py — Other Multi-element widgets follow different conventions: e.g., SplitDateTimeWidget.id_for_label returns a suffixed id for a named subwidget (e.g. '_year' or '_month'), while contrib.postgres SplitArrayWidget.id_for_label also appends '_0' (same pattern as MultiWidget). These are separate locations encoding the same root-pattern (label targeting a specific subwidget), and they must be considered together when reasoning about consistent semantics.

6) django/forms/boundfield.py — BoundField.label_tag calls widget.id_for_label(id_) and uses its return value as the label's 'for' attribute if truthy. Therefore, any widget.id_for_label implementation directly controls the rendered label 'for' attribute.

7) Tests: tests/forms_tests/field_tests/test_multivaluefield.py assert current behavior (labels like '<label for="id_field1_0">...'), which documents and depends on the present MultiWidget.id_for_label behavior. bug_report.Title: forms.URLField.clean raises ValueError (from urlsplit) instead of ValidationError for malformed URLs
bug_report.Description: Calling forms.URLField().clean() on certain malformed inputs (example: '////]@N.AN') results in a ValueError propagating from urlsplit (message: "Invalid IPv6 URL") instead of raising a django ValidationError. The failure occurs during URLValidator.__call__ while validators are run.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) URLValidator.__call__ performs unguarded calls to urllib.parse.urlsplit(value) after the initial regex/IDN handling. Locations: django/core/validators.py, URLValidator.__call__. Evidence: the method calls urlsplit(value).netloc inside a regex search (host_match = re.search(..., urlsplit(value).netloc)) and also calls urlsplit(value).hostname in the length check (if len(urlsplit(value).hostname) > 253:). These later calls are not wrapped in try/except, so any ValueError raised by urlsplit can propagate.

2) The IDN (punycode) branch inside URLValidator.__call__ does guard an initial urlsplit call and translates ValueError into ValidationError, but that guarded call is distinct from the later unguarded calls. Location: django/core/validators.py, URLValidator.__call__. Evidence: the code has a try/except around scheme, netloc, path, query, fragment = urlsplit(value) that converts ValueError into ValidationError, but subsequent urlsplit(value) uses are unguarded.

3) The underlying URL parsing routine raises ValueError for malformed bracketed/IPv6 hosts (message: "Invalid IPv6 URL"). Location: django/utils/http.py (function _urlsplit) and stdlib urllib.parse.urlsplit; traceback shows the ValueError originates from urlsplit. Evidence: django/utils/http._urlsplit explicitly raises ValueError("Invalid IPv6 URL") when brackets are unbalanced in the netloc.

4) Field.run_validators expects validators to raise django.core.exceptions.ValidationError and only catches ValidationError. Location: django/forms/fields.py, Field.run_validators. Evidence: run_validators iterates over validators and only handles exceptions of type ValidationError; other exceptions (like ValueError) will propagate.

5) The same root cause affects other code paths that rely on URLValidator: e.g., django/db/models/fields.URLField uses validators.URLValidator as a default validator, so model-level URL validation is also subject to an uncaught ValueError from urlsplit. Location: django/db/models/fields (URLField.default_validators references validators.URLValidator()).

Consequence: Because some urlsplit calls inside URLValidator.__call__ are not translated into ValidationError, malformed inputs that cause urlsplit to raise ValueError (for example, "////]@N.AN") will result in ValueError propagating out of the validator. Field.run_validators does not catch ValueError, so the forms/models validation flow crashes instead of producing a user-visible ValidationError.
StepsToReproduce: In a Django project shell or a small script, run:
from django import forms
forms.URLField().clean('////]@N.AN')
Observe the exception raised.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Calling forms.URLField().clean on malformed URL inputs should raise django.core.exceptions.ValidationError indicating the URL is invalid (user-visible validation error), not propagate a raw ValueError or crash the caller.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: A ValueError is raised and propagates out (traceback shows urllib.parse.urlsplit raising ValueError: "Invalid IPv6 URL"), causing the validation flow to crash instead of returning a ValidationError that the forms framework can handle.

Checkpoint 5: Final report

Root cause (short)
- ExpressionWrapper.as_sql blindly returned the compiled SQL of its inner expression. When the inner expression was a WhereNode produced by ~Q(pk__in=[]), WhereNode.as_sql returns an empty string ('') to signal "matches everything." Passing that '' unchanged into the SELECT clause produced an empty SELECT expression (i.e., "SELECT AS ..."), which is invalid SQL. ExpressionWrapper didn't distinguish WHERE semantics ('', match-everything) from SELECT semantics (non-empty SQL expected).

All locations that need to change
- Primary location to change:
  - django/db/models/expressions.py — class ExpressionWrapper:
    - Method to change: as_sql(self, compiler, connection)
    - Current behavior: return compiler.compile(self.expression)
    - Problem: does not handle inner expression compiling to '' or None.
    - Fix: handle EmptyResultSet, sql is None, and sql == '' specifically:
      - Re-raise EmptyResultSet unchanged (so SQLCompiler.get_select will handle as before and use '0' fallback).
      - If compiled sql is None: raise EmptyResultSet (treat as "empty").
      - If compiled sql == '' and wrapper.output_field is BooleanField or inner expression is conditional, return '1', [] — canonical SQL for True (mirrors existing '0' for False).
      - Otherwise, return compiled (sql, params) unchanged.

- No other code location needs direct changes:
  - WhereNode (django/db/models/sql/where.py): no change — it correctly returns '' for match-everything and raises EmptyResultSet for match-nothing.
  - SQLCompiler.get_select (django/db/models/sql/compiler.py): no change — it already handles EmptyResultSet by substituting '0' (false) or other empty_result_set_value logic; the fix uses that by re-raising EmptyResultSet where appropriate.

Why this is a "complete" fix
- The bug arises solely because ExpressionWrapper forwarded the '' sentinel (match-everything) directly into SELECT building. Resolving it inside ExpressionWrapper is the proper place because ExpressionWrapper is the adapter used to place expressions (including boolean Q/WhereNode) into a SELECT clause. It must translate WhereNode semantics to SELECT semantics. Adjusting ExpressionWrapper.as_sql completes this mapping and leaves WhereNode semantics intact for WHERE clause contexts.

Patch (conceptual) for django/db/models/expressions.py
- Replace:

    def as_sql(self, compiler, connection):
        return compiler.compile(self.expression)

- With:

    def as_sql(self, compiler, connection):
        try:
            sql, params = compiler.compile(self.expression)
        except EmptyResultSet:
            # Preserve EmptyResultSet for callers (SQLCompiler.get_select)
            # to handle with its existing fallback logic.
            raise
        # If compiled SQL is None, treat it as an empty result set.
        if sql is None:
            raise EmptyResultSet
        # If compiled SQL is an empty string, this often means "matches
        # everything" for WhereNode. For boolean outputs, emit a TRUE
        # literal so that the SELECT expression is valid.
        if sql == '':
            if getattr(self.expression, 'conditional', False) or isinstance(self.output_field, fields.BooleanField):
                return '1', []
            return sql, params
        return sql, params

Returning '1' for match-everything (True) is consistent and produces valid SELECT expressions for typical backends. For backends that don't support raw boolean expressions in SELECT, select_format (on WhereNode or BaseExpression) will wrap the expression appropriately (e.g., CASE WHEN ... - Why I need the file: The draft asserts WhereNode.as_sql uses special return values: '' for "matches everything", (None, []) for "empty", and raising EmptyResultSet for "can't match anything". I expected to find a docstring and logic implementing that contract.

  - where.py (lines 79-105) shows the compilation loop and the logic:

    - If empty_needed reaches 0 and self.negated: return '', [] (matches everything for the negated case), else raise EmptyResultSet.

bug_report.Title: ExpressionWrapper with negated empty Q(~Q(pk__in=[])) produces empty SELECT expression
bug_report.Description: Annotating a queryset with ExpressionWrapper(~Q(pk__in=[]), output_field=BooleanField()) produces invalid SQL with an empty expression in the SELECT list (e.g. "SELECT AS \"foo\" FROM ..."). The non-negated case ExpressionWrapper(Q(pk__in=[])) compiles to a false literal (SELECT 0 AS \"foo\") and works.
bug_report.RootCause:
1. ExpressionWrapper.as_sql (django/db/models/expressions.py, method ExpressionWrapper.as_sql) unconditionally returns the compiled SQL of its inner expression by delegating to compiler.compile(self.expression). The implementation is: return compiler.compile(self.expression). (expressions.py lines 981-983).

2. WhereNode.as_sql (django/db/models/sql/where.py) uses sentinel return values to represent three semantics for boolean nodes: '' (empty string) means "matches everything"; (None, []) means "empty"; raising EmptyResultSet means "matches nothing". The docstring and logic explicitly implement these return values (where.py lines 65-71 and lines 95-105).

3. The In lookup (django/db/models/lookups.py, class In) raises EmptyResultSet when its RHS becomes empty (e.g., pk__in=[]). In.process_rhs contains "if not rhs: raise EmptyResultSet" (lookups.py lines 408-418). Therefore Q(pk__in=[]) yields a child lookup that raises EmptyResultSet during compilation.

4. WhereNode.as_sql transforms a child's EmptyResultSet differently depending on negation: for a non-negated WHERE, an EmptyResultSet from a child is propagated to signal "matches nothing"; for a negated node (~Q(...)), an EmptyResultSet in a child can cause WhereNode.as_sql to return '' (match-everything) for the whole node (where.py lines 95-105). Concretely, Q(pk__in=[]) results in EmptyResultSet (match-nothing) while ~Q(pk__in=[]) results in '' (match-everything).

5. SQLCompiler.get_select (django/db/models/sql/compiler.py, method get_select) expects compile() either to raise EmptyResultSet (so get_select can fall back to a literal '0' or to an expression based on empty_result_set_value) or to return a non-empty SQL fragment. get_select does not special-case an empty string '' return value; it forwards the compiled SQL to col.select_format and then to the final SELECT construction. When the compiled SQL is the empty string, the SELECT column expression becomes empty, producing invalid SQL like "SELECT AS \"foo\" ..." (compiler.py lines 271-285 and compile() behavior at 465-471).

6. The adapter that places a WhereNode into a SELECT (ExpressionWrapper) is not translating WhereNode's "match everything" sentinel ('') into a valid SELECT expression. For boolean annotations the expected mapping is: EmptyResultSet -> select '0' (already handled by SQLCompiler.get_select's EmptyResultSet fallback); "matches everything" ('' from WhereNode) -> should correspond to a boolean TRUE literal in SELECT context (for consistency with the existing '0' for False, a SQL '1' literal is the appropriate representation). Because ExpressionWrapper forwards '' unchanged, the select column becomes empty and the SQL is invalid.

Locations affected by the same root-cause pattern: any use of ExpressionWrapper to place a WhereNode or other conditional expression into a SELECT (examples in the test suite include tests/annotations/tests.py, tests/lookup/tests.py).

Annotate the queryset using ExpressionWrapper with a negated empty Q: queryset.annotate(foo=ExpressionWrapper(~Q(pk__in=[]), output_field=BooleanField())).values('foo').query
Print or evaluate the resulting SQL (e.g., print(queryset.annotate(...).values('foo').query))
Observe the generated SQL select fragment is empty and invalid, e.g. "SELECT AS \"foo\" FROM \"app_book\""

Diagnosis (clear statement of the bug)
- Bug: MigrationRecorder will create (and write to) the django_migrations table on any database connection it is given, regardless of database router allow_migrate rules.
- Primary code responsible: django/db/migrations/recorder.py, specifically ensure_schema (creates the django_migrations table unconditionally if it's missing) and record_applied/record_unapplied (which call ensure_schema and then create/delete rows).
- Result: In multi-db setups where a router forbids migrations on some connections, Django still tries to create the django_migrations table and write migration records on those connections during test DB creation or migrations, violating router.allow_migrate.

Checkpoint 4 — Propose a fix, then immediately challenge it

Proposed fix (summary)
- Change Django's MigrationRecorder so it respects database router rules when creating/writing the django_migrations table.
  - Do not create the django_migrations table on connections for which router.allow_migrate(connection.alias, 'migrations', ...) returns False.
  - Do not write (record_applied/record_unapplied) to the django_migrations table on connections for which allow_migrate returns False.
  - Keep applied_migrations() as-is (it already returns {} if the table doesn't exist); ensure_schema should not create the table when disallowed, so applied_migrations will correctly return {}.

Concrete code changes (single-file patch)
- File changed: django/db/migrations/recorder.py
- Changes:
  - In ensure_schema: consult router.allow_migrate(...) and return early without creating the table if allow_migrate is False.
  - In record_applied and record_unapplied: consult router.allow_migrate(...) and no-op (return) if allow_migrate is False (so they don't call ensure_schema/create/delete and don't error).
  - Keep has_table and applied_migrations behavior the same: they will report no applied migrations if the table is absent, and because we no longer create the table on disallowed DBs, that covers the intended effect.

Exact implementation (conceptual diff)
- At top of ensure_schema/record_* methods import router (local import to avoid top-level import cycles), e.g.:

- Call:

Detailed reasoning for each changed method
- ensure_schema:
  - Current assumption: it can create the django_migrations table on any DB connection if missing.
  - Change: if the router disallows migrating the 'migrations' app on this DB, do not attempt to create the table (no-op). This prevents creating tables on DBs that should not have any managed tables.
- record_applied / record_unapplied:
  - Current assumption: safe to create/write/delete migration records on any DB connection.
  - Change: if router disallows migrating the 'migrations' app on this DB, do not write/delete migration records (no-op).
- applied_migrations:
  - No change needed: it already returns {} when the django_migrations table doesn't exist. With ensure_schema no longer creating the table on disallowed DBs, applied_migrations will stay empty for those DBs.

4a) "What assumption does my fix change?"
- Current assumption removed: The code assumes that the migration recorder is free to create and modify the django_migrations table on any database connection without consulting database routers. The fix changes that to: the recorder must consult router.allow_migrate and avoid creating or writing the django_migrations table on connections where migrations are not allowed.

4b) "What hardcoded values encode this assumption?"
- Hardcoded values in the Migration inner model:

  - Yes. These values remain valid: the migration table is still named django_migrations and its app_label is 'migrations'. What changes is whether we attempt to create or write the table on a given DB — not the name or schema of the table. These hardcoded values do not need to become dynamic. They are used as the canonical names by which routers are asked (app_label = 'migrations'), so they must remain stable.

4c) "What about the reverse operation?"
- Reverse operation here = reading/applied_migrations vs writing/record_applied.

- Effects and tracing:

MigrationExecutor will continue, but migrations' operations themselves check router.allow_migrate per-model or per-operation (operations call router.allow_migrate_model / router.allow_migrate inside operations), so operations are already guarded.

With ensure_schema no longer creating the table, applied_migrations will return {} on DBs where router disallows migrations (which is the desired behavior).
- Trace through parent's complementary methods:

The change makes ensure_schema a no-op and recording methods no-op when migrations disallowed. That keeps reading (applied_migrations) consistent with writing (record_applied) because we won't create table/writes when router disallows, and applied_migrations will reflect that (empty set). Checkpoint 5 — Final report (complete analysis and required code changes)

Root cause
- MigrationRecorder assumed it was always allowed to create and write the django_migrations table on any DB connection. It unconditionally created the django_migrations table (ensure_schema) and unconditionally wrote migration rows (record_applied/record_unapplied). That ignored the database routing policy expressed by database routers via allow_migrate.

Any hardcoded values that need to become dynamic?
- No. The hardcoded db_table = 'django_migrations' and app_label = 'migrations' do not need to change. They are the canonical names for the migration-record table. We only change whether the recorder creates/writes that table on particular connections based on routing rules.

Potential side-effects and rationale
- For database connections where router.allow_migrate(...) returns False, applied_migrations() will return {} (unless the corresponding table already exists on that DB). That is correct: we should treat those DBs as having no recorded migrations.

If you prefer a stricter policy (reads blocked too), we could deny reads when router disallows, but that is less flexible and not necessary for the reported problem.

bug_report.Title: MigrationRecorder ignores db_router.allow_migrate and creates/writes django_migrations on disallowed DBs
bug_report.Description: In a multi-database setup with a router that disallows migrations on non-default connections, Django still creates the django_migrations table and records migration rows on every database connection when migrations or test database creation runs. This behaviour is visible during test database setup and when MigrationExecutor calls the recorder.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) MigrationRecorder.ensure_schema (django/db/migrations/recorder.py: ensure_schema) unconditionally creates the migration table named 'django_migrations' if it is missing on the connection, without consulting the database router. The floating Migration inner model defines Meta.app_label = 'migrations' and db_table = 'django_migrations' (recorder.py lines 35–38), and ensure_schema calls connection.schema_editor().create_model(self.Migration) when the table is not present (recorder.py lines 63–68).

2) MigrationRecorder.record_applied (django/db/migrations/recorder.py: record_applied) unconditionally calls ensure_schema() and then creates a Migration row on the given connection, without checking router.allow_migrate for the 'migrations' app (recorder.py lines 84–87). This causes write attempts on connections that a router may have marked as non-migrate targets.

3) MigrationRecorder.record_unapplied (django/db/migrations/recorder.py: record_unapplied) likewise unconditionally calls ensure_schema() and performs deletions, ignoring router.allow_migrate for the 'migrations' app (recorder.py lines 89–92).

4) MigrationRecorder.flush (django/db/migrations/recorder.py: flush) deletes all migration records via migration_qs.all().delete() on the connection without consulting the router (recorder.py lines 94–96); this encodes the assumption that mutation of the django_migrations table is always allowed on any connection.

5) MigrationLoader and MigrationExecutor construct a MigrationRecorder for each connection that is being inspected or migrated. MigrationExecutor.__init__ constructs a recorder per connection (django/db/migrations/executor.py line 19) and migrate() calls recorder.ensure_schema() unconditionally before applying migration operations (executor.py line 100). As a result, ensure_schema() is invoked for every connection the executor is used with, which triggers creation/writes on every connection regardless of routing rules.

6) applied_migrations returns an empty dict if the django_migrations table does not exist (recorder.py lines 72–82). The core inconsistency is that ensure_schema creates the table on any connection (causing writes), whereas other code paths and many operations consult router.allow_migrate for per-app/per-model routing. The canonical way to ask routing about migratability is router.allow_migrate(db, app_label, **hints) (django/db/utils.py lines 272–292). In this context, the appropriate diagnostic/router query for the migration-record model would include the migrations app label and model hints, e.g.:
    router.allow_migrate(
        self.connection.alias,
        'migrations',
        model=self.Migration,
        model_name=self.Migration._meta.model_name,
    )
If that call returns False for a given connection, creating the 'django_migrations' table and writing/deleting migration rows on that connection is inconsistent with the routing decision (i.e., the recorder currently lacks that check and so will create/write regardless).
StepsToReproduce: Configure a Django project with multiple database connections (DATABASES has 'default' plus at least one additional connection).
Include managed=False models or other non-default DB usage so multiple connections exist.
Run test database creation or run migrations across connections (e.g. ./manage.py test or the test runner that triggers setup_databases, or otherwise trigger create_test_db for all connections).
Observe that the django_migrations table is created and migration rows are recorded on the non-default connections even though allow_migrate returned False for those connections.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When a database router's allow_migrate returns False for the 'migrations' app on a given connection, Django should not create the django_migrations table on that connection and should not record applied/unapplied migrations there. Only connections where allow_migrate allows the 'migrations' app should have the django_migrations table and migration records.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: During test DB creation or migration runs, Django creates the 'django_migrations' table (db_table = 'django_migrations') and inserts/deletes migration records on every configured connection, including those for which the database router's allow_migrate returns False for the 'migrations' app.

def get_field_names_from_opts(opts):
    return set(chain.from_iterable(
        (f.name, f.attname) if f.concrete else (f.name,)
        for f in opts.get_fields()
    ))


def get_children_from_q(q):
    for child in q.children:
        if isinstance(child, Node):
            yield from get_children_from_q(child)
        else:
            yield child
