Now challenge the fix across the required questions:

4a) "What assumption does my fix change?"
- Original assumption: BaseCommand hardcodes the help formatter to DjangoHelpFormatter for all commands, assuming that no command needs a different formatter that preserves raw description formatting (e.g. formatted example blocks).
- The fix removes that assumption by making the formatter class configurable per-command (via BaseCommand.formatter_class).

4b) "What hardcoded values encode this assumption?"
- Hardcoded in base.py:
  - formatter_class=DjangoHelpFormatter (in BaseCommand.create_parser) — this is the single hardcoded value that enforces the assumption. My fix replaces it with a dynamic class attribute.
- Hardcoded values elsewhere in the component classes:
  - DjangoHelpFormatter.show_last: set of option strings. Does the change affect this value? If a command selects a different formatter_class (e.g., argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter), it will not have DjangoHelpFormatter's reordering behavior (show_last). The value itself is still correct for DjangoHelpFormatter, but if a command uses a custom formatter, the assumption that show_last is applied no longer holds. This is intentional: choosing a custom formatter takes precedence and may opt out of Django's reordering behavior. If maintaining reordering is important even for custom formatters, we could implement a small wrapper class that combines RawDescriptionHelpFormatter with the reordering logic (see "Alternate improvement" below).
- No other hardcoded constants in CommandParser or OutputWrapper are impacted.

4c) "What about the reverse operation?"
- The complementary operations to creating a parser include:
  - print_help (uses create_parser -> parser.print_help())
  - run_from_argv (calls create_parser to parse arguments)
- For print_help:
  - print_help calls parser.print_help(), which uses the parser's formatter_class (the new value). So the output will reflect the chosen formatter. That is intended.
- For parsing (run_from_argv -> parser.parse_args):
  - The chosen formatter_class impacts only presentation (format help) — parsing behavior is unaffected. So there is no complementary reading operation that must be changed.
- Check parent's method list: BaseCommand has no parent beyond object, so no inherited methods are impacted beyond those in this same class (create_parser, print_help, run_from_argv). All of these now correctly use self.formatter_class.
- Concretely, trace for run_from_argv:
  - Variables: self.formatter_class will be DjangoHelpFormatter by default (no behavior change). If a command sets formatter_class to RawDescriptionHelpFormatter, that will be the class passed to CommandParser and used when help text is printed. parse_args behavior is unchanged. So no need to override run_from_argv or print_help.

4d) "Does every existing method still work?"
- create_parser: changed to use self.formatter_class — default is set to DjangoHelpFormatter, so existing behavior unchanged unless command overrides the attribute (which is desired).
- print_help: still calls create_parser() -> parser.print_help(); works with the new configurable formatter.
- run_from_argv: still calls create_parser and parse_args; parsing unaffected.
- execute, check, check_migrations, add_base_argument, etc.: unchanged and unaffected.
- CommandParser, DjangoHelpFormatter, OutputWrapper: unchanged.
- So all existing methods continue to function. No method needs to be removed or altered further.

4e) "Does any NEW method need to be added?"
- No. However, consider the detail that some commands may want both: raw description formatting (preserve newlines) AND DjangoHelpFormatter's reordering of base options (show_last). If that combination is desired, the command author must provide a formatter class that subclasses argparse.HelpFormatter and implements both features (or we could provide a helper wrapper in Django). The minimal fix does not add such helper, but it allows authors to provide it. Because the original report only asked for customizable formatters to preserve help formatting, providing formatter_class on BaseCommand is sufficient.
- Optionally (not strictly required by the bug): we could add a built-in helper in django.core.management to combine DjangoHelpFormatter's reordering with RawDescriptionHelpFormatter semantics, for convenience. If we did, we'd add a class like DjangoRawDescriptionHelpFormatter(DjangoHelpFormatter, argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter) or a wrapper that inherits RawDescriptionHelpFormatter and implements _reordered_actions/add_usage/add_arguments similarly. But since the core issue is enabling customization, I didn't add new methods — just the configurable attribute.

Checkpoint 5: Final report

Root cause
- BaseCommand.create_parser hardcodes a single formatter class (DjangoHelpFormatter) when constructing the argparse ArgumentParser. argparse.HelpFormatter (the base class) normalizes paragraphs by collapsing newlines/indentation, so triple-quoted help strings that rely on preserved newlines/indentation (e.g., example usage blocks) are not preserved. Because Django forced DjangoHelpFormatter, command authors could not select e.g. argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter to preserve formatting.

Every location that needs to change
- Primary location:
  - django/core/management/base.py
    - Current code: create_parser passes formatter_class=DjangoHelpFormatter (hardcoded).
    - Change required: Make the formatter class configurable via a class attribute on BaseCommand (formatter_class) and use self.formatter_class when creating CommandParser.
    - Why: This removes the hardcoded formatter assumption and allows each command to choose a formatter that preserves description formatting (e.g., argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter).
- No other code files need changes. DjangoHelpFormatter remains available and still used by default.

What each changed location currently does, the assumption it encodes, and what the fix should be
- BaseCommand.create_parser:
  - Current: uses DjangoHelpFormatter for all commands.
  - Assumption encoded: all commands want DjangoHelpFormatter’s behavior (specifically reordering), and no command needs alternate formatting semantics.
  - Fix: replace with dynamic use of self.formatter_class and add default class attribute formatter_class = DjangoHelpFormatter.

Any hardcoded values that need to become dynamic
- The hardcoded class reference formatter_class=DjangoHelpFormatter is the main one; replacing it with self.formatter_class makes it dynamic.
- DjangoHelpFormatter.show_last is a hardcoded set of option strings. It does not need to change for this fix, but note that commands that pick a different formatter_class will not get this reordering automatically. If you want to preserve reordering even when a custom formatter is used, you could add a small utility formatter that combines raw-description semantics with Django’s reordering behavior and document it.

Any methods that need to be added or overridden
- None required for correctness of this change. All existing BaseCommand methods remain valid.
- Optional: add a convenience formatter that combines DjangoHelpFormatter’s reordering with RawDescriptionHelpFormatter behavior (not strictly required by the bug). Example helper (optional) could be:

    import argparse
    class DjangoRawDescriptionHelpFormatter(DjangoHelpFormatter, argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter):
        pass

  This could be added to the file and documented; then command authors can set formatter_class = DjangoRawDescriptionHelpFormatter to get both features without writing their own subclass.

How a command author uses the fix
- After the change, a command author can write:

    import argparse
    class Command(BaseCommand):
        formatter_class = argparse.RawDescriptionHelpFormatter
        help = '''
        Import a contract from tzkt.
        Example usage:
            ./manage.py tzkt_import 'Tezos Mainnet' KT1HTDtMBRCKoNHjfWEEvXneGQpCfPAt6BRe
        '''

- Or set formatter_class to a custom subclass if they want both raw description and Django-like reordering.

Summary patch (one-line summary)
- Add to BaseCommand: formatter_class = DjangoHelpFormatter
- Change create_parser to use formatter_class=self.formatter_class instead of hardcoded DjangoHelpFormatter.

Why this is safe
- Default behavior unchanged: BaseCommand.formatter_class defaults to DjangoHelpFormatter, so existing command output is preserved.
- Backwards-compatible: commands that don't set formatter_class keep previous behavior; commands that do set it get the formatter they want.
- Minimal: single-file change & no other code paths modified.

bug_report.Title: Management command help collapses newlines/indentation because formatter_class is hardcoded to DjangoHelpFormatter
bug_report.Description: Triple-quoted help/description text in Django management commands (example blocks, blank lines and indentation) is not preserved in the output of './manage.py help <command>'. Newlines and indentation from the command's help string are collapsed or wrapped in the printed help output.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) BaseCommand.create_parser hardcodes the argparse formatter class when constructing the parser (django/core/management/base.py). The code constructs the parser with description=self.help and formatter_class=DjangoHelpFormatter (exact code: create_parser passes formatter_class=DjangoHelpFormatter). Because DjangoHelpFormatter subclasses argparse.HelpFormatter (class DjangoHelpFormatter(HelpFormatter):), the parser uses HelpFormatter-style description formatting, which normalizes paragraphs and does not preserve raw newlines/indentation. Commands whose help text depends on preserved newlines/indentation (for example, example usage blocks) therefore cannot rely on the printed help preserving that formatting.

2) DjangoHelpFormatter contains a hardcoded set of option strings that are reordered to appear last in help output (django/core/management/base.py: the show_last set contains "--version", "--verbosity", "--traceback", "--settings", "--pythonpath", "--no-color", "--force-color", "--skip-checks"). The reordering logic (_reordered_actions/add_usage/add_arguments) is implemented only in DjangoHelpFormatter, so choosing a different formatter class would not get that Django-specific reordering behavior automatically. Both the hardcoded formatter_class in create_parser and the hardcoded show_last set in DjangoHelpFormatter are concrete, co-located assumptions in django/core/management/base.py that together explain the observed behavior and the related side-effect on option ordering.
StepsToReproduce:
Create a management command with a triple-quoted help string, e.g.:
class Command(BaseCommand):
    help = '''
    Import a contract from tzkt.
    Example usage:
        ./manage.py tzkt_import 'Tezos Mainnet' KT1HTDtMBRCKoNHjfWEEvXneGQpCfPAt6BRe
    '''
Run: ./manage.py help tzkt_import
Observe the help description output and compare spacing/indentation to the help string in the command.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The command help output preserves blank lines and indentation from the command's help string. For the example above the description should show: a line 'Import a contract from tzkt.' followed by a blank line and an indented 'Example usage:' block with the indented example command on the next line.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: The help output collapses the help description into wrapped paragraphs with lost blank line and indentation. In the example the lines appear run together (e.g. 'Import a contract from tzkt Example usage: ./manage.py tzkt_import ...') and the example's indentation/blank line is not preserved.

bug_report.Title: json_script hardcodes DjangoJSONEncoder; cannot pass custom JSON encoder
bug_report.Description: django.utils.html.json_script always calls json.dumps(..., cls=DjangoJSONEncoder), preventing callers from supplying a custom JSONEncoder subclass for custom encoding behavior. The template filter wrapper also does not accept or forward an encoder parameter.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django.utils.html.json_script (module: django/utils/html.py; function: json_script) hardcodes the JSON encoder by calling json.dumps(value, cls=DjangoJSONEncoder). This encodes the assumption that DjangoJSONEncoder is the only encoder to use.

2) django.template.defaultfilters.json_script (module: django/template/defaultfilters.py; function: json_script) does not accept or forward an encoder parameter to the utility function, so the wrapper cannot propagate a custom encoder from Python-level calls.

3) The only hardcoded value encoding the defective assumption is the explicit use of DjangoJSONEncoder as the cls argument to json.dumps in django/utils/html.py::json_script. The correct relationship is that json.dumps should be called with cls equal to the caller-provided JSONEncoder subclass if supplied; otherwise it should fall back to DjangoJSONEncoder (i.e., cls = provided_cls or DjangoJSONEncoder).

4) Module-level escape mapping used by json_script (_json_script_escapes = {ord('>'): '\\u003E', ord('<'): '\\u003C', ord('&'): '\\u0026'}) is required for safe HTML embedding and is independent of the encoder choice and must be preserved.

5) DjangoJSONEncoder internals (module: django/core/serializers/json.py; class: DjangoJSONEncoder) contain hardcoded formatting slices and timezone assumptions (e.g., r[:23] + r[26:], r[:-6], r[:12]) for ISO formatting of datetime/time strings. These are internal to that encoder and do not depend on json_script's use of that encoder; allowing a custom encoder does not require changing these values.
StepsToReproduce: 1. In a Django project, call django.utils.html.json_script(value) where value contains a Python object that is not handled by DjangoJSONEncoder the way you want (e.g., you want a custom representation).

2. Observe that the JSON output is encoded using DjangoJSONEncoder behavior (e.g., default conversions for datetimes, decimals, UUIDs) and there is no way to pass a custom JSONEncoder subclass to change that behavior.

3. Alternatively, inspect django/utils/html.py and note json.dumps(value, cls=DjangoJSONEncoder) is hardcoded and that django/template/defaultfilters.py's json_script wrapper does not accept or forward any encoder parameter.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The utility function django.utils.html.json_script should allow callers to specify a JSONEncoder subclass (via an optional parameter) to control JSON encoding. When no custom encoder is supplied, it should continue to use DjangoJSONEncoder. The template wrapper should accept the same optional parameter and forward it so Python callers can pass an encoder class.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: json_script always uses DjangoJSONEncoder for json.dumps; there is no parameter that allows using a different encoder. The template filter wrapper also does not accept or forward any encoder parameter.

        # instance, so we access an internal instead of using public interface
        # for performance reasons.
        rel_qs._prefetch_related_lookups = ()

    all_related_objects = list(rel_qs)

    rel_obj_cache = {}
    for rel_obj in all_related_objects:

        # of prefetch_related), so what applies to first object applies to all.

        except exceptions.FieldDoesNotExist:
            pass
        else:

    leaf = len(lookup.prefetch_through.split(LOOKUP_SEP)) - 1 == level

            val = vals[0] if vals else None
            if as_attr:
                # A to_attr has been given for the prefetch.
                setattr(obj, to_attr, val)
            elif is_descriptor:
                # cache_name points to a field name in obj.
                # This field is a descriptor for a related object.
                setattr(obj, cache_name, val)

                # No to_attr has been given for this prefetch operation and the
                # cache_name does not point to a descriptor. Store the value of
                # the field in the object's field cache.
                obj._state.fields_cache[cache_name] = val

class RelatedPopulator:
    """
    RelatedPopulator is used for select_related() object instantiation.

    The idea is that each select_related() model will be populated by a
    different RelatedPopulator instance. The RelatedPopulator instances get
    klass_info and select (computed in SQLCompiler) plus the used db as
    input for initialization. That data is used to compute which columns
    to use, how to instantiate the model, and how to populate the links
    between the objects.

    The actual creation of the objects is done in populate() method. This
    method gets row and from_obj as input and populates the select_related()
    model instance.
    """

    def __init__(self, klass_info, select, db):
        self.db = db
        # Pre-compute needed attributes. The attributes are:
        #  - model_cls: the possibly deferred model class to instantiate
        #  - either:
        #    - cols_start, cols_end: usually the columns in the row are
        #      in the same order model_cls.__init__ expects them, so we
        #      can instantiate by model_cls(*row[cols_start:cols_end])
        #    - reorder_for_init: When select_related descends to a child
        #      class, then we want to reuse the already selected parent
        #      data. However, in this case the parent data isn't necessarily
        #      in the same order that Model.__init__ expects it to be, so
        #      we have to reorder the parent data. The reorder_for_init
        #      attribute contains a function used to reorder the field data
        #      in the order __init__ expects it.
        #  - pk_idx: the index of the primary key field in the reordered
        #    model data. Used to check if a related object exists at all.
        #  - init_list: the field attnames fetched from the database. For
        #    deferred models this isn't the same as all attnames of the
        #    model's fields.
        #  - related_populators: a list of RelatedPopulator instances if

Checkpoint 5 — Final report (complete analysis and fix locations)

Root cause (concise)
- Query.deferred_to_data builds the per-model set of fields that must be included in the SELECT when .only()/.defer() are used. While walking relationship chains the code used opts = cur_model._meta (the Meta for the traversed model). If cur_model is a proxy model, using the proxy _meta causes inconsistent keys in the internal mappings (must_include/seen) that are compared with concrete model fields used later by the compiler and RelatedPopulator. The inconsistency can result in the concrete model primary key column being omitted from the SELECT, and RelatedPopulator then raises ValueError when it cannot find the pk attname in the selected attnames.

Every location that needs to change
1) django/db/models/sql/query.py (primary change)
- Current:
    opts = cur_model._meta
- Problem: cur_model may be a proxy model; using its _meta leads to operating on the proxy's metadata rather than the concrete DB-owning model's metadata.
- Fix:
    opts = cur_model._meta.concrete_model._meta
- Why this is the correct fix:
    - concrete_model returns the concrete class owning the DB table, so using its _meta ensures we refer to the correct db-mapped fields (including pk) when deciding which columns to select.

Why no other files needed changing
- SQLCompiler already builds klass_info based on the actual final select columns produced from the Query configuration (which, after our fix, will include the PKs required). RelatedPopulator already uses concrete_fields in determining which init_list items correspond to a model's fields. The mismatch was caused by deferred_to_data's use of proxy _meta while other parts assumed concrete fields. Fixing the one inconsistent spot makes the overall flow consistent and correct.

Concrete code patch (context and replacement)
- File: django/db/models/sql/query.py
- Within Query.deferred_to_data, inside the for name in parts[:-1] loop, replace these lines:

    if is_reverse_o2o(source):
        cur_model = source.related_model
    else:
        cur_model = source.remote_field.model

    if is_reverse_o2o(source):
        cur_model = source.related_model
    else:
        cur_model = source.remote_field.model
    # Work with the concrete model opts to avoid proxy-meta/concrete-meta mismatches.
    opts = cur_model._meta.concrete_model._meta

Notes / edge cases
- cur_model._meta.concrete_model resolves to cur_model itself if cur_model is already the concrete class. So the code is safe on both concrete and proxy classes.
- The rest of deferred_to_data already uses orig_opts.concrete_model and other concrete_model usages; this fix simply makes the traversal consistent with that.

Testing recommendations
- Add a regression test capturing the original scenario:
  - Define models CustomModel (concrete), ProxyCustomModel (proxy subclass), AnotherModel with ForeignKey to ProxyCustomModel.
  - Query: AnotherModel.objects.select_related("custom").only("custom__name").all() — ensure it evaluates without exception and that the related object's name is available and model instances are of the proxy class (i.e., ProxyCustomModel instances).
- Also test combinations:
  - select_related + only where only selects related__pk explicitly (should work).
  - select_related + only where only selects related__field only (the concrete pk must still be selected by the ORM to allow relation population).

Summary (one-paragraph)
- The bug is caused by Query.deferred_to_data using cur_model._meta (which can be a proxy model's options) when deciding which fields to include for deferred/immediate loading; that produces an inconsistent mapping that can omit the concrete model's primary key column from the SELECT. The correct approach is to always use the concrete model's _meta during this traversal (opts = cur_model._meta.concrete_model._meta). Changing that single line makes the computation of must_include/seen consistent with the rest of the query/compilation pipeline and fixes the ValueError observed when using select_related().only() with proxy models. No other file changes or new methods are required.

bug_report.Title: QuerySet.only() after select_related() crashes when related target is a proxy model
bug_report.Description: When evaluating a QuerySet that uses select_related() to follow a ForeignKey to a proxy model and only() to limit selected fields on that related model (for example only('custom__name')), the ORM raises a ValueError during result population because the concrete related model's primary-key column is omitted from the selected columns.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/db/models/sql/query.py :: Query.deferred_to_data: the method initializes must_include with the original model's concrete_model (must_include = {orig_opts.concrete_model: {orig_opts.pk}}) but, while traversing relationship parts, assigns opts using the traversed class's _meta (opts = cur_model._meta). Because cur_model can be a proxy class, deferred_to_data keys and values can be recorded using proxy classes rather than the concrete model class that owns the DB table. (See the code around lines where must_include is initialized and where opts = cur_model._meta is executed.)

2) django/db/models/sql/compiler.py :: SQLCompiler.get_related_selections: the compiler consults the deferred-to-columns mapping produced by Query.deferred_to_data using the concrete model class as the lookup key (it calls only_load.get(field_model) where field_model = f.model._meta.concrete_model). If deferred_to_data used proxy-class keys, only_load.get(concrete_model) will be a miss and the compiler can therefore omit required concrete-model columns (notably the primary key) from the SELECT for the related model. This mismatch between the keys produced by deferred_to_data and the keys the compiler expects causes omission of concrete columns.

3) django/db/models/query.py :: RelatedPopulator.__init__: RelatedPopulator builds init_list from the selected columns using klass_info["model"]._meta.concrete_fields and then expects the related model's primary key attname to be present in that list (self.pk_idx = self.init_list.index(self.model_cls._meta.pk.attname)). If the concrete model's PK column was omitted from the SELECT (because of the mismatch described above), this index() call raises ValueError ('<pk_attname>' is not in list). RelatedPopulator receives klass_info entries whose "model" value can be a proxy class (klass_info is built from Query.model or f.remote_field.model), so it uses that model's _meta to determine expected attnames while the compiler's column-selection logic works from concrete-model keys.
StepsToReproduce: Define models:
class CustomModel(models.Model):
name = models.CharField(max_length=16)
class ProxyCustomModel(CustomModel):
class Meta: proxy = True
class AnotherModel(models.Model):
custom = models.ForeignKey(ProxyCustomModel, on_delete=models.SET_NULL, null=True, blank=True)
Evaluate the queryset that triggers the issue (example management command handler):
list(AnotherModel.objects.select_related('custom').only('custom__name').all())
Observe the exception during evaluation (ValueError about missing pk attname).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The queryset should evaluate without exception. The ORM should include the concrete model's primary-key column where necessary for related-object population and return AnotherModel instances with their .custom relation populated (ProxyCustomModel instances) and the requested related fields (e.g. name) available.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Evaluating the queryset raises ValueError: 'id' is not in list. Stack trace shows RelatedPopulator.__init__ attempting to find the related model PK attname in the list of selected attnames and failing because the concrete model PK column was not included in the SELECT.

def normalize_together(option_together):
    """
    option_together can be either a tuple of tuples, or a single
    tuple of two strings. Normalize it to a tuple of tuples, so that
    calling code can uniformly expect that.
    """
    try:
        if not option_together:

        if not isinstance(option_together, (tuple, list)):
            raise TypeError
        first_element = option_together[0]
        if not isinstance(first_element, (tuple, list)):

        return option_together

Thought: We must modify inspectdb to generate related_name attributes when generating relations to same model to avoid E304 clashes. In inspectdb.handle_inspection, when it encounters relation columns, it sets rel_to and field_type but doesn't set related_name. We need to produce related_name params when rel_to == self model or when multiple relations point to same target. The bug mentions "relations to same entities" — multiple FKs in the same model to the same target causing reverse accessor name clash. The right fix is to generate related_name on fields when target model is same as source (self relations) or when multiple FKs from one model to another. But inspectdb only knows about current table and relations mapping for that table; to detect multiple FKs referencing same remote table from different columns, it might need to inspect all tables and their relations.

Proposed fix (summary)
- Change inspectdb (django/core/management/commands/inspectdb.py) to auto-generate and emit a related_name argument for ForeignKey/OneToOneField fields when necessary so that reverse accessor name clashes are avoided. Concretely:
  - Before iterating the table_description for a table, analyze the relations mapping for that table to find how many foreign-key columns reference each target table.
  - When emitting a field for a foreign key:
    - If the referenced table is the same table being inspected (self-reference) OR there are multiple columns in this table referencing the same target table (i.e., count > 1), then add extra_params["related_name"] = "<source_model_lower>_<field_name>" where:
      - source_model_lower = table2model(table_name).lower()
      - field_name = the normalized attribute name we are emitting (att_name)
  - Emit this related_name in the generated field constructor (it will be represented as related_name='model_field1' in the generated code).

Rationale:
- The duplicate reverse accessor name by default is model_name + "_set". If two FKs from the same source table point to the same target, they would both attempt to create the same reverse accessor on the target. Generating unique related_name values that incorporate the source model name and the field name produces deterministic names which avoid conflicts and are intuitive (they indicate which source model and which attribute are the origin).

- Add code to compute a mapping of referenced tables -> list of referencing columns (from relations) before the loop that iterates table_description.
- For each relation field, if len(target_refs[ref_db_table]) > 1 or ref_db_table == table_name, add related_name to extra_params with the value shown above.

Root cause
- inspectdb didn't generate related_name on ForeignKey/OneToOne fields. When a table contains multiple foreign keys that point to the same target table (including self-reference), Django's default reverse accessor name (target_model_name + "_set") is the same for each relation, causing a reverse accessor name clash (fields.E304).

- Django's relationship machinery (RelatedField, reverse-related objects) uses remote_field.related_name when present as the final accessor name. Emitting a unique related_name avoids the default duplicate accessor name.
- This fix is local to inspectdb-generated source and doesn't require any changes to the ORM codebase.

bug_report.Title: inspectdb does not emit related_name for multiple FKs to the same target => E304 reverse accessor clash
bug_report.Description: When inspectdb generates models from an existing database, ForeignKey/OneToOne fields that point to the same target model (including self-references or multiple FK columns from one table to the same target) are emitted without a related_name. Django then computes identical default reverse accessor names (target_model_name + '_set') for each relationship, triggering fields.E304 (reverse accessor clash) during model checks.
bug_report.RootCause: 1) django/core/management/commands/inspectdb.py::Command.handle_inspection currently emits relation fields without an explicit related_name parameter. The generator builds rel_type and rel_to and collects extra_params (primary_key, unique, to_field, db_column, null/blank, etc.) but does not add related_name; as a result Django falls back to its default naming. 2) Django's default reverse accessor name is computed as opts.model_name + '_set' (see django/db/models/fields/reverse_related.py), so when two or more incoming relations from the same source table target the same model (including when the source table references itself), the default accessor name is identical for each relation and Django raises fields.E304. 3) For the inspected cases, a deterministic explicit related_name is needed in the generated model source to avoid duplicate default accessors. A suitable deterministic pattern (available from the pieces inspectdb already computes) is related_name="<source_model_lower>_<field_name>" where source_model_lower = table2model(table_name).lower() and field_name is the normalized attribute name produced by inspectdb.normalize_col_name(). This pattern addresses both cases equally: (a) self-referential FKs (ref_db_table == table_name) and (b) when more than one column in the source table references the same target table.
StepsToReproduce: Create a database table 'module_model' with two foreign key columns both referencing the same target table (or referencing the same table itself).
Run python manage.py inspectdb --database=<yourdb> > models.py (or run inspectdb and capture output).
Place the generated models.py into a Django project or run manage.py check against the project.
Observe Django system checks raise fields.E304 about reverse accessor name clashes between the generated fields (e.g. 'module.Model.field1' clashes with 'module.Model.field2').
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: inspectdb-generated model code should include deterministic related_name attributes for relation fields when needed so the generated models import cleanly and do not produce reverse accessor clashes (E304) during Django checks. For multiple FKs from the same source table to the same target (including self-reference), each generated relation in the source model should have a unique related_name that prevents duplicate reverse accessor names on the target.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: inspectdb emits ForeignKey/OneToOne fields without related_name. When a table contains multiple FKs to the same target (or to itself), Django computes the same default reverse accessor name (target_model_name + '_set') for each relationship, causing fields.E304 reverse accessor clashes and requiring the developer to manually edit the generated models to add related_name values.

Django uses this if the database ENGINE setting is empty (None or empty string).

Each of these API functions, except connection.close(), raise

from django.core.exceptions import ImproperlyConfigured

from django.db.backends.base.client import BaseDatabaseClient
from django.db.backends.base.creation import BaseDatabaseCreation
from django.db.backends.base.introspection import BaseDatabaseIntrospection
from django.db.backends.base.operations import BaseDatabaseOperations
from django.db.backends.dummy.features import DummyDatabaseFeatures


def complain(*args, **kwargs):
    raise ImproperlyConfigured(
        "settings.DATABASES is improperly configured. "
        "Please supply the ENGINE value. Check "
        "settings documentation for more details."
    )


def ignore(*args, **kwargs):
    pass


class DatabaseOperations(BaseDatabaseOperations):
    quote_name = complain


class DatabaseClient(BaseDatabaseClient):
    runshell = complain


class DatabaseCreation(BaseDatabaseCreation):
    create_test_db = ignore
    destroy_test_db = ignore


class DatabaseIntrospection(BaseDatabaseIntrospection):
    get_table_list = complain
    get_table_description = complain
    get_relations = complain
    get_indexes = complain


class DatabaseWrapper(BaseDatabaseWrapper):
    operators = {}
    # Override the base class implementations with null
    # implementations. Anything that tries to actually
    # do something raises complain; anything that tries
    # to rollback or undo something raises ignore.
    _cursor = complain
    ensure_connection = complain
    _commit = complain
    _rollback = ignore
    _close = ignore
    _savepoint = ignore
    _savepoint_commit = complain
    _savepoint_rollback = ignore
    _set_autocommit = complain
    # Classes instantiated in __init__().
    client_class = DatabaseClient
    creation_class = DatabaseCreation
    features_class = DummyDatabaseFeatures
    introspection_class = DatabaseIntrospection
    ops_class = DatabaseOperations

    def is_usable(self):
        return True
import subprocess

from django.core.management.base import BaseCommand, CommandError
from django.db import DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS, connections


class Command(BaseCommand):
    help = (
        "Runs the command-line client for specified database, or the "
        "default database if none is provided."
    )

    requires_system_checks = []

    def add_arguments(self, parser):
        parser.add_argument(
            "--database",
            default=DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS,
            help=(
                "Nominates a database onto which to open a shell. Defaults to the "
                '"default" database.'
            ),
        )
        parameters = parser.add_argument_group("parameters", prefix_chars="--")
        parameters.add_argument("parameters", nargs="*")

    def handle(self, **options):
        connection = connections[options["database"]]
        try:
            connection.client.runshell(options["parameters"])
        except FileNotFoundError:
            # Note that we're assuming the FileNotFoundError relates to the
            # command missing. It could be raised for some other reason, in
            # which case this error message would be inaccurate. Still, this
            # message catches the common case.
            raise CommandError(
                "You appear not to have the %r program installed or on your path."
                % connection.client.executable_name
            )
        except subprocess.CalledProcessError as e:
            raise CommandError(
                '"%s" returned non-zero exit status %s.'
                % (
                    " ".join(e.cmd),
                    e.returncode,
                ),
                returncode=e.returncode,
            )

bug_report.Title: PostgreSQL dbshell: parameters must be placed before database name when building psql args
bug_report.Description: When manage.py dbshell passes extra parameters to psql (PostgreSQL), the parameters are currently appended after the database name in the generated command-line. psql expects options/parameters to come before the DBNAME; placing them after causes psql to treat them as extraneous positional arguments (warnings or ignored options). The offending behavior is in the PostgreSQL DatabaseClient that constructs the argument list.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect args ordering in django/db/backends/postgresql/client.py::DatabaseClient.settings_to_cmd_args_env — the method appends the DBNAME to args before extending args with the extra parameters (code sequence: args += [dbname] then args.extend(parameters)). psql requires options/parameters to appear before DBNAME, so the current code places parameters after DBNAME causing psql to treat them as extra positional arguments.

2) The same code-level ordering pattern (database/connection argument appended before parameters) is present in other backend clients (examples: django/db/backends/mysql/client.py, django/db/backends/sqlite3/client.py, django/db/backends/oracle/client.py). In those files the code similarly performs args += [database/connection] and then args.extend(parameters). Those files exhibit the same pattern (the same root-cause code-level sequence), although their respective client executables have different command-line semantics and are not necessarily broken by that ordering. All such occurrences share the same root-cause pattern and are listed here with equal weight.

3) Tests currently encode the old ordering for PostgreSQL: tests/dbshell/test_postgresql.py::test_parameters expects (['psql', 'dbname', '--help'], None). The test expectation reflects the current (incorrect for psql) ordering and therefore will need to be updated to reflect the correct ordering where parameters appear before DBNAME (for example, ['psql', '--help', 'dbname']).
StepsToReproduce: 1) Create a Django project configured to use PostgreSQL and set DATABASES NAME to some_database.
2) Run: ./manage.py dbshell -- -c "select * from some_table;"

3) Observe that psql prints warnings: "psql: warning: extra command-line argument \"-c\" ignored" and "psql: warning: extra command-line argument \"select * from some_table;\" ignored" and then drops you into the database prompt without executing the -c command.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: When passing extra parameters (e.g., -c "SQL") to manage.py dbshell for PostgreSQL, those parameters are given to psql as options (before the DBNAME) so psql executes them. For example, manage.py dbshell -- -c "select * from some_table;" should run that SQL and exit (or behave as psql normally would when -c is provided).
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Parameters passed after the DBNAME are treated as extraneous positional arguments by psql, which issues warnings that the parameters were ignored and does not execute the intended command (example warnings: "psql: warning: extra command-line argument "-c" ignored").

        if min_length is not None:
            self.validators.append(validators.MinLengthValidator(int(min_length)))

        self.validators.append(validators.ProhibitNullCharactersValidator())

        """Return a string."""
        if value not in self.empty_values:
            value = str(value)
            if self.strip:
                value = value.strip()
        if value in self.empty_values:
            return self.empty_value
        return value

    def widget_attrs(self, widget):
        attrs = super().widget_attrs(widget)
        if self.max_length is not None and not widget.is_hidden:
            # The HTML attribute is maxlength, not max_length.
            attrs["maxlength"] = str(self.max_length)
        if self.min_length is not None and not widget.is_hidden:
            # The HTML attribute is minlength, not min_length.
            attrs["minlength"] = str(self.min_length)

        if min_value is not None:
            self.validators.append(validators.MinValueValidator(min_value))
        if step_size is not None:
            self.validators.append(validators.StepValueValidator(step_size))

        """

        of int() or None for empty values.

        if value in self.empty_values:
            return None
        if self.localize:
            value = formats.sanitize_separators(value)

        try:
            value = int(self.re_decimal.sub("", str(value)))
        except (ValueError, TypeError):
            raise ValidationError(self.error_messages["invalid"], code="invalid")

        attrs = super().widget_attrs(widget)
        if isinstance(widget, NumberInput):
            if self.min_value is not None:

            if self.max_value is not None:
                attrs["max"] = self.max_value
            if self.step_size is not None:

        return attrs

        min_value=None,
        max_digits=None,
        decimal_places=None,
        **kwargs,
    ):
        self.max_digits, self.decimal_places = max_digits, decimal_places
        super().__init__(max_value=max_value, min_value=min_value, **kwargs)
        self.validators.append(validators.DecimalValidator(max_digits, decimal_places))

    def to_python(self, value):
        """
        Validate that the input is a decimal number. Return a Decimal
        instance or None for empty values. Ensure that there are no more
        than max_digits in the number and no more than decimal_places digits
        after the decimal point.

        if value in self.empty_values:
            return None
        if self.localize:
            value = formats.sanitize_separators(value)
        try:
            value = Decimal(str(value))
        except DecimalException:
            raise ValidationError(self.error_messages["invalid"], code="invalid")
        return value

    def validate(self, value):
        super().validate(value)
        if value in self.empty_values:
            return
        if not value.is_finite():
            raise ValidationError(
                self.error_messages["invalid"],
                code="invalid",
                params={"value": value},
            )

    def widget_attrs(self, widget):
        attrs = super().widget_attrs(widget)
        if isinstance(widget, NumberInput) and "step" not in widget.attrs:
            if self.decimal_places is not None:

class BaseTemporalField(Field):
    def __init__(self, *, input_formats=None, **kwargs):
        super().__init__(**kwargs)
        if input_formats is not None:
            self.input_formats = input_formats

    def to_python(self, value):
        value = value.strip()
        # Try to strptime against each input format.
        for format in self.input_formats:
            try:
                return self.strptime(value, format)
            except (ValueError, TypeError):
                continue
        raise ValidationError(self.error_messages["invalid"], code="invalid")

    def strptime(self, value, format):
        raise NotImplementedError("Subclasses must define this method.")

        """

        if isinstance(value, datetime.datetime):

        if isinstance(value, datetime.date):

Checkpoint 4: Propose a fix, then immediately challenge it

Proposed fix (summary)
- Add an override of render() to ManagementForm so that when rendering is invoked without an explicit template_name, the ManagementForm produces its hidden input fields directly (i.e., concatenation of the form's hidden fields) and does not call RenderableMixin.render and therefore does not trigger the default.html deprecation warning.
- Preserve the existing behavior when a template_name is explicitly passed (so tests and external code that explicitly render the management form with a template are unaffected), and preserve use of widget templates for each hidden input (so we still get HiddenInput rendering behavior).

Rationale:
- The management form is only a carrier for hidden IntegerFields used by the formset; its HTML is only the set of hidden inputs. The template chosen to render the management form (the general form template) is not semantically important. Emitting the deprecation warning when the only rendered output is hidden input tags is noisy.
- By rendering only the hidden fields directly when template_name is not provided, we avoid rendering through the generic form template and thus avoid the spurious deprecation warning.

Concrete patch (change to django/forms/formsets.py)

- Add an import:
  from django.utils.safestring import mark_safe

- Add this render override to the ManagementForm class (inside the class, after clean()):

    def render(self, template_name=None, context=None, renderer=None):
        """
        For management forms, if no explicit template is requested, render
        only the hidden inputs directly. This avoids emitting the default.html
        deprecation warning when management_form is included at the top of a
        FormSet template. If a template_name is explicitly passed, fall back
        to the normal rendering behavior (which can emit warnings).
        """
        if template_name is None:
            # Render only the hidden inputs (the management form only contains
            # hidden IntegerFields). Use str() on BoundField objects so we use
            # widget rendering (widget templates) for each hidden input.
            return mark_safe("".join(str(f) for f in self.hidden_fields()))
        return super().render(template_name, context, renderer)

Why this is a complete fix:
- ManagementForm is the only place where a Form with only hidden fields is automatically included by a template (FormSet templates include management_form directly).
- The change is local to ManagementForm and doesn't change global RenderableMixin behavior or change the default renderer/template names.
- It preserves behavior when a template_name is explicitly passed.
- HiddenInput widgets still render via their widget templates; we simply avoid going through the form-level template system (which is where the deprecation check is done).

bug_report.Title: Deprecation warning for 'django/forms/default.html' emitted when rendering FormSet.management_form (ManagementForm)
bug_report.Description: Rendering a FormSet that includes its management form (ManagementForm) triggers the template-deprecation warning for the default form template even when the management form only outputs hidden inputs. The warning is raised while producing the management form HTML (the ManagementForm instance is stringified), not because the developer rendered user-facing form markup.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Template-selection assumption: Form instances use the renderer's form-level template when no explicit template is provided. Location: django/forms/forms.py (BaseForm.template_name property returns self.renderer.form_template_name).

2) Default values: The default renderer encodes the deprecated template names as defaults: BaseRenderer.form_template_name == "django/forms/default.html" and BaseRenderer.formset_template_name == "django/forms/formsets/default.html". Location: django/forms/renderers.py (BaseRenderer).

3) Deprecation trigger: RenderableMixin.render issues DEFAULT_TEMPLATE_DEPRECATION_MSG when the selected template equals either exact string "django/forms/default.html" or "django/forms/formsets/default.html" (exact equality check). Location: django/forms/utils.py (RenderableMixin.render).

4) How the management form gets affected: ManagementForm is a plain Form subclass (django/forms/formsets.py: class ManagementForm(Form)) that does not override the inherited rendering flow. BaseFormSet.management_form constructs ManagementForm with renderer=self.renderer, so when the formset uses the default renderer the ManagementForm inherits renderer.form_template_name and is rendered via that (no explicit template_name is passed). Location: django/forms/formsets.py (ManagementForm class and BaseFormSet.management_form property).

5) Why the warning is noisy in this case: The ManagementForm only declares hidden IntegerFields (TOTAL_FORMS, INITIAL_FORMS, MIN_NUM_FORMS, MAX_NUM_FORMS) using HiddenInput widgets, so its intended HTML is only a set of hidden inputs. Rendering it through the form-level default template causes the deprecation warning even though the visible output is hidden inputs and the enclosing formset template (e.g. p/div/table/ul) is the meaningful user-facing template. Location: django/forms/formsets.py (ManagementForm field declarations).
StepsToReproduce: Create a form and a formset (e.g. with formset_factory) using the default form renderer (settings.FORM_RENDERER -> default).
Render the formset (for example, call formset.as_p() or include {{ formset.management_form }} at the top of a formset template).
Observe that a deprecation warning referencing "django/forms/default.html" (DEFAULT_TEMPLATE_DEPRECATION_MSG) is emitted even though the management form only produces hidden input tags.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Including or rendering a FormSet's management form (the hidden-only ManagementForm) should not produce the default-template deprecation warning in the common case where the management form only emits hidden inputs. Deprecation warnings should still be emitted when an actual default form or formset template ("django/forms/default.html" or "django/forms/formsets/default.html") is being used to render visible form/formset markup.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: When a FormSet is rendered (or when its management_form is stringified), Django emits the DEFAULT_TEMPLATE_DEPRECATION_MSG because the ManagementForm falls back to renderer.form_template_name == "django/forms/default.html" (or the formset default), even though the management form only outputs hidden fields.

    def safe_exec(self, string, value=None):
        d = {}
        try:
            exec(string, globals(), d)
        except Exception as e:
            if value:
                self.fail(
                    "Could not exec %r (from value %r): %s" % (string.strip(), value, e)
                )
            else:
                self.fail("Could not exec %r: %s" % (string.strip(), e))
        return d

    def serialize_round_trip(self, value):
        string, imports = MigrationWriter.serialize(value)
        return self.safe_exec(
            "%s\ntest_value_result = %s" % ("\n".join(imports), string), value
        )["test_value_result"]

    def assertSerializedEqual(self, value):
        self.assertEqual(self.serialize_round_trip(value), value)

        self.assertEqual(MigrationWriter.serialize(value), target)

    def assertSerializedFieldEqual(self, value):
        new_value = self.serialize_round_trip(value)
        self.assertEqual(value.__class__, new_value.__class__)
        self.assertEqual(value.max_length, new_value.max_length)

    class EnumSerializer(BaseSerializer):
        def serialize(self):
            enum_class = self.value.__class__
            module = enum_class.__module__
            imports = {"import %s" % module}

            # If it has a concrete name, serialize normally.
            name = getattr(self.value, "name", None)
            if name is not None:
                return ("%s.%s[%r]" % (module, enum_class.__qualname__, name), imports)

            # For Flag/IntFlag combinations, decompose into named members and OR them.
            if issubclass(enum_class, enum.Flag):
                parts = []
                # Include zero-valued member only if the value equals that member.
                for member in enum_class:
                    if member.value == 0:
                        if self.value == member:
                            parts.append("%s.%s[%r]" % (module, enum_class.__qualname__, member.name))
                    else:
                        # For non-zero members, include if bit is set in value.
                        if (self.value & member) == member:
                            parts.append("%s.%s[%r]" % (module, enum_class.__qualname__, member.name))
                if parts:
                    return (" | ".join(parts), imports)

            # Fallback: represent value using repr() (no module import)
            return (repr(self.value), set())

- It preserves existing serialization for single-member enums (name present).
- When enum is a Flag (combinable) and has no single name, it decomposes into known named members and emits an expression that, when executed, reconstructs the same Flag value.
- If decomposition finds nothing, we fall back to repr(self.value) to fail loudly/meaningfully rather than produce module.Class[None].

    class EnumSerializer(BaseSerializer):
        def serialize(self):
            enum_class = self.value.__class__
            module = enum_class.__module__
            imports = {"import %s" % module}

            # If it has a concrete name, serialize normally.
            name = getattr(self.value, "name", None)
            if name is not None:
                return ("%s.%s[%r]" % (module, enum_class.__qualname__, name), imports)

            # For Flag/IntFlag combinations, decompose into named members and OR them.
            if issubclass(enum_class, enum.Flag):
                parts = []
                # Include zero-valued member only if the value equals that member.
                for member in enum_class:
                    if member.value == 0:
                        if self.value == member:
                            parts.append("%s.%s[%r]" % (module, enum_class.__qualname__, member.name))
                    else:
                        # For non-zero members, include if bit is set in value.
                        if (self.value & member) == member:
                            parts.append("%s.%s[%r]" % (module, enum_class.__qualname__, member.name))
                if parts:
                    return (" | ".join(parts), imports)

            # Fallback: represent value using repr() (no module import)
            return (repr(self.value), set())

Notes and justifications:
- We restrict decomposition to issubclass(enum_class, enum.Flag) so normal Enums are unaffected.
- We handle the zero-valued member case to preserve correct serialization of zero-valued named members.
- Using OR expressions comprised of module-qualified Enum member lookups ensures that executing the generated migration code reconstructs the exact combined flag value.
- We left the import set for named-member-based expressions as {"import <module>"}, matching existing behavior.

bug_report.Title: EnumSerializer produces invalid serialization for combined Flag/IntFlag values (e.g. RegexFlag[None])
bug_report.Description: When serializing Enum values (including Flag/IntFlag subclasses) the migrations serializer uses the enum value's .name unconditionally. For combined Flag values (e.g. re.UNICODE | re.IGNORECASE) .name is None, so EnumSerializer emits module.EnumClass[None] (for example default=re.RegexFlag[None]) instead of an expression that reconstructs the combined flags.
bug_report.RootCause:
1. Assumption: EnumSerializer.serialize unconditionally assumes every enum value corresponds to a single named member and therefore always uses self.value.name. Location: django/db/migrations/serializer.py, class EnumSerializer, method serialize. Evidence: the code formats "%s.%s[%r]" % (module, enum_class.__qualname__, self.value.name) and returns it with an import set.

2. Encoding: Because self.value.name can be None for combined Flag/IntFlag values, the unconditional formatting produces strings like re.RegexFlag[None] (repr(None) == 'None'), which are invalid/surprising as migration expressions. Location: same as above; exact code: return ("%s.%s[%r]" % (module, enum_class.__qualname__, self.value.name), {"import %s" % module},).

3. Missing decomposition handling: The serializer contains no special handling for enum.Flag / enum.IntFlag combined values; it does not decompose a multi-bit Flag into its named constituent members to emit an expression that reconstructs the combined value (e.g., module.EnumClass['A'] | module.EnumClass['B']). Location: django/db/migrations/serializer.py, class EnumSerializer, method serialize.

4. Zero-valued member corner-case: When decomposing Flag values, zero-valued named members must be treated specially: a member with value 0 should only be emitted if the whole enum value equals that member (otherwise zero members would be incorrectly included or omitted). This logic would need to be present in decomposition code. Location: decomposition logic to be added in django/db/migrations/serializer.py, class EnumSerializer, method serialize.

5. Fallback behavior: If decomposition finds no named members (for bits that do not correspond to declared members), the serializer should not emit module.EnumClass[None]; instead it should fall back to a safer representation (e.g., repr(self.value)) so that the migration contains a valid Python representation or fails more explicitly. Location: django/db/migrations/serializer.py, class EnumSerializer, method serialize.
StepsToReproduce: Create a model field or object that uses combined re.RegexFlag values, for example: regex_flags = models.IntegerField(default=re.UNICODE | re.IGNORECASE)
Run makemigrations to generate a migration that captures this default value
Open the generated migration file and inspect the serialized default value
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Combined Flag/IntFlag enum values should be serialized as valid Python expressions that reconstruct the same combined enum value when evaluated in the migration. For example a combined re.RegexFlag value should appear as: re.RegexFlag['UNICODE'] | re.RegexFlag['IGNORECASE'] (with the necessary import), not re.RegexFlag[None].
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Combined Flag/IntFlag enum values are serialized using the enum value's .name unconditionally; when .name is None for combined values, this results in output such as re.RegexFlag[None] (invalid/surprising representation) in generated migrations.

class DeclarativeFieldsMetaclass(MediaDefiningClass):

            for key, value in list(attrs.items())
            if isinstance(value, Field)

        new_class = super().__new__(mcs, name, bases, attrs)

Proposed fix (high level):
- In BaseFormSet.empty_form, obtain the kwarg dict from self.get_form_kwargs(None) first, remove any keys that are also explicitly supplied to self.form in the call (the keys are: "auto_id", "prefix", "empty_permitted", "use_required_attribute", "renderer"), and then expand that sanitized dict into the form constructor. This ensures that explicit, known values cannot be duplicated by user-supplied form_kwargs and that user-supplied custom kwargs (e.g., custom_kwarg) still flow through.

Current code (lines ~258–269):
- (existing)
  @property
  def empty_form(self):
      form = self.form(
          auto_id=self.auto_id,
          prefix=self.add_prefix("__prefix__"),
          empty_permitted=True,

Proposed replacement:
  @property
  def empty_form(self):
      # Collect user-supplied form kwargs for the empty form (index None).
      form_kwargs = self.get_form_kwargs(None).copy()
      # Remove keys that would conflict with the explicit arguments below.
      for key in ("auto_id", "prefix", "empty_permitted", "use_required_attribute", "renderer"):
          form_kwargs.pop(key, None)
      form = self.form(
          auto_id=self.auto_id,
          prefix=self.add_prefix("__prefix__"),
          empty_permitted=True,
          use_required_attribute=False,
          renderer=self.renderer,
          **form_kwargs,
      )
      self.add_fields(form, None)
      return form

This is a minimal, focused change that:
- keeps the explicit, required behavior for empty_form (empty_permitted=True, use_required_attribute=False),
- continues to allow custom kwargs (custom_kwarg) through to the empty form,
- avoids duplicate keyword errors when a user (mistakenly or deliberately) sets keys like empty_permitted in form_kwargs.

Checkpoint 5: Final report (root cause, every affected location, and the complete fix)

Root cause
- BaseFormSet.empty_form calls the form constructor with explicit keyword arguments AND expands the dict returned from get_form_kwargs(None) afterwards. If the user-supplied dict includes any of the same keys (notably 'empty_permitted'), Python tries to pass the same keyword twice to the Form.__init__, causing a runtime error when accessing formset.empty_form (observed as an exception in the rendering path).
- The code assumes get_form_kwargs(None) will not include keys that empty_form sets explicitly. This assumption is invalid because form_kwargs is user-supplied and may include those keys. empty_permitted is a legitimate Form kwarg so it's plausible a user will pass it.

Every location that needs to change (only the minimal necessary):
1) django/forms/formsets.py — BaseFormSet.empty_form
   - Current behavior:
     - Calls self.get_form_kwargs(None) and expands the returned dict after giving explicit keywords to the form constructor:
       form = self.form(auto_id=..., prefix=..., empty_permitted=True, use_required_attribute=False, **self.get_form_kwargs(None), renderer=self.renderer)
     - This allows duplicate keys (e.g., 'empty_permitted') to be passed twice.
   - Problem: Duplicate keywords cause runtime exception.
   - Fix:
     - Build a copy of the dict returned by get_form_kwargs(None), remove any keys that would collide with explicit keywords (auto_id, prefix, empty_permitted, use_required_attribute, renderer), then expand the sanitized dict.
   - Patch (full replacement for the empty_form property):
     @property
     def empty_form(self):
         # Collect user-supplied form kwargs for the empty form (index None).
         form_kwargs = self.get_form_kwargs(None).copy()
         # Remove keys that would conflict with the explicit arguments below.
         for key in ("auto_id", "prefix", "empty_permitted", "use_required_attribute", "renderer"):
             form_kwargs.pop(key, None)
         form = self.form(
             auto_id=self.auto_id,
             prefix=self.add_prefix("__prefix__"),
             empty_permitted=True,
             use_required_attribute=False,
             renderer=self.renderer,
             **form_kwargs,
         )
         self.add_fields(form, None)
         return form

Why this fix is complete
- It prevents duplicate keyword errors by ensuring the explicit keywords cannot be duplicated by the ** expansion.
- It preserves the intended semantics:
  - empty_form always gets empty_permitted=True (as it should).
  - custom user keys (e.g., custom_kwarg) still reach empty_form.
  - other code paths (non-empty forms produced via _construct_form) are unchanged and remain able to override defaults via form_kwargs.
- It avoids mutating the user's original form_kwargs dict because it operates on a copy.

Any other locations considered and why they didn't need to change
- _construct_form: uses a single dict (defaults) and then defaults.update(kwargs) before calling form = self.form(**defaults). This is safe (no duplicate-key problem) and therefore unchanged.
- BaseModelFormSet and modelformset_factory: they do not create empty_form by themselves; they rely on BaseFormSet.empty_form, so changing BaseFormSet.empty_form resolves the issue for model formsets too.
- No other references to get_form_kwargs(None) call patterns were found that would expand user kwargs after explicit keywords — I searched for get_form_kwargs(None) and found only the usage in empty_form.

Tests / expected behavior
- Existing tests (test_form_kwargs_empty_form) expect custom kwargs to be present on empty_form; that test still passes with this change.
- The bug repro case in the report (form_kwargs = {'empty_permitted': True} or False) will no longer crash when rendering formset.empty_form.
- empty_form.empty_permitted remains True (test at tests/forms_tests/tests/test_formsets.py:579 expects that).

Notes / small implementation details
- Use .copy() on the dict returned by get_form_kwargs(None). The default BaseFormSet.get_form_kwargs returns self.form_kwargs.copy(), but subclasses may override get_form_kwargs and return the actual shared dict. Using copy() ensures we don't mutate the returned object or the formset's stored form_kwargs.
- I removed only the explicit conflicting keys; this keeps user control over other kwargs they may pass.
- I preserved a direct call to renderer=self.renderer (and popped 'renderer' from the user dict) so that empty_form always uses the same renderer the formset is configured with.

bug_report.Title: Accessing formset.empty_form raises exception when form_kwargs contains empty_permitted
bug_report.Description: Constructing a formset with form_kwargs that include Form keyword(s) that BaseFormSet.empty_form also supplies (for example 'empty_permitted') causes an exception when a template or code accesses formset.empty_form. The failure occurs during empty_form construction in the formset implementation.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/forms/formsets.py :: BaseFormSet.empty_form — The empty_form property calls the form constructor with explicit keyword arguments (auto_id=self.auto_id, prefix=self.add_prefix("__prefix__"), empty_permitted=True, use_required_attribute=False, renderer=self.renderer) and also expands the dictionary returned by self.get_form_kwargs(None) into the same call (the code uses **self.get_form_kwargs(None)). Because get_form_kwargs(None) is user-controlled (it returns a copy of self.form_kwargs by default and may be overridden), it may include any valid Form kwargs. If that dict contains any of the same keys that empty_form supplies explicitly (notably 'empty_permitted', but also 'auto_id', 'prefix', 'use_required_attribute', or 'renderer'), Python will attempt to pass the same keyword argument twice to Form.__init__, resulting in a runtime error (Python raises a TypeError for duplicate keyword arguments). Location: django/forms/formsets.py :: BaseFormSet.empty_form (lines where form(...) is invoked with explicit kwargs then **self.get_form_kwargs(None)).

2) Incorrect assumption encoded in BaseFormSet.empty_form — The implementation assumes the dict returned by get_form_kwargs(None) will not include keys that empty_form supplies explicitly. That assumption is invalid because 'empty_permitted' (and the other explicit names) are legitimate Form.__init__ kwargs and callers may include them in form_kwargs or via custom get_form_kwargs. Form.__init__ accepts empty_permitted (django/forms/forms.py :: BaseForm.__init__), so passing empty_permitted via form_kwargs is a valid/expected caller action; empty_form creation must therefore tolerate such inputs without causing duplicate-key errors.

3) Contrast with non-empty form construction — BaseFormSet._construct_form avoids this duplicate-key risk by creating a single defaults dict, conditionally setting values (including defaults['empty_permitted'] when appropriate), updating it with kwargs returned by get_form_kwargs(i), and then calling self.form(**defaults). This single-dict pattern prevents duplicate keyword delivery because user-supplied kwargs override defaults rather than being passed twice. Location: django/forms/formsets.py :: BaseFormSet._construct_form.

4) Extent of impact — Any formset class that inherits BaseFormSet (including BaseModelFormSet and formsets produced by modelformset_factory) uses BaseFormSet.empty_form and is thus affected. The issue can occur whether form_kwargs is supplied as a static dict when constructing the formset or provided dynamically via an overridden get_form_kwargs(index) that returns a dict for index None.
StepsToReproduce: Define a model Model with a_field and a view that constructs a modelformset_factory for that model.
Instantiate the formset with queryset=Model.objects.none() and form_kwargs={'empty_permitted': True} (or False).
Render a template that references {{ formset }} and {{ formset.empty_form }} (e.g., include {{ formset.empty_form }} outside the form).
Load the view in a browser or request the URL that renders the template; observe the exception when the template accesses formset.empty_form.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Rendering a template that accesses formset.empty_form succeeds even if the formset was constructed with form_kwargs that include any Form.__init__ kwargs (including 'empty_permitted'). The empty_form should have empty_permitted set to True (empty_form is inherently permitted to be empty) and non-conflicting custom form_kwargs should be applied to empty_form.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Accessing formset.empty_form raises a runtime exception during empty_form construction because duplicate keyword arguments are passed into the Form constructor when form_kwargs (or get_form_kwargs(None)) contains a key that BaseFormSet.empty_form also supplies (notably 'empty_permitted'). Python reports this as a TypeError because the same keyword argument is being provided more than once.

from decimal import Decimal

from django.conf import settings
from django.utils.safestring import mark_safe


def format(
    number,
    decimal_sep,
    decimal_pos=None,
    grouping=0,
    thousand_sep="",
    force_grouping=False,
    use_l10n=None,
):
    """
    Get a number (as a number or string), and return it as a string,
    using formats defined as arguments:

    * decimal_sep: Decimal separator symbol (for example ".")
    * decimal_pos: Number of decimal positions
    * grouping: Number of digits in every group limited by thousand separator.
        For non-uniform digit grouping, it can be a sequence with the number
        of digit group sizes following the format used by the Python locale
        module in locale.localeconv() LC_NUMERIC grouping (e.g. (3, 2, 0)).
    * thousand_sep: Thousand separator symbol (for example ",")
    """
    use_grouping = (
        use_l10n or (use_l10n is None and settings.USE_L10N)
    ) and settings.USE_THOUSAND_SEPARATOR
    use_grouping = use_grouping or force_grouping
    use_grouping = use_grouping and grouping != 0
    # Make the common case fast
    if isinstance(number, int) and not use_grouping and not decimal_pos:
        return mark_safe(number)
    # sign
    sign = ""
    # Treat potentially very large/small floats as Decimals.
    if isinstance(number, float) and "e" in str(number).lower():
        number = Decimal(str(number))
    if isinstance(number, Decimal):

        if decimal_pos is not None:
            # If the provided number is too small to affect any of the visible
            # decimal places, consider it equal to '0'.
            cutoff = Decimal("0." + "1".rjust(decimal_pos, "0"))
            if abs(number) < cutoff:
                number = Decimal("0")

        # Format values with more than 200 digits (an arbitrary cutoff) using
        # scientific notation to avoid high memory usage in {:f}'.format().
        _, digits, exponent = number.as_tuple()
        if abs(exponent) + len(digits) > 200:
            number = "{:e}".format(number)
            coefficient, exponent = number.split("e")
            # Format the coefficient.
            coefficient = format(
                coefficient,
                decimal_sep,
                decimal_pos,
                grouping,
                thousand_sep,
                force_grouping,
                use_l10n,
            )
            return "{}e{}".format(coefficient, exponent)
        else:
            str_number = "{:f}".format(number)
    else:
        str_number = str(number)
    if str_number[0] == "-":
        sign = "-"
        str_number = str_number[1:]
    # decimal part
    if "." in str_number:
        int_part, dec_part = str_number.split(".")
        if decimal_pos is not None:
            dec_part = dec_part[:decimal_pos]
    else:
        int_part, dec_part = str_number, ""
    if decimal_pos is not None:
        dec_part = dec_part + ("0" * (decimal_pos - len(dec_part)))
    dec_part = dec_part and decimal_sep + dec_part
    # grouping
    if use_grouping:
        try:
            # if grouping is a sequence
            intervals = list(grouping)
        except TypeError:
            # grouping is a single value
            intervals = [grouping, 0]
        active_interval = intervals.pop(0)
        int_part_gd = ""
        cnt = 0
        for digit in int_part[::-1]:
            if cnt and cnt == active_interval:
                if intervals:
                    active_interval = intervals.pop(0) or active_interval
                int_part_gd += thousand_sep[::-1]
                cnt = 0
            int_part_gd += digit
            cnt += 1
        int_part = int_part_gd[::-1]
    return sign + int_part + dec_part

Primary location of bug:

    str_number = str(number)
    if str_number[0] == "-":
        sign = "-"
        str_number = str_number[1:]

If str_number is an empty string (''), attempting str_number[0] raises IndexError: string index out of range. That is the crash reported.

Clear statement of the bug and primary responsible method/class:
- Bug: numberformat.format() indexes the first character of str(number) without checking whether the resulting string is empty; this raises IndexError when an empty string is passed as the number (which can happen in some contexts when formatting values for admin list_display).
- Primary responsible function: django.utils.numberformat.format.

All functions defined in file:

Class-level attributes: none (no classes).

  (This returns mark_safe(number) where number is an int. mark_safe will coerce to str internally; it's safer to explicitly pass a string — see fix section.)

- Else it does str_number = str(number)

Checkpoint 4: Propose a fix, then immediately challenge it

Proposed fix (summary):
1) In django/utils/numberformat.py, make the function robust to empty strings by checking for empty str_number after converting number to str(). If str_number is empty, return it as-is (an empty string).
2) Also make the earlier fast-path explicit and safe by converting the int to a string before calling mark_safe (i.e., mark_safe(str(number))). This prevents passing non-strings to mark_safe and is a small robustness improvement that doesn't change behavior.

Concrete patch (diff-style, showing the minimal changes):

In django/utils/numberformat.py:

Replace:

    # Make the common case fast
    if isinstance(number, int) and not use_grouping and not decimal_pos:
        return mark_safe(number)
    # sign
    sign = ""
    ...
    else:
        str_number = str(number)
    if str_number[0] == "-":
        sign = "-"
        str_number = str_number[1:]

With:

    # Make the common case fast
    if isinstance(number, int) and not use_grouping and not decimal_pos:
        return mark_safe(str(number))
    # sign
    sign = ""
    ...
    else:
        str_number = str(number)
    # Guard against empty string inputs (avoid IndexError on str_number[0])
    if not str_number:
        return str_number
    if str_number[0] == "-":
        sign = "-"
        str_number = str_number[1:]

Rationale:
- The immediate cause of IndexError is indexing an empty string. Guarding with if not str_number avoids that.
- Returning the empty string preserves the caller's expectation (if input was '', return ''). This is the least surprising behavior.
- Converting int to string in the fast path when calling mark_safe avoids passing a non-string to mark_safe (defensive fix).

4a) "What assumption does my fix change?"
- One-sentence: The current code assumes that str(number) always produces a non-empty string; my fix removes this assumption, allowing empty strings to be formatted without raising an IndexError.

- There are no hardcoded numeric constants whose correctness depends on the assumption that the input string is non-empty. The main hardcoded constants in the module are:

  - Default grouping (grouping=0) and default thousand_sep="" — these are defaults but not tied to the empty-string assumption.
- Conclusion: None of these need to become dynamic because of the empty-string fix. They encode other assumptions (size cutoff, grouping policy) that the fix does not change.

4c) "What about the reverse operation?"
- The "reverse operation" would be parsing or normalizing numeric input strings (e.g., django.utils.formats.sanitize_separators).
- I re-read formats.sanitize_separators (it accepts strings and tries to normalize localized decimal and thousand separators into a decimal-dot normalized string). That function expects a string input and handles empty strings gracefully — if value is a string, it builds parts and can return value ".".join(reversed(parts)). If value is empty string, the method's behavior is safe (it will set parts=[] then append value at the end and ultimately return value).

bug_report.Description: Formatting a numeric value that becomes an empty string (for example, a value represented as '') can raise IndexError: "string index out of range" inside django.utils.numberformat.format. bug_report.RootCause:
