Location: django/utils/numberformat.py, function format(...). Evidence: code paths set str_number = str(number) (line 70) and then test if str_number[0] == '-' (line 71); if str_number == '' this raises IndexError: 'string index out of range'.

2) Secondary observation — inconsistent fast-path argument type: the function contains an early fast-path that returns mark_safe(number) for ints without explicitly converting number to a string. Location: django/utils/numberformat.py, early fast-path in format(...). Evidence: lines 34–35 show return mark_safe(number). Note: mark_safe will coerce the argument to a string (see django/utils/safestring.py), so this is an inconsistency/robustness observation rather than the direct cause of the reported IndexError.

3) Caller context that exposes the issue: the formatting wrapper django.utils.formats.number_format forwards its value argument directly to django.utils.numberformat.format (location: django/utils/formats.py), and admin utilities check for value is None and return early (django/contrib/admin/utils.py lines 417 and 443). Because callers can still pass empty strings (''), an empty-string value can reach numberformat.format and trigger the unguarded indexing. Evidence: formats.number_format forwards value (lines 175–196), and admin utilities return early for None but do not prevent callers from passing empty strings to the formatter (django/contrib/admin/utils.py lines 417–426 and 438–456).
StepsToReproduce: Start a Python session with Django on the PYTHONPATH (or within a Django project context).
Import the formatter directly: from django.utils.numberformat import format as number_format
Call number_format('', '.') — i.e. pass an empty string as the number and '.' as the decimal separator (matching numberformat.format signature).
Observe IndexError: 'string index out of range' raised from django/utils/numberformat.py (originating at the line that checks str_number[0]).
Alternate reproduction: call django.utils.formats.number_format('') (the formats wrapper), which forwards the empty string to django.utils.numberformat.format and triggers the same error.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Passing an empty string to the number formatter should not raise an unhandled exception. The formatter should handle empty-string inputs gracefully and return a sensible string (for example, the empty string) so that callers (admin list_display, templates, or other code) do not crash when presented with empty inputs.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: An IndexError: 'string index out of range' is raised inside django/utils/numberformat.py when format() converts the input to a string and checks str_number[0] on an empty string, causing callers (such as code rendering admin list_display or code calling formats.number_format) to fail with an uncaught exception.

Step 1b — locate relevant files - Found the classes and relevant code in: - django/contrib/auth/forms.py (UserChangeForm, ReadOnlyPasswordHashField, ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget, UsernameField, PasswordResetForm, etc.) - django/contrib/auth/admin.py (UserAdmin and user_change_password URL/view) - django/contrib/admin/options.py (ModelAdmin.changeform handling, _to_field handling) - django/contrib/admin/widgets.py (RelatedFieldWidgetWrapper producing change link URLs for related lookups) - tests/auth_tests/... (tests that assert the password link behavior) Step 1c — open relevant source - I read django/contrib/auth/forms.py (entire file), django/contrib/auth/admin.py, django/contrib/admin/options.py, django/contrib/admin/widgets.py, django/forms/models.py (ModelForm / BaseModelForm), and the tests that verify the password link (tests/auth_tests/test_views.py and tests/auth_tests/test_forms.py). Step 1d — statement of the bug - Root symptom: When the admin change form for a User is opened from a related lookup that uses to_field (so the change URL uses the non-PK value in the path, e.g. /admin/auth/user//change/?_to_field=uuid), the help_text link in the ReadOnly password field points to a relative URL ("../password/") that resolves to /admin/auth/user//password/ and thus calls the password-change view with id=. The password-change view expects the PK (so get_object is called without the to_field parameter) and fails to find the User, producing a 404. - Primary responsible code: UserChangeForm.__init__ in django/contrib/auth/forms.py, specifically the line password.help_text = password.help_text.format("../password/") This hardcoded relative path assumes the change URL always contains the PK as the path segment immediately before "change/". That assumption is invalid when the change view is being referenced via a different field (to_field). Checkpoint 2 — Read the full file and catalog everything (forms.py) I read the full file django/contrib/auth/forms.py. Classes defined (in file order), their parent classes, class-level attributes and methods: 1) ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget (parent: forms.Widget) - class-level attrs: template_name = "auth/widgets/read_only_password_hash.html", read_only = True - methods: get_context(self, name, value, attrs), id_for_label(self, id_) 2) ReadOnlyPasswordHashField (parent: forms.Field) - class-level attrs: widget = ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget - methods: __init__(self, *args, **kwargs) — sets required=False, disabled=True then calls super() 3) UsernameField (parent: forms.CharField) - methods: to_python(self, value), widget_attrs(self, widget) 4) UserCreationForm (parent: forms.ModelForm) - class-level attrs: error_messages, password1, password2, inner Meta: model = User, fields = ("username",), field_classes = {"username": UsernameField} - methods: __init__, clean_password2, _post_clean, save 5) UserChangeForm (parent: forms.ModelForm) <-- primary class - class-level attrs: - password = ReadOnlyPasswordHashField(label=..., help_text=_('Raw passwords ... this form.')) - inner Meta: model = User, fields = "__all__", field_classes = {"username": UsernameField} - methods: __init__(self, *args, **kwargs) - In __init__, it gets password field and does: password.help_text = password.help_text.format("../password/") then optimizes user_permissions queryset select_related("content_type"). 6) AuthenticationForm (parent: forms.Form) 7) PasswordResetForm (parent: forms.Form) - etc. 8) SetPasswordForm, PasswordChangeForm, AdminPasswordChangeForm (many further classes in the file, but they don't affect the particular bug). Component classes referenced by the primary class UserChangeForm (class-level attributes that point to other classes): - ReadOnlyPasswordHashField (the password field) - UsernameField (in Meta.field_classes) - User (the model in Meta.model is django.contrib.auth.models.User) Checkpoint 3 — Map the architecture 3a) Inspect component classes in full (we already read them in forms.py) - ReadOnlyPasswordHashField: - widget = ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget - __init__ sets required False and disabled True - No hardcoded URL/path values. - ReadOnlyPasswordHashWidget: - template_name and read_only = True - get_context constructs a summary depending on the stored hash and identify_hasher() - No hardcoded URLs. - UsernameField: - minor widget attrs, no hardcoded values important for this bug. The only hardcoded URL/path-like constant involved is in UserChangeForm.__init__: "../password/" This is a relative URL fragment used to format the help_text link. 3b) Parent class for UserChangeForm - UserChangeForm inherits from forms.ModelForm. - ModelForm itself is a thin subclass (no additional methods) of BaseModelForm. - BaseModelForm (in django/forms/models.py) defines all important ModelForm behavior. Methods include (non-exhaustive list — the key ones): - __init__(...) — sets self.instance (model instance), fills fields, etc. - _get_validation_exclusions - clean - _update_errors - _post_clean - validate_unique - save (defined near top of file — constructs instance, saves m2m) - Several other helpers (construct_instance, etc.) Which methods does UserChangeForm override? - UserChangeForm only overrides __init__. - It inherits all other ModelForm/BaseModelForm methods unchanged. Why this matters: - The __init__ method is executed after BaseModelForm.__init__ has set self.instance (possibly to the model() default when instance not provided). So self.instance is available in UserChangeForm.__init__. 3c) Sibling patterns - There is a sibling UserCreationForm (also a ModelForm) but it doesn't set any URL-based help_text. - RelatedFieldWidgetWrapper in django/contrib/admin/widgets.py creates related change/add links and includes to_field var when building the querystring. That code properly supports to_field. That is why related lookup popups can request change views by non-PK values (the popups include the TO_FIELD_VAR param), and admin changeform_view will use that TO_FIELD_VAR to look up objects by that field. But the password-change view URL (UserAdmin.get_urls) is a separate URL pattern //password/ and that view uses get_object with the id path param; it does not receive the TO_FIELD_VAR (the password change link does not include the TO_FIELD_VAR), and so it always tries to fetch by the model PK. Therefore the help_text link must point to the pk-based password-change URL. 3d) Call graph around primary class - The change form is constructed in ModelAdmin._changeform_view: - ModelForm = self.get_form(request, obj, change=not add, fields=...) - form = ModelForm(instance=obj) - UserAdmin.get_urls includes path("/password/", self.user_change_password, name="auth_user_password_change"). - user_change_password uses self.get_object(request, unquote(id)) to load the user (using pk unless a to_field param is passed — but the URL does not include to_field). Checkpoint 4 — Propose a fix, then challenge it Proposed fix (code change) - Replace the brittle relative link formatting in UserChangeForm.__init__ with a format that resolves to the password-change URL using the object's PK when possible, otherwise fall back to the original relative path. Suggested change in django/contrib/auth/forms.py: Current code: def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) password = self.fields.get("password") if password: password.help_text = password.help_text.format("../password/") ... Proposed code: def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) password = self.fields.get("password") if password: # If the instance has a PK, format the help link to point to the # admin password-change URL for that PK to avoid broken links when # the change form is accessed using a non-PK path segment via # _to_field. Fall back to the original relative link when there's # no PK (e.g. an unsaved instance). if getattr(self.instance, "pk", None) is not None: password.help_text = password.help_text.format(f"../../{self.instance.pk}/password/") else: password.help_text = password.help_text.format("../password/") Rationale: - Using the instance PK ensures that the link targets the URL pattern used by UserAdmin.user_change_password (which expects the PK). - Using "../../{pk}/password/" as a relative link relative to the current change URL (/...//change/) produces /...//password/ regardless of whether the current in the path is a PK or a different field value (to_field case). - Fallback to "../password/" for instances without PK keeps behavior for add/unsaved instances and avoids introducing “None” into the URL. Now the required checks from the protocol: 4a) "What assumption does my fix change?" - The code originally assumed that the change view URL's path segment is always the model instance's primary key; the fix removes that assumption by constructing a help link that points to the password-change URL using the instance's actual PK (when available), rather than assuming the current path segment equals the PK. 4b) "What hardcoded values encode this assumption?" - The hardcoded "../password/" encodes the assumption that the change view URL structure is always ...//change/, so stepping up one path segment and appending "password/" yields ...//password/. - If we remove the assumption, "../password/" is not robust; the new value f"../../{self.instance.pk}/password/" encodes the assumption that the change URL has at least two directory levels and that stepping up two levels and appending "/password/" constructs the correct path. But this is safe for current admin URL structure: change URL is "...//change/" and password URL is "...//password/". Two-level relative construction (../..//password/) transforms both: - /...//change/ + "../..//password/" -> /...//password/ - /...//change/ + "../..//password/" -> /...//password/ - Note: To be robust, we use the instance.pk value rather than the path's current id segment. The hardcoded relative navigation remains ("../../") but it's acceptable because we control both sides of the URL within the admin URL namespace and the change URL and password URL are siblings within the model's admin URL space. The fallback "../password/" preserves behavior when instance.pk is None. 4c) "What about the reverse operation?" - The "reverse" complementary operations would be code that resolves and uses the password-change URL when the password-change form finishes. UserAdmin.user_change_password constructs a redirect after successful password change using: reverse("%s:%s_%s_change" % (self.admin_site.name, user._meta.app_label, user._meta.model_name), args=(user.pk,)) i.e., it expects the password-change endpoint is called with the user's PK, and it redirects to the change view using user.pk. The new help_text link (using instance.pk) points to the same expected password-change endpoint, so it matches the reverse/dependent behavior of user_change_password and response redirect. Therefore no complementary method needs changing. - Specifically, ModelAdmin.get_urls and UserAdmin.user_change_password expect PK-based password-change URLs, so our constructed URL (using instance.pk) is consistent with that. 4d) "Does every existing method still work?" - Methods in UserChangeForm: only __init__ is modified. Behavior for other methods (save, _post_clean, etc.) is not affected. - The __init__ change: - When instance has a PK (typical change form), help_text now uses "../..//password/" — this yields the correct link both in normal and to_field access patterns. - When instance has no PK (unsaved instance, or code constructs the form without instance), we fall back to "../password/" to preserve previous behavior and avoid inserting "None" into the URL. This preserves tests that create the form without instance (test_bug_14242 creates MyUserForm({}) just to ensure it constructs without error). - ModelAdmin and UserAdmin behavior: Unchanged; user_change_password view still works as before. The password change form and flow are consistent. 4e) "Does any NEW method need to be added?" - No new methods are needed. The change is local to UserChangeForm.__init__. - We do not need to change admin URL patterns or UserAdmin.user_change_password, because the password-change URL remains PK-based and our link will target it correctly. Additional test suggestions to avoid regressions - There is an existing test test_user_change_password in tests/auth_tests/test_views.py which asserts the link in the User change page resolves to the password change URL in the normal case. This test will continue to pass. - Ideally, add a regression test to assert that when the change view is accessed with a different path id value (simulating the behavior when _to_field is present), the help_text link still resolves to the PK-based password change URL. Creating a full test that replicates the admin popup -> to_field flow requires registering an auxiliary model that references User with to_field and is non-trivial; I recommend adding such an integration test in tests/admin_widgets or tests/admin_views where to_field lookup scenarios are already set up. Checklist / locations to change - File to change: - django/contrib/auth/forms.py - Change in UserChangeForm.__init__, lines where password.help_text is formatted. - No other files need changes. Concrete patch (conceptual — apply to django/contrib/auth/forms.py): Replace (current): def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) password = self.fields.get("password") if password: password.help_text = password.help_text.format("../password/") user_permissions = self.fields.get("user_permissions") ... With (proposed): def __init__(self, *args, **kwargs): super().__init__(*args, **kwargs) password = self.fields.get("password") if password: # If instance.pk is available, point the help link at the password # change URL for that PK (avoids broken links when change form is # accessed via a non-PK path segment using _to_field). bug_report.Title: UserAdmin password-change link broken (404) when User change page is accessed via related to_field
bug_report.Description: When the Django User change form is opened from another model's admin via a related lookup that uses to_field (so the change URL is like .../user/<to_field_value>/change/?_to_field=uuid), the "this form" link in the read-only password field points to a URL that results in a 404.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Hardcoded relative link in UserChangeForm.__init__ (django/contrib/auth/forms.py) — the code formats the help text with the literal string "../password/":
   password.help_text = password.help_text.format("../password/")
   This encodes the incorrect assumption that the path segment immediately before "change/" in the admin change URL is always the object's primary key (PK). The current hardcoded value is "../password/".

2) UserAdmin password-change URL/view expects a PK in the path (django/contrib/auth/admin.py) — get_urls registers the pattern "<id>/password/" and user_change_password calls self.get_object(request, unquote(id)) without passing a from_field, i.e. it looks up by the model PK and treats the path segment as a primary key (the view's Http404 message explicitly references "primary key"). Therefore the password-change view requires the id path segment to be the object's PK.

3) Admin related-lookup/to_field flow can produce change URLs that use a non-PK identifier and include the _to_field query parameter (django/contrib/admin/widgets.py and django/contrib/admin/options.py) — RelatedFieldWidgetWrapper and other admin widgets add the TO_FIELD_VAR ("_to_field") query parameter when producing related-change links, and client-side code substitutes the related-field value into the change URL template. ModelAdmin.get_object supports a from_field argument and can resolve objects by a non-PK field when that parameter is supplied. As a result, the admin related-lookup flow can produce a change URL whose path segment is a to_field value rather than the PK.

Net effect (how these three facts combine): because UserChangeForm.__init__ injects the relative fragment "../password/", the link resolves relative to whatever path segment is currently in the change URL. If that path segment is a to_field value (not the PK), the link resolves to /.../<to_field_value>/password/ and user_change_password receives id=<to_field_value> and fails to find the user (404), since it expects a PK. 

Diagnosis of the hardcoded value: current wrong value: "../password/". The correct link target (when an instance PK is available) must point to the PK-based password-change URL; an exact correct formatted value consistent with admin URL layout is "../../{self.instance.pk}/password/" (with fallback to "../password/" for unsaved instances where no PK is present).
StepsToReproduce: Register a model that has a relation to User using to_field (example: ForeignKey(User, to_field='uuid')).
Open the admin for that model and use the related-lookup to open the linked User's change page (the URL will be like /.../user/<to_field_value>/change/?_to_field=uuid).
On the User change page, locate the read-only Password field's help text and click the "this form" link.
Observe that the link leads to a 404 page (password-change URL was constructed with the to_field value instead of the user's PK).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: The "this form" link in the User change form's password field opens the password-change page for the correct user (no 404), regardless of whether the User change page was reached via the User's PK or via a related lookup using to_field.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: When the User change page is reached via a to_field-based related lookup (URL contains _to_field and a non-PK path segment), the password-field help link points to a URL containing that to_field value and the password-change view fails to find the user (404).

    def as_widget(self, widget=None, attrs=None, only_initial=False):
        """
        Render the field by rendering the passed widget, adding any HTML
        attributes passed as attrs. If a widget isn't specified, use the
        field's default widget.
        """
        widget = widget or self.field.widget
        if self.field.localize:
            widget.is_localized = True
        attrs = attrs or {}
        attrs = self.build_widget_attrs(attrs, widget)
        if self.auto_id and "id" not in widget.attrs:
            attrs.setdefault(
                "id", self.html_initial_id if only_initial else self.auto_id
            )
        # When rendering only the initial (hidden) widget, render the original
        # initial value rather than the bound data. This ensures the
        # 'initial-' hidden input always contains the original initial value
        # (formatted via prepare_value) so change detection can compare against it.
        if only_initial:
            rendered_value = self.field.prepare_value(self.initial)
        else:
            rendered_value = self.value()
        return widget.render(
            name=self.html_initial_name if only_initial else self.html_name,
            value=rendered_value,
            attrs=attrs,
            renderer=self.form.renderer,

Rationale and why this is a complete fix:
- The hidden initial input is supposed to represent the original initial value so change detection on subsequent POSTs can compare posted data to that initial. Previously, due to using self.value() during rendering (which returns bound data on bound forms), the hidden initial was replaced by bound data on re-render, and that bound data then became the "initial" on the next POST — causing change detection to incorrectly think the field had not changed and skip validation/processing for extra forms/inlines.
- By ensuring only_initial rendering uses the original initial (evaluated and prepared for presentation), the hidden initial remains the true initial across bound/unbound re-renders and across multiple posts; BoundField._has_changed will then function correctly and inlines will not be silently dismissed on subsequent submits.
- The change is small and localized to BoundField.as_widget. It is the single place responsible for producing the hidden initial input. No other sites use only_initial=True. The reverse reading code in BoundField._has_changed already expects the initial to be in the format widget outputs (because it calls field.to_python on the POSTed initial) — so no other changes needed.

bug_report.Title: Admin inline with ArrayField(default=list): hidden initial rendered with bound value causes inline to be dismissed on re-submit
bug_report.Description: When a ModelForm field is created from a model field with a callable default (e.g. ArrayField(default=list)) the hidden "initial-..." input is rendered with the submitted (bound) value after an error. On a subsequent submit that hidden value is used as the original initial for change-detection, which can make the inline appear unchanged and cause the inline to be dismissed / validation to be bypassed.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Field.formfield encodes callable defaults as an initial and requests a hidden initial: django/db/models/fields/__init__.py :: Field.formfield sets defaults['initial'] = self.default and defaults['show_hidden_initial'] = True when the model field's default is callable. (lines showing: defaults['initial'] = self.default; defaults['show_hidden_initial'] = True)

2) The form evaluates callable initial values before rendering: django/forms/forms.py :: Form.get_initial_for_field evaluates callable initial values (by calling value()) so BoundField.initial is the evaluated initial value, not the callable. (lines showing: if callable(value): value = value())

3) Hidden-initial rendering uses the bound value on bound forms: django/forms/boundfield.py :: BoundField.as_widget currently supplies the widget value using self.value() even when only_initial=True. Because BoundField.value, on a bound form, uses bound data (it calls self.field.bound_data(self.data, data) and returns field.prepare_value(data)), the hidden "initial-..." input rendered on a re-rendered (bound) form contains the user's submitted value rather than the original initial.

4) Change-detection trusts the posted hidden-initial: django/forms/boundfield.py :: BoundField._has_changed reads the posted "initial-..." value via the form's widget data routines, passes it through field.to_python(initial_value), and then calls field.has_changed(initial_value, data). Because the hidden initial may have been rendered with the previous submitted value, subsequent submits compare posted data against that submitted value and can erroneously report "no change", causing extra forms/inlines to be skipped/dismissed and validation to be bypassed.

5) Serialization expectation for widget-roundtrip: django/contrib/postgres/forms/array.py :: SimpleArrayField implements prepare_value (serializes list -> delimiter-joined string) and to_python (parses the string back to a list). The hidden initial must be rendered in the widget's presentation format (prepare_value(self.initial)) so that field.to_python(posted_initial) round-trips correctly. The immediate defect is that the value placed into the hidden initial is the bound/submitted value on re-render (due to BoundField.as_widget using self.value()), not that the array field's prepare_value/to_python are mismatched.

6) Scope: Because Field.formfield sets show_hidden_initial for any model field with a callable default, any such field (not only ArrayField) is subject to the same problem: the hidden initial can be replaced with bound data on a re-render and then used as the canonical initial on a subsequent submit.
StepsToReproduce: Go to /admin/my_app/thing/add/ (Thing has an inline for RelatedModel, and RelatedModel.plop is ArrayField(default=list)).
In the inline row for RelatedModel (plop is the ArrayField) type any value into plop.
Submit -> the form shows an error on the inline (e.g. RelatedModelForm.clean() raises ValidationError).

Submit the form again without changing the inline -> the inline error is gone, the inline is dismissed and the plop value becomes empty/unfilled (the previously submitted value is treated as the initial and the inline is considered unchanged).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: After the first submit that raises a validation error, re-rendering the form should preserve the original initial/default values in the hidden "initial-..." inputs (presented in the widget's presentation format). On a subsequent submit the formset should correctly detect changes vs the original initial and not silently dismiss inlines or bypass validation; the inline should continue to validate and display the same validation errors until the user corrects the input.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: After a validation error on an inline containing an ArrayField(default=list), the re-rendered form contains an "initial-..." hidden input whose value equals the user's submitted value (because BoundField.as_widget used the bound value when rendering the initial-only widget). On the next submit that hidden value is used as the original initial, so the inline is treated as unchanged and dismissed; validation is bypassed and the field appears unfilled.

    def test_sitemap_last_modified(self):
        "Last-Modified header is set correctly"
        response = self.client.get("/lastmod/sitemap.xml")
        self.assertEqual(
            response.headers["Last-Modified"], "Wed, 13 Mar 2013 10:00:00 GMT"
        )

    def test_sitemap_last_modified_date(self):
        """
        The Last-Modified header should be support dates (without time).
        """
        response = self.client.get("/lastmod/date-sitemap.xml")
        self.assertEqual(
            response.headers["Last-Modified"], "Wed, 13 Mar 2013 00:00:00 GMT"
        )

    def test_sitemap_last_modified_tz(self):
        """
        The Last-Modified header should be converted from timezone aware dates
        to GMT.
        """

        self.assertEqual(
            response.headers["Last-Modified"], "Wed, 13 Mar 2013 15:00:00 GMT"
        )

    def test_sitemaps_lastmod_ascending(self):

Proposed fix (concrete patch)

    if callable(self.lastmod):
        try:
            return max([self.lastmod(item) for item in self.items()])
        except TypeError:
            return None

    - collects lastmod values,
    - filters out None,
    - returns max of the remaining values, and
    - catches both TypeError and ValueError, returning None if either occurs.

Suggested implementation:

    def get_latest_lastmod(self):
        if not hasattr(self, "lastmod"):
            return None
        if callable(self.lastmod):
            values = [self.lastmod(item) for item in self.items()]
            # Filter out None values; comparing None with dates raises TypeError
            non_none_values = [v for v in values if v is not None]
            try:
                return max(non_none_values)
            except (TypeError, ValueError):
                # TypeError: incomparable types in list (e.g. mixing date and non-date)
                # ValueError: empty sequence (no items or all lastmod values were None)

            return self.lastmod

Checkpoint 5: Final report (root cause, all required changes, and exact code)

Root cause
- Sitemap.get_latest_lastmod called max([self.lastmod(item) for item in self.items()]) when lastmod is a callable. If self.items() returned an empty list, max() raised ValueError ("max() arg is an empty sequence") and the code caught only TypeError, not ValueError. Therefore the ValueError propagated and crashed sitemap index generation.

All locations that need change
1) django/contrib/sitemaps/__init__.py — Sitemap.get_latest_lastmod

What the current code does (lines 165-174)
- If lastmod is callable, it tries to compute max(self.lastmod(item) for item in self.items()) and catches only TypeError; it does not handle empty items (ValueError).

Assumption encoded by current code
- It implicitly assumes that when lastmod is callable, self.items() will be non-empty (or that catching TypeError will be sufficient), which is not always true.

Proposed change
- Replace the current body of get_latest_lastmod with the robust implementation that:
    - collects lastmod values from items,
    - filters out None values,
    - returns max of remaining values,
    - and returns None if the max cannot be computed (either because there are no non-None values or the values are incomparable), by catching both ValueError and TypeError.

Exact patch (diff-like snippet):

--- a/django/contrib/sitemaps/__init__.py
+++ b/django/contrib/sitemaps/__init__.py
@@
     def get_latest_lastmod(self):
-        if not hasattr(self, "lastmod"):
-            return None
-        if callable(self.lastmod):
-            try:
-                return max([self.lastmod(item) for item in self.items()])
-            except TypeError:
-                return None
-        else:
-            return self.lastmod
+        if not hasattr(self, "lastmod"):
+            return None
+        if callable(self.lastmod):
+            # Collect lastmod values for each item, filter out None values
+            values = [self.lastmod(item) for item in self.items()]
+            non_none_values = [v for v in values if v is not None]
+            try:
+                return max(non_none_values)
+            except (TypeError, ValueError):
+                # TypeError: incomparable types in list (e.g. mixing date with non-date)
+                # ValueError: empty sequence (no items or all lastmod values were None)
+                return None
+        else:
+            return self.lastmod

Why this fixes everything
- When self.items() is empty, non_none_values will be empty and max(non_none_values) raises ValueError; we catch it and return None — avoiding the crash described in the report.
- If lastmod values include None and some dates, filtering removes None and max works on dates only.
- If lastmod returns incomparable types that cause TypeError, we still return None (matching the previous behavior for TypeError).
- GenericSitemap already implements get_latest_lastmod using database ordering and .first(), which returns None if empty; no change needed there.
- Views.index handles None site_lastmod by omitting lastmod for that sitemap, so behavior will be as tests expect.

Other files examined and why they don't need changes
- django/contrib/sitemaps/views.py — uses get_latest_lastmod and _get_latest_lastmod; no change needed. The view already handles None returns by omitting lastmod headers.
- django/contrib/flatpages/sitemaps.py — inherits Sitemap and will benefit from the fixed base method; no change needed.
- tests in tests/sitemaps_tests/* remain valid; the intended test for "get_latest_lastmod None" maps to the correct behavior (omitted lastmod), and the new implementation ensures no crash for empty sitemaps with callable lastmod.

Notes on an even smaller fix
- If a minimal change is preferred, you could change the existing except TypeError: to except (TypeError, ValueError): — that would catch the empty-sequence ValueError as the bug reporter suggested. However, the slightly more robust change above also filters out None values and is clearer about why ValueError occurs.

Summary (one-line)
- Fix Sitemap.get_latest_lastmod to handle empty item lists and None lastmod values by filtering None values and catching ValueError and TypeError; update django/contrib/sitemaps/__init__.py accordingly.

bug_report.Title: Sitemap index crashes with ValueError when sitemap has callable lastmod but no items
bug_report.Description: When a Sitemap implementation exposes lastmod as a callable and its items() returns an empty sequence, requesting the sitemap index (e.g. /sitemap.xml) triggers a server error (ValueError) and the sitemap index view fails.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) django/contrib/sitemaps/__init__.py :: Sitemap.get_latest_lastmod
   - Incorrect assumption: the implementation assumes it can compute max([self.lastmod(item) for item in self.items()]) when lastmod is callable. It does not account for self.items() being empty.
   - Observed behavior in code: when callable(self.lastmod) the method returns max([self.lastmod(item) for item in self.items()]) inside a try/except that only catches TypeError. If self.items() is empty, max([]) raises ValueError ("max() arg is an empty sequence") which is not caught and therefore propagates.

2) Other sitemap classes that reuse the same base implementation (all share the same root-cause pattern if they do not override get_latest_lastmod)
   - django/contrib/flatpages/sitemaps.py :: FlatPageSitemap (inherits Sitemap and does not override get_latest_lastmod)
   - django/contrib/gis/sitemaps/kml.py :: KMLSitemap (and KMZSitemap) (inherit Sitemap and do not override get_latest_lastmod)
   - User-defined or app-provided sitemaps that inherit Sitemap and expose lastmod as a callable while items() can be empty; test-suite examples in this repository include tests/sitemaps_tests/urls/http.py :: EmptySitemap and CallableLastmodPartialSitemap / CallableLastmodFullSitemap which demonstrate the common usage patterns that lead to this code path.

3) Consumer contract violation: django/contrib/sitemaps/views.py :: index()
   - The index view calls site.get_latest_lastmod() and expects either a date/datetime or None. An unexpected exception (ValueError) from get_latest_lastmod violates this contract and causes a 500 server error while generating the sitemap index.

Notes:
   - GenericSitemap overrides get_latest_lastmod using a queryset order_by(...).values_list(...).first(), which returns None for empty querysets; GenericSitemap is therefore not affected.
   - The immediate cause in code is the uncaught ValueError raised by max([]) when items() is empty and lastmod is callable.
StepsToReproduce: Implement a Sitemap subclass where lastmod is a callable (def lastmod(self, item): ...).
Ensure that Sitemap.items(self) returns an empty list (or otherwise yields zero items).
Include the sitemap in the project's sitemaps dict and urlconf used by django.contrib.sitemaps.views.index.
Request the sitemap index URL (e.g. GET /sitemap.xml).
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Request succeeds (HTTP 200). The sitemap index is returned; for the sitemap that has no items or no computable lastmod, the index treats its latest-lastmod as absent (i.e. omits lastmod/does not set a Last-Modified header for the index) rather than raising an exception.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: Request returns HTTP 500. Traceback ends in django/contrib/sitemaps/__init__.py in get_latest_lastmod: max() arg is an empty sequence (ValueError), causing the sitemap index view to crash.

bug_report.Title: FileBasedCache.has_key race condition causes FileNotFoundError during concurrent access
bug_report.Description: FileBasedCache.has_key checks os.path.exists(fname) and then opens the file. If the file is removed between the exists() check and open() (for example, by _is_expired deleting an expired file), open() can raise FileNotFoundError and that exception propagates to callers (observed from get_or_set -> add -> has_key).
bug_report.RootCause:
1) Incorrect assumption in django/core/cache/backends/filebased.py::FileBasedCache.has_key that os.path.exists(fname) guarantees the file will still be present at open(fname, 'rb'). has_key performs a non-atomic exists-then-open sequence (lines 91–96) which is unsafe under concurrent deletion.

2) django/core/cache/backends/filebased.py::FileBasedCache._is_expired deletes expired cache files by calling self._delete(f.name) while holding a closed file handle (lines 147–158). A concurrent reader that checked exists() but has not yet opened the file can encounter the file being removed by _is_expired in another thread/process.

3) Interaction assumption at the call sites: BaseCache.get_or_set (django/core/cache/backends/base.py::BaseCache.get_or_set) -> FileBasedCache.add -> FileBasedCache.has_key relies on has_key being a safe boolean presence check. Because has_key can raise FileNotFoundError when the file is removed between exists() and open(), callers of add/get_or_set can receive that exception (get_or_set calls add, and add calls has_key; add does not catch this exception).

4) File deletion code django/core/cache/backends/filebased.py::FileBasedCache._delete itself uses an exists() check followed by os.remove and catches FileNotFoundError (lines 81–89); while _delete tolerates races, that exception handling does not prevent the race in has_key because has_key does not catch FileNotFoundError from open().

5) Inconsistent FileNotFoundError handling within the backend: FileBasedCache.get and FileBasedCache.touch explicitly catch FileNotFoundError (get: lines 31–39; touch: lines 61–76), and _delete tolerates FileNotFoundError, but has_key does not. This inconsistency is part of the root cause pattern and explains why some cache operations are resilient to transient deletions while has_key is not.

6) Additional affected call sites: BaseCache.__contains__ delegates to has_key, so use of the "in" operator on this cache backend may also raise FileNotFoundError under the same race conditions (BaseCache.__contains__ calls has_key).
StepsToReproduce: Configure Django to use FileBasedCache (django/core/cache/backends/filebased.py).
Create a cache key whose file is already present but expired (so _is_expired would delete it when read).
Concurrently invoke operations that call cache.get_or_set or cache.add (many threads or processes simultaneously) on that same key so multiple has_key calls run in parallel.
Observe a FileNotFoundError from django/core/cache/backends/filebased.py in has_key when open(fname, 'rb') is attempted after the file was deleted.
bug_report.ExpectedBehavior: Concurrent cache reads/has_key checks should not raise FileNotFoundError. has_key should return True or False (present/unexpired or not) in user-visible terms and callers such as get_or_set/add should not crash due to a transient removal of the file.
bug_report.ObservedBehavior: When multiple threads/processes race to read an expired cache file, a FileNotFoundError is raised from has_key (open(fname, 'rb')) because the file was deleted between os.path.exists() and open(). The exception propagates to callers (e.g., get_or_set -> add) and can crash the operation.

"""
Creates permissions for all installed apps that need permissions.
"""
import getpass
import unicodedata

from django.apps import apps as global_apps
from django.contrib.auth import get_permission_codename
from django.contrib.contenttypes.management import create_contenttypes
from django.core import exceptions
from django.db import DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS, router


def _get_all_permissions(opts):
    """
    Return (codename, name) for all permissions in the given opts.
    """
    return [*_get_builtin_permissions(opts), *opts.permissions]


def _get_builtin_permissions(opts):
    """
    Return (codename, name) for all autogenerated permissions.
    By default, this is ('add', 'change', 'delete', 'view')
    """
    perms = []
    for action in opts.default_permissions:
        perms.append(
            (
                get_permission_codename(action, opts),
                "Can %s %s" % (action, opts.verbose_name_raw),
            )
        )
    return perms


def create_permissions(
    app_config,
    verbosity=2,
    interactive=True,
    using=DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS,
    apps=global_apps,
    **kwargs,
):
    if not app_config.models_module:
        return

    # Ensure that contenttypes are created for this app. Needed if
    # 'django.contrib.auth' is in INSTALLED_APPS before
    # 'django.contrib.contenttypes'.
    create_contenttypes(
        app_config,
        verbosity=verbosity,
        interactive=interactive,
        using=using,
        apps=apps,
        **kwargs,
    )

    app_label = app_config.label
    try:
        app_config = apps.get_app_config(app_label)
        ContentType = apps.get_model("contenttypes", "ContentType")
        Permission = apps.get_model("auth", "Permission")
    except LookupError:
        return

    if not router.allow_migrate_model(using, Permission):
        return

    # This will hold the permissions we're looking for as
    # (content_type, (codename, name))
    searched_perms = []
    # The codenames and ctypes that should exist.
    ctypes = set()
    for klass in app_config.get_models():
        # Force looking up the content types in the current database
        # before creating foreign keys to them.
        ctype = ContentType.objects.db_manager(using).get_for_model(
            klass, for_concrete_model=False
        )

        ctypes.add(ctype)
        for perm in _get_all_permissions(klass._meta):
            searched_perms.append((ctype, perm))

    # Find all the Permissions that have a content_type for a model we're
    # looking for.  We don't need to check for codenames since we already have
    # a list of the ones we're going to create.
    all_perms = set(
        Permission.objects.using(using)
        .filter(
            content_type__in=ctypes,
        )
        .values_list("content_type", "codename")
    )

    perms = [
        Permission(codename=codename, name=name, content_type=ct)
        for ct, (codename, name) in searched_perms
        if (ct.pk, codename) not in all_perms
    ]
    Permission.objects.using(using).bulk_create(perms)
    if verbosity >= 2:
        for perm in perms:
            print("Adding permission '%s'" % perm)


def get_system_username():
    """
    Return the current system user's username, or an empty string if the
    username could not be determined.
    """
    try:
        result = getpass.getuser()
    except (ImportError, KeyError):
        # KeyError will be raised by os.getpwuid() (called by getuser())
        # if there is no corresponding entry in the /etc/passwd file
        # (a very restricted chroot environment, for example).
        return ""
    return result


def get_default_username(check_db=True, database=DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS):
    """
    Try to determine the current system user's username to use as a default.

    :param check_db: If ``True``, requires that the username does not match an
        existing ``auth.User`` (otherwise returns an empty string).
    :param database: The database where the unique check will be performed.
    :returns: The username, or an empty string if no username can be
        determined or the suggested username is already taken.
    """
    # This file is used in apps.py, it should not trigger models import.
    from django.contrib.auth import models as auth_app

    # If the User model has been swapped out, we can't make any assumptions
    # about the default user name.
    if auth_app.User._meta.swapped:
        return ""

    default_username = get_system_username()
    try:
        default_username = (
            unicodedata.normalize("NFKD", default_username)
            .encode("ascii", "ignore")
            .decode("ascii")
            .replace(" ", "")
            .lower()
        )
    except UnicodeDecodeError:
        return ""

    # Run the username validator
    try:
        auth_app.User._meta.get_field("username").run_validators(default_username)
    except exceptions.ValidationError:
        return ""

    # Don't return the default username if it is already taken.
    if check_db and default_username:
        try:
            auth_app.User._default_manager.db_manager(database).get(
                username=default_username,
            )
        except auth_app.User.DoesNotExist:
            pass
        else:
            return ""
    return default_username

What the bug report describes
- When running manage.py migrate --database <some_alias>, migrations run successfully.
- After migrations complete, there is a DB read that runs but does not respect the same database parameter (i.e., it calls the DB router and the router uses thread-local subdomain state to choose a different DB or raise an error because the thread-local subdomain isn't set).
- In the reporter's setup the TenantDatabaseRouter raises InvalidTenantException when no subdomain is set, causing migrate to fail after the migrations have been applied, because some post-migrate handler is triggering a read without using the migrate database alias.

Primary responsible method/class
- The root of the process where the problem happens is the post-migrate signal emission triggered from management command migrate (django/core/management/commands/migrate.py -> emit_post_migrate_signal). The specific post_migrate receiver that is expected to maintain use of the provided database is django.contrib.auth.management.create_permissions (django/contrib/auth/management/__init__.py::create_permissions), and django.contrib.contenttypes.management.create_contenttypes is another receiver used by create_permissions and by contenttypes AppConfig.
- The code path primarily responsible for the unexpected DB read is code executed in post_migrate handlers which perform ORM reads/writes. In particular, create_permissions and create_contenttypes use .using(using) and db_manager(using) for their main DB operations (good), but something executed during post_migrate execution is invoking a DB read via a manager or descriptor that does not have its _db set and therefore calls router.db_for_read. The ConnectionRouter code shows that when router.db_for_read is invoked, routers get the call and may use thread-local state (which is not set in the management command), leading to unexpected behavior.

Clear statement of the bug (short)
- When django.core.management.commands.migrate emits post_migrate signals with using=<db_alias>, some post_migrate handlers or operations invoked during signal handling cause ORM reads via managers/descriptors that don't have an explicit database set; those calls fall through to router.db_for_read and thus ignore the migrate --database parameter. This results in the DB router being invoked during post-migrate processing and, in routers that depend on request-specific thread-local state, raising errors or selecting the wrong DB.

Primary class/method primarily responsible:
- The immediate symptom appears because code called from the post_migrate signal does ORM reads without binding explicit using. The primary suspect is django.contrib.auth.management.create_permissions because it runs during post_migrate and creates Permission objects and prints them. However, create_permissions itself uses .db_manager(using) and .using(using) for DB operations; thus the real issue is that some code invoked (likely printing or attribute access during create_permissions' logging) ends up triggering a related-manager/foreign-key attribute access that uses a manager/descriptor whose db is not set — causing router.db_for_read to be consulted (and the router's db_for_read uses thread-local tenant state). Therefore the bug is an inconsistency: not every post-migrate ORM usage is done through .using(using) or a manager bound to the migrate DB; when code relies on manager.db property or on related descriptors that call router.db_for_read, the explicit migrate DB setting can be ignored.

Concluding summary for Checkpoint 1:
- Root context: migrate emits post_migrate(using=db) and post_migrate receivers (create_contenttypes/create_permissions and others) should respect that using value. The create_permissions and create_contenttypes functions mostly use .using(using) and db_manager(using) correctly, but there is at least one code path during post_migrate handling that executes a read through a manager or related descriptor whose _db is None, causing router.db_for_read to be consulted and the migrate database selection to be ignored. The router call is what prints "read {}" in the reporter's minimal example (TenantDatabaseRouter.db_for_read prints "read" then hints dict), and because the thread-local subdomain isn't set in the management process the router raises the reporter's InvalidTenantException.

Summary of where we are (short)
- Symptom: After running manage.py migrate --database <alias>, post-migrate receivers trigger DB reads that do not respect the migrate --database parameter because those reads end up invoking router.db_for_read without a “using” set; routers that depend on thread-local request/tenant state then mis-select a DB or fail.
- The post-migrate emission path is django/core/management/commands/migrate.py -> emit_post_migrate_signal (django/core/management/sql.py) -> models.signals.post_migrate.send(..., using=db, ...).
- Many post-migrate handlers (contenttypes, auth, sites, etc.) are careful to use .using(using) or db_manager(using) for their DB work, but some code still performs read operations during signal handling that may call router.db_for_read because the manager/queryset doesn't have an explicit DB (manager._db is None and manager._hints is empty).
- The core problem: there is no mechanism that makes router.db_for_read automatically pick the --database value emitted with the post_migrate signal when code (in signal handlers or things they call) constructs QuerySets/managers without an explicit using. As a result router.db_for_read is consulted with no hints and routers that expect a request-specific hint may misbehave.

Root cause (concise)
- During emit_post_migrate_signal, read operations invoked by signal handlers sometimes rely on the normal router.db_for_read fallback path; router.db_for_read is called without any information about the migration “using” database (because managers and querysets used by the handler lack a _db and _hints), so routers that rely on thread-local state (request/tenant) are consulted and fail or choose the wrong DB. There is no temporary context that tells router.db_for_read to prefer the migration DB when handlers run without explicit using.

Proposed fix (high-level)
- While we should not change how routers themselves decide DBs in general, we should ensure that during the execution of the post_migrate signal (the block where the management command intends DB operations to be targeted at a specific DB), any router.db_for_read calls that lack better information will prefer the migration DB alias passed to emit_post_migrate_signal.
- Implement this by setting a short-lived, thread-local "migration-using" value while post_migrate signals are emitted. ConnectionRouter._router_func (db_for_read and db_for_write) will consult that thread-local value as a fallback when no router returned a DB and there is no instance._state.db. This mirrors the existing fallback ordering but supplies the migration DB instead of always returning DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS when called without sufficient hints.
- Set and clear the thread-local migration DB around the call to models.signals.post_migrate.send() in emit_post_migrate_signal (django/core/management/sql.py). Do the same for pre_migrate (safer / symmetric), though the user report concerns post_migrate — I'll include both.

Checkpoint 5: Final report — full analysis, root cause, all locations to change, and content of fixes

Root cause (one paragraph)
- emit_post_migrate_signal causes many app-specific setup operations to run. Some of those operations (or code they call) perform ORM reads without binding an explicit database (.using() / db_manager(using)), so manager/db-resolution falls back to ConnectionRouter.db_for_read(). In multi-DB setups with routers that expect request-local/tenant info (thread-local state), calling router.db_for_read() without such state leads to incorrect DB selection or exceptions. There is no mechanism that tells router.db_for_read to prefer the migration’s --database alias during post_migrate, so reads may be routed incorrectly. The fix is to provide a short-lived, thread-local “migration DB” fallback that ConnectionRouter uses when routers don't choose and no instance DB is present.

Every location that needs to change
1) django/db/utils.py
   - What it currently does:
     - ConnectionRouter._router_func iterates routers; if none returns a DB, it checks instance._state.db then returns DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS.
   - Why change:
     - Provide a targeted fallback (migration DB) used during signal emission.
   - What to change:
     - Add module-level thread-local storage plus helpers:
         import threading
         _migration_state = threading.local()
         def _set_temporary_migration_db(db): _migration_state.db = db
         def _clear_temporary_migration_db(): _migration_state.db = None
     - Modify _route_db to check the temporary migration DB after instance._state.db and before DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS.
   - Assumption encoded and changed:
     - Previously the final fallback was DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS; we make that final fallback still exist but insert the migration DB as a higher-priority fallback in the migration context.
   - Tests/notes:
     - This is small, thread-local and cleared in all code paths (finally). It won't leak across threads.

2) django/core/management/sql.py
   - What it currently does:
     - emit_pre_migrate_signal and emit_post_migrate_signal call models.signals.pre_migrate/post_migrate.send(...) with using=db in kwargs.
   - Why change:
     - The signal kwargs alone do not reach router.db_for_read calls made later (those calls derive hints from managers/querysets). We need to create a temporary, thread-local context that router can consult.
   - What to change:
     - Import the helper functions from django.db.utils and surround the send() calls with set/clear in try/finally. Example:
         from django.db.utils import _set_temporary_migration_db, _clear_temporary_migration_db
         _set_temporary_migration_db(db)
         try:
             models.signals.post_migrate.send(...using=db,...)
         finally:
             _clear_temporary_migration_db()
   - Assumption encoded and changed:
     - Previously the code assumed the using kwarg passed to the signal is sufficient; in practice it isn't for router decision-making down the stack. Now we make it also available to router as a fallback.

Other files reviewed and found OK (no change)
- django/contrib/auth/management/__init__.py (create_permissions): uses db_manager(using) and using(using) appropriately — no change required.
- django/contrib/contenttypes/management/__init__.py (create_contenttypes): uses .using(using) correctly — no change required.
- django/contrib/contenttypes/models.py (ContentTypeManager): uses caching keyed by manager.db; unaffected.
- django/db/models/manager.py Manager.db property remains unchanged: router.db_for_read(self.model, **self._hints) (the router now has the migration fallback).
- django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py: many places call router.db_for_read(self.model, instance=self.instance) — unaffected (instance hint takes precedence).
- django/core/management/commands/migrate.py: already passed using db to emit_post_migrate_signal — unchanged.

Hardcoded values that need to become dynamic
- None of the numeric or length constants needed to change. The only “default” that was previously hardcoded (DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS) remains the final fallback; we add a dynamic thread-local fallback for migration time.

Any new methods to add or existing ones to override
- Add small helpers in django/db/utils.py: _set_temporary_migration_db and _clear_temporary_migration_db (module-level).
- No model classes need to add or override methods.

Full justification of correctness
- The change is narrow: it only affects the router fallback path and only within a tiny time window (during pre/post migrate signal emission) by using thread-local storage set and cleared synchronously around the signal emission. It maintains existing precedence (router returns > instance._state.db > migration_db > DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS) and therefore preserves expected behavior for most cases while fixing the migration scenario where managers lack explicit DB hints.
- It avoids requiring every post_migrate handler to be perfect (i.e., to always use .using(using) on every QuerySet created). It is defensive and reduces surprising behavior in real-world multi-DB & tenant routing setups.
- This approach also avoids changing or weakening router semantics globally; routers still are consulted first and can override the migration DB.

Notes on tests and compatibility
- Tests that assert router.db_for_read behavior might need to be updated if they expected DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS inside post_migrate handlers that run with a different using. But that behavior is arguably incorrect: when running migrate --database=X, handlers should operate on X and not on default; the change makes the framework more consistent with that intent.
- The change is thread-local; for async contexts it relies on Python threads (Django already uses thread-critical for connections). If the management code is executed within an async event loop but synchronously emitting signals, thread-local is the correct approach (consistent with other Django thread-local uses).

I will now summarize the verification I performed, what I expected to learn with each code read, and what I found. For each method/file named in the draft report I fetched the source and checked whether the draft's claims are supported by the code. All tool calls were preceded by a short reasoning of why the file was needed (documented in the call comments). Below are the verification results and any gaps I found.

1) Does migrate emit post_migrate with the selected database alias?
- What I checked: the migrate command to see how it passes the database alias to post_migrate.
- Evidence: django/core/management/commands/migrate.py
  - Lines 381–390 call emit_post_migrate_signal(self.verbosity, self.interactive, connection.alias, ...)
  - This confirms the migrate command obtains the selected alias from options["database"] (line 98) and passes connection.alias to emit_post_migrate_signal.
- Conclusion: The draft claim that emit_post_migrate is sent with using=db is correct.

2) What does emit_post_migrate_signal send to receivers?
- What I checked: the emit_post_migrate_signal function to see exactly what kwargs it passes to signal.send.
- Evidence: django/core/management/sql.py
  - Lines 52–58 call models.signals.post_migrate.send(..., using=db, **kwargs)
- Conclusion: The signal is sent with using=db. The draft's statement that "emit_post_migrate is sent with using=db" is accurate.

3) Do the standard post_migrate handlers use the 'using' value for their DB operations?
- What I checked: django.contrib.auth.management.create_permissions and django.contrib.contenttypes.management.create_contenttypes.
- Evidence: django/contrib/auth/management/__init__.py
  - create_permissions has signature create_permissions(..., using=DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS, ...) (lines 37–44).
  - It calls create_contenttypes(..., using=using, ...) (lines 51–58).
  - It explicitly uses ContentType.objects.db_manager(using).get_for_model(...) (lines 79–81).
  - It uses Permission.objects.using(using).filter(...).values_list(...) (lines 91–96) and Permission.objects.using(using).bulk_create(perms) (line 103).
  - It prints the newly-created Permission instances after bulk_create (lines 104–106).
- Evidence: django/contrib/contenttypes/management/__init__.py
  - create_contenttypes(..., using=using, ...) calls ContentType.objects.clear_cache() and ContentType.objects.using(using).filter(app_label=...) (lines 32–39).
- Conclusion: The core auth/contenttypes handlers noted in the draft do use db_manager(using) / .using(using) for their main reads/writes. The draft's claim that the handlers "do use db_manager(using)/.using(using)" is correct.

4) But can code run during those handlers perform unbound ORM reads that fall back to the router?
- What I checked: how manager/db resolution and related-object descriptors determine the DB when no explicit .using() is present.
- Evidence: django/db/models/manager.py
  - BaseManager.db property returns self._db or router.db_for_read(self.model, **self._hints) (line 144).
  - get_queryset constructs a QuerySet with using=self._db, hints=self._hints (line 155). If _db is None the QuerySet will have no explicit DB, and later ORM operations will call router.db_for_read to pick a DB.
- Evidence: django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py
  - ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.get_queryset returns self.field.remote_field.model._base_manager.db_manager(hints=hints).all() (lines 152–154). Related-object accessors construct QuerySets/managers that can have no explicit using set (depending on how they are used), and so can rely on router.db_for_read for DB selection.
- Evidence: django/contrib/contenttypes/models.py
  - ContentTypeManager.get_for_model explicitly uses self.get(...) (lines 50–53) to ensure db_for_read is used (see the comment "Start with get() and not get_or_create() in order to use the db_for_read (see #20401)").
  - The manager caches results keyed by self.db (lines 14–16, lines 129–136); the cache key depends on the manager's db attribute.
- Conclusion: It is accurate that unbound managers/querysets or related-object descriptors can trigger router.db_for_read because Manager.db resolves by calling the router. Thus, even though the canonical handlers use .using(using), code reachable from them (attribute access, related descriptors, manager.db property, or helpers that construct managers without explicit using) can perform ORM reads/writes that are not bound to the migrate alias and therefore go through routers.

5) How does the ConnectionRouter decide a DB if routers return None?
- What I checked: ConnectionRouter._router_func implementation and the fallback order.
- Evidence: django/db/utils.py
  - The _router_func's inner function loops configured routers and calls their method (db_for_read/db_for_write) first (lines 220–229).
  - If no router returned a DB, it gets instance = hints.get("instance") and if instance._state.db set returns that (lines 230–232).
  - Otherwise it returns DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS (line 233).
- Conclusion: The draft's description of the router fallback order (routers -> instance._state.db -> DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS) is accurate. This supports the draft's claim that unbound reads will call routers first, and if routers depend on request-local state then such routers will be invoked in manage.py migrate context where that state is absent.

6) The user-provided TenantDatabaseRouter example
- What I checked: the original bug report's example (provided in the "Original bug report" input).
- Evidence: The user example shows a thread-local local_state used by TenantDatabaseRouter._default_db and db_for_read/db_for_write printing "read" / "write" then returning _default_db. This is consistent with the printed "read {}" observed by the user during migrate.
- Conclusion: While this is user code (not in Django core), the example precisely demonstrates the failure mode: a router that assumes a thread-local tenant exists will be called during post_migrate if an ORM read occurs that is unbound, and in the management process the thread-local is unset, so the router may raise.

7) Completeness check / secondary findings
- I checked for other post_migrate receivers and code that run during signal handlers. Many app handlers do use .using(using) correctly (auth, contenttypes, sites, etc.). However, the root cause pattern (unbound manager/queryset -> router.db_for_read invoked -> router depends on thread-local tenant) can occur in any handler or any code called from them (including third-party apps or custom signal receivers).

I also confirmed related descriptors (ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.__get__ & get_queryset) will create QuerySets/managers that could be unbound and therefore call the router (related_descriptors.py lines ~152–159, ~196–199).

8) Claims in the draft that could not be verified or required softening
- The draft states "the correct relationship is: ORM reads/writes executed during post_migrate must be performed via a manager/queryset bound to the desired DB (e.g. .using(using) or db_manager(using)) if they are to target the migrate database." - The draft also asserts that "post_migrate handlers assume all DB access performed while the handler runs will automatically use the using kwarg provided to post_migrate." I softened that to indicate that many handlers already use .using(using) for their main operations (evidence above) but that other code paths they call may not and therefore can trigger router resolution. I changed any absolute language to reflect what the code shows: handlers *tend* to use .using(using) but unbound code paths still exist and cause the observed problem.

- Verified and supported claims:
  - migrate passes the selected DB alias into emit_post_migrate_signal (migrate.py -> sql.py).

bug_report.Title: migrate management command: post-migrate DB reads ignore --database and trigger DB router
bug_report.Description: When running manage.py migrate --database=<alias>, migrations complete but a subsequent DB access performed during post-migrate handling can be routed via the project's DATABASE_ROUTERS instead of using the specified database alias. In multi-tenant setups where routers depend on request-local state, this leads to router errors (or wrong DB selection) in the management process because the request-local tenant context is not present.
bug_report.RootCause:
1) The migrate command emits the post_migrate signal with using=<db_alias>, but that 'using' sentinel is only a kwarg on the signal and is not automatically forced as the active DB for arbitrary ORM operations performed while handlers run (locations: django/core/management/commands/migrate.py -> django/core/management/sql.py::emit_post_migrate_signal). The incorrect assumption here is: "passing using=db to post_migrate guarantees all ORM accesses during signal handling will target that database." The correct relationship is diagnostic: only managers/querysets that are explicitly bound to a DB (via .using(using) or db_manager(using)) can guarantee they will operate on the migrate database; otherwise DB selection falls back to normal routing.

2) The built-in post_migrate handlers that create content types and permissions do use managers bound to the provided using value for their main queries/changes (locations: django/contrib/contenttypes/management/__init__.py::create_contenttypes and django/contrib/auth/management/__init__.py::create_permissions — e.g. ContentType.objects.db_manager(using).get_for_model(...) and Permission.objects.using(using).bulk_create(...)). However, code paths reachable from those handlers (attribute access, related-object descriptors, manager.db property, or helper utilities) can perform ORM reads without an explicit DB bound and therefore invoke the router. The relevant code locations that demonstrate how an unbound access consults the router are: django/db/models/manager.py::BaseManager.db (returns self._db or router.db_for_read(self.model, **self._hints)) and related-object accessors in django/db/models/fields/related_descriptors.py (e.g. ForwardManyToOneDescriptor.get_queryset uses the model's manager and can produce QuerySets without an explicit .using). ContentTypeManager.get_for_model intentionally uses self.get(...) so that db_for_read is involved (django/contrib/contenttypes/models.py), which shows that these code paths are expected to consult routers in the absence of an explicit manager DB.

3) ConnectionRouter consults configured routers before considering instance._state.db and, if routers return None, falls back to DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS (location: django/db/utils.py::ConnectionRouter._router_func). The observable decision order is therefore: consult routers (router.db_for_read/db_for_write) -> instance._state.db (if an instance is provided in hints) -> DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS. Because routers are consulted first for unbound managers/querysets, routers that depend on request-local tenant information are invoked in the management process where that request-local state is not present; that causes incorrect DB selection or exceptions. The incorrect assumption encoded in the fallback is: "DEFAULT_DB_ALIAS is always an appropriate fallback when routers return None." From an application/management-command point of view, unbound reads that occur while post_migrate is running are often expected to target the migrate command's using alias rather than the default DB.

4) User-defined routers that assume request-bound context (the user's TenantDatabaseRouter in the report is an example) will raise or mis-route when db_for_read/db_for_write are called without the request/tenant context (user example: TenantDatabaseRouter._default_db, db_for_read, db_for_write). The incorrect assumption in such routers is: "db_for_read/db_for_write will only be called in request-handling contexts where a tenant value is set on thread-local storage." That assumption does not hold for management commands and signal handlers run in the CLI process, and thus such routers can raise or return the wrong alias when invoked during post_migrate.
StepsToReproduce: Install a tenant-aware DB router and middleware like the example in the original report (TenantSubdomainMiddleware that sets thread-local.local_state.subdomain and TenantDatabaseRouter that uses local_state.subdomain and prints in db_for_read/db_for_write).
Add the middleware, TENANT_MAP, and DATABASE_ROUTERS = ['utils.tenant_db_router.TenantDatabaseRouter'] to settings.py.
